docs.title: Human Annotator Cognitive Fatigue & Quality Decay Dynamics
docs.text:
In continuous active learning workflows, human oracles are not static, stateless functions. Specialist annotators (e.g., corporate litigation attorneys, board-certified radiologists, intelligence analysts) suffer from cognitive fatigue over extended shifts (Lowell et al., 2019).

Empirical studies demonstrate that after four consecutive hours of labeling difficult edge-case instances, an annotator's error rate \(\eta(t)\) exhibits exponential drift:

\[\eta(t) = \eta_0 + (\eta_{\max} - \eta_0) \left(1 - e^{-\lambda_{\text{fatigue}} t}\right)\]

where \(\eta_0 \in [0.05, 0.10]\) is the baseline rested error rate, \(\eta_{\max} \in [0.25, 0.40]\) is the fatigued error ceiling, and \(\lambda_{\text{fatigue}} > 0\) is the task-specific cognitive depletion rate.

Furthermore, active learning exacerbates fatigue because it selectively serves the most ambiguous, boundary-adjacent instances in the entire pool, depriving human reviewers of the cognitive respite provided by easy, clear-cut instances. Production MLOps architectures counteract fatigue drift through: - Synthetic Honey-Pot Injections: Interleaving known gold-standard validation instances at random intervals (\(5 - 10\%\) frequency) to detect error drift in real time. - Dynamic Task Throttling: Automatically rotating annotators off boundary-active queues to routine verification or rest breaks when individual rolling accuracy drops below \(90\%\). - Cognitive Workload Smoothing: Interleaving high-confidence representative instances into active batches to maintain reviewer baseline engagement and prevent cognitive burnout.

docs.title: Cold Start Initialization Strategies
docs.text:
Before the active query loop can compute meaningful uncertainty estimates \(\alpha(\mathbf{x})\), the learner requires a seeded labeled corpus \(\mathcal{L}_0\). In enterprise cold-start regimes where zero labeled instances exist, naive random sampling risks failing to discover rare minority classes. Production architectures employ three advanced initialization paradigms:

1. Unsupervised Geometric Clustering (\(k\)-Means++): Compute penultimate embeddings using self-supervised foundation backbones (e.g., DINOv2, CLIP, or modern sentence transformers). Run \(k\)-Means++ on unlabeled pool \(\mathcal{U}\) to extract \(K_{\text{clusters}}\) cluster exemplars as the initial seed \(\mathcal{L}_0\), guaranteeing representation across the entire feature manifold.

2. Programmatic Weak Supervision Seed: Apply domain-heuristic keyword rules or regex filters (Weak Supervision, covered in Lesson 11.5) to generate high-confidence initial pseudo-labels, bootstrapping the active model without initial manual review expenditure.

3. Zero-Shot Foundation Model Distillation: Prompt a frontier multimodal foundation model to generate initial soft probability distributions across an exploratory partition of \(\mathcal{U}\). The active learner selects instances where the foundation model exhibits high confidence to initialize parameters, then transitions to human active querying for nuanced domain-specific boundary edge cases.

docs.title: 📐 Formal Mathematical Foundations
docs.text: To formalize enterprise active learning systems, we establish four rigorous mathematical definitions governing batch diversity optimization, automated stopping gates, noisy oracle consensus, and PAC stopping bounds.

docs.title: Definition 11.4.1: Batch-Mode Active Selection with Intra-Batch Diversity Regularization
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{U} = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_U\}\) denote the unlabeled pool, and let \(\phi(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) be the feature embedding. Let \(\alpha_{\text{unc}}(\mathbf{x}) \in [0, 1]\) be an uncertainty scoring function (e.g., Margin Sampling or Shannon Entropy).

When querying a batch \(\mathcal{B} \subset \mathcal{U}\) of cardinality \(|\mathcal{B}| = B > 1\), pure uncertainty queries suffer from extreme spatial clustering. The Intra-Batch Diversity Regularized Objective balances individual informativeness against pairwise geometric redundancy (Sener & Savarese, 2018; Ash et al., 2020):

\[\max_{\mathcal{B} \subset \mathcal{U}, |\mathcal{B}| = B} \mathcal{J}(\mathcal{B}) = \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{B}} \alpha_{\text{unc}}(\mathbf{x}) - \lambda \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j \in \mathcal{B}, i \neq j} \operatorname{sim}(\phi(\mathbf{x}_i), \phi(\mathbf{x}_j))\]

where \(\lambda \ge 0\) is the diversity penalty coefficient, and \(\operatorname{sim}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\) is the Gaussian RBF kernel similarity.

Because exact combinatorial optimization is NP-hard, the Greedy Forward Diversity Selector initializes \(\mathcal{B}_0 = \emptyset\) and at step \(m \in \{1, \dots, B\}\) selects:

\[\mathbf{u}^* = \arg\max_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U} \setminus \mathcal{B}_{m-1}} \left[ (1 - \lambda) \widetilde{\alpha}_{\text{unc}}(\mathbf{u}) - \lambda \max_{\mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{L} \cup \mathcal{B}_{m-1}} \operatorname{sim}(\phi(\mathbf{u}), \phi(\mathbf{v})) \right]\]

This ensures that each newly selected instance simultaneously exhibits high uncertainty and maximum geometric distance from both previously labeled data \(\mathcal{L}\) and all candidates already admitted into the current batch \(\mathcal{B}\).

docs.title: Definition 11.4.2: Automated Stopping Criteria (Validation Plateau, Prediction Stability, and Uncertainty Decay)
docs.text:
In production MLOps, continuing active learning past the point of convergence wastes specialist budget and risks overfitting to difficult boundary noise (Lowell et al., 2019). Automated termination is certified through three complementary stopping gates:

1. Rolling Window Performance Plateau Gate: Let \(\mathcal{M}_t\) denote a validation evaluation metric (e.g., Macro-\(F_1\) score or Mean Average Precision) computed at round \(t\). Over a rolling window of size \(W \ge 3\), the performance delta between consecutive windows is:

\[\Delta \text{Perf}_t = \left| \frac{1}{W}\sum_{w=0}^{W-1} \mathcal{M}_{t-w} - \frac{1}{W}\sum_{w=W}^{2W-1} \mathcal{M}_{t-w} \right|\]

Active learning terminates when \(\Delta \text{Perf}_t \le \epsilon_{\text{plateau}}\) (typically \(\epsilon_{\text{plateau}} = 0.005\)) for two consecutive rounds.

2. Cohen's Kappa Prediction Stability on Unlabeled Pool (Bloodgood & Vijay-Shanker, 2009): Let \(\hat{Y}_{t-1} = \{\hat{y}_{t-1}(\mathbf{u})\}_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U}_{\text{eval}}}\) and \(\hat{Y}_t = \{\hat{y}_t(\mathbf{u})\}_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U}_{\text{eval}}}\) denote the discrete class predictions generated on a held-out unlabelled evaluation pool \(\mathcal{U}_{\text{eval}}\) by the models trained at rounds \(t-1\) and \(t\).

Cohen's Kappa statistic measures the chance-corrected agreement between consecutive model versions:

\[\kappa\left(\hat{Y}_t, \hat{Y}_{t-1}\right) = \frac{P_o - P_e}{1 - P_e}\]

where observed agreement \(P_o\) and chance agreement \(P_e\) are defined as:

\[P_o = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}_{\text{eval}}|} \sum_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U}_{\text{eval}}} \mathbb{I}\left(\hat{y}_t(\mathbf{u}) = \hat{y}_{t-1}(\mathbf{u})\right), \quad P_e = \sum_{k=1}^K P_t(k) P_{t-1}(k)\]

where \(P_t(k) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}_{\text{eval}}|} \sum_{\mathbf{u}} \mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_t(\mathbf{u}) = k)\).

When \(\kappa \ge \tau_{\text{stability}}\) (typically \(\tau_{\text{stability}} = 0.98\)), the decision boundary is certified to have stabilized across the entire instance space: subsequent batch labeling alters predictions on less than \(1\%\) of the dataset, justifying immediate termination.

3. Maximum Pool Uncertainty Decay Gate: Active learning halts when the most uncertain remaining candidate in pool \(\mathcal{U}\) falls below an acceptable threshold:

\[\max_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U}} \alpha_{\text{Margin}}(\mathbf{u}) \le \tau_{\text{unc\_stop}}\]

docs.title: Definition 11.4.3: Noisy Oracle Consensus & Dynamic Quality Compensation (Dawid-Skene / Sheng et al.)
docs.text:
In real-world data collection, human annotators are imperfect oracles. Let \(A\) annotators provide labels for instance \(\mathbf{x}\), where annotator \(a \in \{1, \dots, A\}\) has latent error rate \(\eta_a \in (0, 0.5)\).

1. Dawid-Skene Bayesian Consensus Model: Under the Dawid-Skene formulation, each annotator is parameterized by a confusion matrix \(\theta_{a, j, k} = P(y_a = k \mid y^* = j)\). Given a vector of observed labels \(\mathbf{y} = [y_1, \dots, y_A]^\top\), the posterior probability that true class \(y^* = k\) is:

\[P(y^* = k \mid \mathbf{y}) = \frac{\pi_k \prod_{a=1}^A \theta_{a, k, y_a}}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \prod_{a=1}^A \theta_{a, j, y_a}}\]

where \(\pi_k = P(y^* = k)\) is the class prior distribution.

2. Sheng's Repeat Labeling Tradeoff (Sheng et al., 2008): Given a fixed financial annotation budget, an active learning manager must choose between two competing actions: - Action 1 (Explore): Query a brand-new unlabelled instance \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{new}} \in \mathcal{U}\). - Action 2 (Consolidate): Request a second or third label for an existing ambiguous instance \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{existing}} \in \mathcal{L}\) where annotators disagreed.

Let \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{loss}}(y^*)\) be the expected model parameter error induced by label uncertainty. Sheng et al. proved that when annotator noise \(\eta \ge 0.20\), the expected reduction in model classification error per unit cost satisfies:

\[\frac{\Delta \mathcal{L}_{\text{error}}(\mathbf{x}_{\text{repeat}})}{\text{Cost}} > \frac{\Delta \mathcal{L}_{\text{error}}(\mathbf{x}_{\text{new}})}{\text{Cost}}\]

Whenever the current posterior consensus confidence \(P(y^* = \hat{y} \mid \mathbf{y}) < 0.75\), acquiring an additional redundant label for an existing high-uncertainty point yields greater parameter update fidelity than labeling a clean, unambiguous new point.

docs.title: Definition 11.4.4: Successive Elimination & Budget-Constrained Stopping Bounds
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{H}\) be a finite hypothesis class. Under Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning guarantees, an active stopping rule must guarantee that the selected classifier \(f_{\hat{\theta}}\) achieves true generalization error within \(\epsilon\) of the empirical risk minimizer with confidence \(1 - \delta\).

1. PAC Stopping Sample Complexity Bound: By Hoeffding's inequality and the union bound over \(\mathcal{H}\), active learning can be guaranteed to stop safely once the number of labeled samples \(N_{\text{labeled}}\) satisfies:

\[N_{\text{labeled}} \ge \frac{1}{2\epsilon^2} \ln \left(\frac{2|\mathcal{H}|}{\delta}\right)\]

In active learning under Alexander capacity condition \(\theta_A\), this bound contracts to logarithmic sample complexity:

\[N_{\text{active}} \ge \mathcal{O}\left(\theta_A \cdot d \cdot \ln \left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right) \cdot \ln \left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\right)\]

2. Marginal Cost-Utility Ratio (MCUR): Let \(C(\mathcal{B})\) denote the financial cost of labeling batch \(\mathcal{B}\) (e.g., USD 1.50 per document). The marginal cost-utility ratio at round \(t\) is:

\[\text{MCUR}_t = \frac{\mathcal{M}_t - \mathcal{M}_{t-1}}{C(\mathcal{B}_t)}\]

Active learning terminates when \(\text{MCUR}_t < \gamma_{\text{stop}}\), indicating that acquiring additional data costs more than the expected business value of the accuracy gain.

docs.title: 💻 Production Pydantic V2 Implementation
docs.text:
The following production script implements PracticalActiveLearningEngine, integrating greedy batch diversity selection, Cohen's Kappa prediction stability, Dawid-Skene noisy consensus estimation, and multi-gate automated stopping criteria with strict Pydantic V2 validation contracts.

"""Production Practical Active Learning Pipeline: Batch Mode, Stopping Criteria, and Quality Compensation."""

import numpy as np
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import List, Dict, Literal, Tuple, Optional


class BatchActiveRequest(BaseModel):
    batch_size: int = Field(default=10, ge=1, description="Batch query size")
    diversity_penalty: float = Field(default=0.5, ge=0.0, le=1.0, description="Tradeoff parameter")
    stability_threshold: float = Field(default=0.98, ge=0.80, le=1.0, description="Cohen's Kappa stopping threshold")


class StoppingCriteriaStatus(BaseModel):
    iteration: int
    labeled_count: int
    prediction_stability_kappa: float
    performance_plateau_delta: float
    max_uncertainty: float
    should_stop: bool
    stopping_reason: Optional[str]


class PracticalActiveLearningEngine:
    """Production implementation of Batch Selection, Prediction Stability, and Stopping Gates."""

    @staticmethod
    def greedy_batch_diversity_selection(
        uncertainty_scores: np.ndarray,
        embeddings: np.ndarray,
        batch_size: int,
        diversity_lambda: float = 0.5
    ) -> List[int]:
        """Greedy batch selection trading off individual uncertainty against pairwise intra-batch similarity."""
        n = len(uncertainty_scores)
        if n <= batch_size:
            return list(range(n))

        u_norm = (uncertainty_scores - np.min(uncertainty_scores)) / (np.ptp(uncertainty_scores) + 1e-12)

        first_idx = int(np.argmax(u_norm))
        selected = [first_idx]
        selected_mask = np.zeros(n, dtype=bool)
        selected_mask[first_idx] = True

        dists_first = np.linalg.norm(embeddings - embeddings[first_idx], axis=1)
        sigma = float(np.median(dists_first)) + 1e-6
        max_sims = np.exp(- (dists_first ** 2) / (2.0 * sigma ** 2))

        for _ in range(batch_size - 1):
            combined_scores = (1.0 - diversity_lambda) * u_norm - diversity_lambda * max_sims
            combined_scores[selected_mask] = -np.inf

            best_idx = int(np.argmax(combined_scores))
            selected.append(best_idx)
            selected_mask[best_idx] = True

            new_dists = np.linalg.norm(embeddings - embeddings[best_idx], axis=1)
            new_sims = np.exp(- (new_dists ** 2) / (2.0 * sigma ** 2))
            max_sims = np.maximum(max_sims, new_sims)

        return selected

    @staticmethod
    def compute_cohens_kappa_stability(
        preds_prev: np.ndarray,
        preds_curr: np.ndarray,
        num_classes: int
    ) -> float:
        """Cohen's Kappa agreement between two consecutive models on unlabelled pool."""
        n = len(preds_prev)
        if n == 0:
            return 1.0

        p_o = float(np.mean(preds_prev == preds_curr))

        counts_prev = np.bincount(preds_prev, minlength=num_classes) / float(n)
        counts_curr = np.bincount(preds_curr, minlength=num_classes) / float(n)
        p_e = float(np.sum(counts_prev * counts_curr))

        if p_e >= 1.0:
            return 1.0
        kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1.0 - p_e)
        return float(np.clip(kappa, -1.0, 1.0))

    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_stopping_criteria(
        iteration: int,
        labeled_count: int,
        perf_history: List[float],
        kappa_stability: float,
        max_pool_uncertainty: float,
        plateau_window: int = 3,
        plateau_delta: float = 0.005,
        stability_threshold: float = 0.98,
        uncertainty_threshold: float = 0.08,
        budget_limit: int = 150
    ) -> StoppingCriteriaStatus:
        """Evaluates whether active learning should terminate based on plateau, stability, or budget."""
        should_stop = False
        reason = None

        if labeled_count >= budget_limit:
            should_stop = True
            reason = f"Labeling budget limit reached ({labeled_count} >= {budget_limit})"

        delta_perf = 1.0
        if len(perf_history) >= 2 * plateau_window:
            recent_mean = float(np.mean(perf_history[-plateau_window:]))
            prior_mean = float(np.mean(perf_history[-2 * plateau_window:-plateau_window]))
            delta_perf = abs(recent_mean - prior_mean)
            if delta_perf <= plateau_delta and not should_stop:
                should_stop = True
                reason = f"Performance plateau reached (delta={delta_perf:.4f} <= {plateau_delta})"

        if kappa_stability >= stability_threshold and not should_stop:
            should_stop = True
            reason = f"Prediction stability converged (kappa={kappa_stability:.4f} >= {stability_threshold})"

        if max_pool_uncertainty <= uncertainty_threshold and not should_stop:
            should_stop = True
            reason = f"Maximum uncertainty exhausted (max_unc={max_pool_uncertainty:.4f} <= {uncertainty_threshold})"

        return StoppingCriteriaStatus(
            iteration=iteration,
            labeled_count=labeled_count,
            prediction_stability_kappa=round(kappa_stability, 4),
            performance_plateau_delta=round(delta_perf, 4),
            max_uncertainty=round(max_pool_uncertainty, 4),
            should_stop=should_stop,
            stopping_reason=reason
        )


def run_unit_tests():
    """Unit test suite verifying batch selection, prediction stability, and stopping gates."""
    np.random.seed(42)

    # 1. Test Greedy Batch Diversity Selection
    cluster_a = np.random.randn(10, 2) * 0.1 + np.array([0.0, 0.0])
    cluster_b = np.random.randn(10, 2) * 0.1 + np.array([5.0, 5.0])
    embeddings = np.vstack([cluster_a, cluster_b])
    unc_scores = np.array([0.95] * 10 + [0.85] * 10)

    selected = PracticalActiveLearningEngine.greedy_batch_diversity_selection(
        uncertainty_scores=unc_scores,
        embeddings=embeddings,
        batch_size=4,
        diversity_lambda=0.6
    )
    print("Selected batch indices:", selected)
    has_a = any(idx < 10 for idx in selected)
    has_b = any(idx >= 10 for idx in selected)
    assert has_a and has_b, "Batch selection failed to enforce inter-cluster diversity!"

    # 2. Test Cohen's Kappa Prediction Stability
    p_prev = np.random.choice([0, 1, 2], size=1000)
    p_curr = p_prev.copy()
    p_curr[:5] = (p_curr[:5] + 1) % 3  # flip 5 predictions (99.5% agreement)
    kappa = PracticalActiveLearningEngine.compute_cohens_kappa_stability(p_prev, p_curr, num_classes=3)
    print(f"Cohen's Kappa (99.5% match): {kappa:.4f}")
    assert kappa >= 0.98, "Cohen's Kappa stability calculation failed!"

    # 3. Test Stopping Criteria Evaluation
    status = PracticalActiveLearningEngine.evaluate_stopping_criteria(
        iteration=10,
        labeled_count=100,
        perf_history=[0.85, 0.86, 0.87, 0.89, 0.90, 0.901, 0.902, 0.902],
        kappa_stability=0.992,
        max_pool_uncertainty=0.04
    )
    print("Stopping Status:", status.model_dump())
    assert status.should_stop is True, "Stopping criteria failed to trigger!"

    print("All practical active learning batch and stopping assertions verified successfully!")

docs.title: 🔬 Industrial Case Studies
docs.text: To understand how batch active learning and automated stopping criteria function in production, we examine two enterprise deployments: Relativity's Continuous Active Learning (TAR 2.0) in federal legal discovery and Paige AI's clinical pathology whole-slide triage.

docs.title: Case Study 1: Relativity — Continuous Active Learning (TAR 2.0) in Legal E-Discovery
docs.text:
RELATIVITY CONTINUOUS ACTIVE LEARNING (TAR 2.0)
 ┌───────────────────┐       ┌────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ 1.5M Email Corpus │ ────► │ TF-IDF + Embeddings    │ ────► │ Diverse Batch B=250  │
 │ Unreviewed Docs   │       │ Linear Classifier W    │       │ Margin + Diversity   │
 └───────────────────┘       └────────────────────────┘       └──────────┬───────────┘
                                                                         │
                      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                      ▼
         ┌────────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────┐
         │ Certified Attorneys    │ ─────► │ Statistical Stopping   │ ──► Subpoena Defense
         │ USD 350/Hour Review    │        │ Recall >= 95% Verified │     Production Cert
         └────────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────┘

In corporate litigation and antitrust investigations, legal counsel must review millions of confidential emails and contracts to identify evidence responsive to regulatory subpoenas. Manually reviewing \(1.5\text{ million}\) emails with certified corporate attorneys billing USD 350.00 per hour would cost upwards of USD 10.5 million and take over six months (Bloodgood & Vijay-Shanker, 2009; Cormack & Grossman, 2014).

The Engineering Challenge: 1. Asynchronous Batching: Legal teams comprise dozens of attorneys working simultaneously; the platform cannot pause review to retrain after single documents. 2. Strict Legal Standards: Under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Rule 26, courts mandate statistical proof that stopping active review has uncovered at least \(85\%\) of all legally responsive documents across the entire corpus.

The Architectural Solution: Relativity deployed Continuous Active Learning (CAL / TAR 2.0) (Cormack & Grossman, 2014): - Batches of \(B = 250\text{ documents}\) are populated via diversity-regularized active selection and distributed across attorney review queues. - At the end of each review round, a randomized statistical validation control set estimates total corpus recall \(\hat{R}\). - Active review stops automatically when the estimated recall exceeds \(95.0\%\) and the rolling marginal discovery rate falls below \(1\) responsive document per \(100\) reviewed documents.

The Empirical Outcome: Attorneys reviewed only \(180,000\text{ documents}\) (\(12.0\%\) of the corpus) before the stopping rule certified \(96.4\%\) recall, slashing review costs from USD 10.5 million to USD 1.26 million (saving USD 9.24 million).

Litigation Review Parameter Exhaustive Manual Review Relativity Continuous Active Learning Documents Reviewed by Attorneys \(1,500,000\text{ Documents}\) \(180,000\text{ Documents}\) (\(88.0\%\) reduction) Verified Responsive Document Recall \(95.0\%\) (target threshold) \(96.4\%\) (statistically certified) Specialist Attorney Review Hours \(30,000\text{ Hours}\) \(3,600\text{ Hours}\) (\(26,400\text{ Hours}\) saved) Total Legal Review Expenditure USD 10,500,000.00 USD 1,260,000.00 (USD 9.24M saved)

docs.title: Case Study 2: Paige AI — Clinical Digital Pathology Triage & Stopping Certification
docs.text:
PAIGE AI CLINICAL BIOPSY TRIAGE
 ┌───────────────────┐       ┌────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ 5,000 Whole Slide │ ────► │ Patch Embeddings       │ ────► │ Batch Selection B=50 │
 │ Biopsy Images     │       │ ResNet-50 / ViT        │       │ Margin + Core-Set    │
 └───────────────────┘       └────────────────────────┘       └──────────┬───────────┘
                                                                         │
                      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                      ▼
         ┌────────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────┐
         │ Surgical Pathologists  │ ─────► │ Cohen's Kappa >= 0.985 │ ──► FDA CE-Mark
         │ Gleason Grade Groups   │        │ Prediction Stability   │     Diagnostic Lock
         └────────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────┘

In cancer diagnostics, whole-slide digital biopsy images contain millions of cells across thousands of microscopic image patches. Annotating non-cancerous stroma patches wastes pathologist time, while stopping active labeling prematurely could cause false-negative diagnoses (Citovsky et al., 2021; Sheng et al., 2008).

The Engineering Challenge: Pathologists exhibit inter-observer variability: two board-certified pathologists agree on borderline Gleason grade 3 vs. 4 in only \(78\%\) of cases. The active learning engine must detect pathologist disagreement and stop only when the diagnostic classification surface is demonstrably stable.

The Architectural Solution: Paige AI deployed an MLOps active triage pipeline: - Active batches of \(B = 50\text{ patches}\) are selected using diversity regularization. - Borderline patches with high annotator variance trigger Sheng's repeat labeling consensus. - The pipeline tracks Cohen's Kappa prediction stability on a held-out set of \(25,000\) patient biopsy patches, terminating active learning when \(\kappa \ge 0.985\) and validation AUC delta is \(\le 0.002\).

The Empirical Outcome: The active stopping criterion certified diagnostic equivalence after reviewing only \(21.0\%\) of biopsy patches, slashing pathologist annotation time from \(5,000\) to \(1,050\text{ hours}\) (\(79.0\%\) reduction) while achieving \(99.1\%\) diagnostic concordance with full-cohort supervision.

Clinical Parameter Full Manual Annotation Active Triage with Stability Stopping Biopsy Slide Patches Reviewed \(500,000\text{ Patches}\) \(105,000\text{ Patches}\) (\(79.0\%\) reduction) Pathologist Review Hours \(5,000\text{ Hours}\) \(1,050\text{ Hours}\) (\(3,950\text{ Hours}\) saved) Diagnostic Concordance (AUC) \(0.988\) \(0.987\) (Clinical equivalence) Total Annotation Expenditure USD 1,250,000.00 USD 262,500.00 (USD 987.5k saved)

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Test your mathematical and operational grasp of batch active learning and automated stopping rules.

Self-Assessment 1: Exact Numerical Derivation of Cohen's Kappa Prediction Stability

An active learning model at round \(t-1\) and round \(t\) classifies a held-out unlabelled evaluation pool of \(N = 10,000\) instances into \(K = 2\) classes (Positive and Negative).

The confusion matrix of predictions between round \(t-1\) (rows) and round \(t\) (columns) is:

\[\begin{array}{c|cc|c} & \hat{y}_t = 1 & \hat{y}_t = 0 & \text{Total} \\ \hline \hat{y}_{t-1} = 1 & 3,920 & 80 & 4,000 \\ \hat{y}_{t-1} = 0 & 60 & 5,940 & 6,000 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 3,980 & 6,020 & 10,000 \end{array}\]

1. Calculate the observed proportion of agreement \(P_o\).

2. Calculate the chance-expected proportion of agreement \(P_e\).

3. Compute Cohen's Kappa statistic \(\kappa\). Under stopping threshold \(\tau = 0.98\), does the active learning pipeline terminate?

Reveal Detailed Solution & Step-by-Step Derivation

1. Observed Agreement (\(P_o\)): The number of instances where both models predicted the identical class is:

\[N_{\text{agree}} = 3,920 + 5,940 = 9,860\] \[P_o = \frac{9,860}{10,000} = \mathbf{0.9860 \quad (98.60\%)}\]

2. Chance Expected Agreement (\(P_e\)): - Probability round \(t-1\) predicts Positive: \(P_{t-1}(1) = \frac{4,000}{10,000} = 0.4000\). - Probability round \(t\) predicts Positive: \(P_t(1) = \frac{3,980}{10,000} = 0.3980\). - Probability round \(t-1\) predicts Negative: \(P_{t-1}(0) = \frac{6,000}{10,000} = 0.6000\). - Probability round \(t\) predicts Negative: \(P_t(0) = \frac{6,020}{10,000} = 0.6020\).

\[P_e = P_{t-1}(1) P_t(1) + P_{t-1}(0) P_t(0)\] \[P_e = (0.4000 \times 0.3980) + (0.6000 \times 0.6020) = 0.1592 + 0.3612 = \mathbf{0.5204 \quad (52.04\%)}\]

3. Cohen's Kappa Calculation:

\[\kappa = \frac{P_o - P_e}{1 - P_e} = \frac{0.9860 - 0.5204}{1.0 - 0.5204} = \frac{0.4656}{0.4796} \approx \mathbf{0.9708}\]

Decision: Because \(\kappa = 0.9708 < \tau = 0.9800\), the model decision boundary has not yet achieved certified stability. Approximately \(140\) predictions out of \(10,000\) flipped between rounds (\(1.4\%\)), indicating active learning updates are still altering classification outcomes. The pipeline continues to the next active batch.

Self-Assessment 2: Sheng's Repeat Labeling Tradeoff under Annotator Noise

An annotation manager employs crowdsourced annotators with independent error rate \(\eta = 0.25\) (\(75\%\) accuracy).

A candidate instance \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{existing}}\) has received a single label \(y_1 = 1\). The prior class distribution is balanced (\(\pi_1 = \pi_0 = 0.50\)).

1. Under Bayes' rule, what is the posterior probability \(P(y^* = 1 \mid y_1 = 1)\)?

2. If a second independent annotator labels the same instance and agrees (\(y_2 = 1\)), calculate the updated posterior probability \(P(y^* = 1 \mid y_1 = 1, y_2 = 1)\).

3. If the cost of labeling is USD 0.50 per query, explain why paying USD 0.50 for a second confirmation label on a boundary point provides greater risk reduction than acquiring an uncertain new point with \(25\%\) error.

Reveal Detailed Solution & Step-by-Step Derivation

1. Posterior with Single Label: Given \(P(y_1 = 1 \mid y^* = 1) = 1 - \eta = 0.75\) and \(P(y_1 = 1 \mid y^* = 0) = \eta = 0.25\):

\[P(y^* = 1 \mid y_1 = 1) = \frac{0.75 \times 0.50}{(0.75 \times 0.50) + (0.25 \times 0.50)} = \frac{0.375}{0.375 + 0.125} = \mathbf{0.7500 \quad (75.0\%)}\]

The single label carries a \(25.0\%\) probability of being wrong!

2. Posterior with Second Concordant Label (\(y_1 = 1, y_2 = 1\)): By conditional independence given true class \(y^*\):

\[P(y_1 = 1, y_2 = 1 \mid y^* = 1) = (0.75)^2 = 0.5625\] \[P(y_1 = 1, y_2 = 1 \mid y^* = 0) = (0.25)^2 = 0.0625\] \[P(y^* = 1 \mid y_1 = 1, y_2 = 1) = \frac{0.5625 \times 0.50}{(0.5625 \times 0.50) + (0.0625 \times 0.50)} = \frac{0.28125}{0.28125 + 0.03125} = \frac{0.28125}{0.3125} = \mathbf{0.9000 \quad (90.0\%)}\]

3. Tradeoff Analysis (Sheng et al., 2008): With a single query, the ground-truth error probability is \(25\%\). If this instance is situated directly on the classifier's decision boundary, training on a reversed label (\(y = 0\) instead of \(y^* = 1\)) induces a substantial gradient penalty in the wrong direction, destabilizing the entire separating hyperplane.

Spending USD 0.50 to acquire a second label reduces the label error rate from \(25.0\%\) to \(10.0\%\) (a \(2.5\times\) error reduction). Conversely, spending USD 0.50 on a new unlabelled instance merely yields another noisy observation with \(25.0\%\) error. Near the decision boundary, data quality strictly dominates data quantity.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & The Software 2.0 Shift
docs.text:
In classical machine learning pipelines, human subject matter experts spend thousands of hours manually hand-labeling individual instances one by one. This hand-labeling paradigm suffers from severe systemic vulnerabilities: it is unversioned, non-auditable, prohibitively expensive, and must be discarded and repeated from scratch whenever schema taxonomies change (Ratner et al., 2016; Ratner et al., 2017). When business requirements or class boundaries evolve, thousands of hand-labeled records become technical debt.

Weak Supervision revolutionizes data curation by shifting from manual instance-level labeling to programmatic data programming (Ratner et al., 2017). Instead of hand-labeling 100,000 documents, domain experts write a suite of dozens of Labeling Functions (LFs)—arbitrary Python functions that encode domain heuristics, regular expressions, pattern dictionaries, automated rule synthesis (Varma & Ré, 2018), ontology-guided clinical extractions (Fries et al., 2021), distant supervision lookups, and zero-shot foundation model prompts (Bach et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021). Fast covariance parameter estimation models such as FlyingSquid further enable near-instantaneous scaling over millions of samples (Chen et al., 2020).

docs.title: The Software 2.0 Paradigm: Code-as-Supervision
docs.text:
In Software 2.0, training data is no longer curated through manual, subjective point clicks in a third-party labeling portal. Instead, supervision is expressed as executable software programs that are subject to the same rigorous engineering lifecycle as application code: version control via Git, continuous integration, regression testing, and collaborative pull requests (Ratner et al., 2017; Varma et al., 2019).

Operational Dimension Software 1.0 (Manual Hand-Labeling) Software 2.0 (Programmatic Weak Supervision) Curation Velocity Weeks to months per dataset Hours to days per iteration Marginal Cost per Label USD 0.10 to USD 5.00+ per instance Near-zero compute cost (\(< \text{USD } 0.0001\)) Auditability & Provenance Subjective, unversioned human clicks 100% auditable Git-versioned Python functions Taxonomy Adaptability Complete manual relabeling required Update LF logic and re-execute pipeline in minutes Noise Resolution Ad-hoc majority vote or annotator consensus Principled generative graphical models & covariance matching Domain Portability Annotator retraining required Reusable regexes, ontologies, and cross-domain heuristics

docs.title: Anatomy of a Labeling Function (LF)
docs.text:
A Labeling Function (LF) \(\lambda_j\) takes an unlabeled instance \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}\) and either outputs a predicted class label or abstains (\(0\)):

\[ \lambda_j(\mathbf{x}): \mathcal{X} \to \{-1, 0, 1\} \quad \text{or} \quad \{1, 2, \dots, K\} \cup \{0\} \]
  • Abstention is Foundational: Unlike a traditional classifier which must emit a guess on every instance, an LF acts only when its specific heuristic pattern is detected. For example, a regex rule detecting clinical drug names abstains on 98% of medical text records and votes only when an explicit drug token is present.
  • Noise Tolerance: Individual LFs are expected to be noisy (typically \(60\% - 85\%\) accuracy), correlate with one another, and frequently disagree.
  • Generative Label Modeling: A statistical factor graph models the joint distribution of observed LF votes and the unobserved latent true label, estimating LF accuracies without requiring ground-truth gold labels (Ratner et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2020).

Industrial Best Practice: Programmatic Labeling with Snorkel

Replace manual token-by-token labeling with Programmatic Weak Supervision: author 20–50 deterministic Labeling Functions (LFs) capturing domain heuristics, regex patterns, external dictionaries, and zero-shot model outputs. Snorkel estimates rule accuracies and outputs probabilistic training labels automatically.

Common Pitfall / Anti-Pattern: Majority Voting Over Correlated Labeling Rules

If five labeling functions depend on the exact same keyword list or sentiment lexicon, a naive majority vote counts their correlated vote five times, artificially inflating confidence and overpowering independent, accurate rules. Always use a generative model that explicitly accounts for conditional covariance between labeling functions (Ratner et al., 2017; Varma et al., 2019).

docs.title: Definition 11.5.1: The Sparse Label Matrix \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) and Data Programming Formulations
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{X} = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_n\}\) denote an unlabeled dataset drawn from an underlying data distribution \(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}\), where each instance has an unobserved latent true label \(y_i^* \in \mathcal{Y} = \{-1, +1\}\) (or \(K\)-ary \(\mathcal{Y} = \{1, \dots, K\}\)). Let \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m)^T\) denote an ensemble of \(m\) labeling functions, where each function is a mapping:

\[ \lambda_j: \mathcal{X} \to \{-1, 0, +1\} \quad (j = 1, \dots, m) \]

with \(\lambda_j(\mathbf{x}_i) = 0\) designating that labeling function \(\lambda_j\) abstains on sample \(\mathbf{x}_i\).

Evaluating the ensemble \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) across all \(n\) unlabeled instances generates the Sparse Label Matrix \(\mathbf{\Lambda} \in \{-1, 0, +1\}^{n \times m}\):

\[ \mathbf{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} \Lambda_{1, 1} & \Lambda_{1, 2} & \dots & \Lambda_{1, m} \\ \Lambda_{2, 1} & \Lambda_{2, 2} & \dots & \Lambda_{2, m} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \Lambda_{n, 1} & \Lambda_{n, 2} & \dots & \Lambda_{n, m} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1(\mathbf{x}_1) & \lambda_2(\mathbf{x}_1) & \dots & \lambda_m(\mathbf{x}_1) \\ \lambda_1(\mathbf{x}_2) & \lambda_2(\mathbf{x}_2) & \dots & \lambda_m(\mathbf{x}_2) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \lambda_1(\mathbf{x}_n) & \lambda_2(\mathbf{x}_n) & \dots & \lambda_m(\mathbf{x}_n) \end{bmatrix} \]

The non-zero entries of \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) define the empirical support mask \(\mathbf{S} \in \{0, 1\}^{n \times m}\), where \(S_{i, j} = \mathbb{I}(\Lambda_{i, j} \ne 0)\). In industrial applications, \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) is highly sparse: each individual LF covers only a small fraction of the input space (\(1\% - 40\%\)), but their union spans the vast majority of the corpus.

docs.title: Definition 11.5.2: Labeling Function Matrix Metrics (Coverage, Overlap, Conflict, and Empirical Accuracy)
docs.text:
For any ensemble of labeling functions \( oldsymbol{\lambda}\) evaluated over corpus \(\mathcal{X}\), the structural properties of \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) are governed by four fundamental mathematical metrics:

  1. Individual LF Coverage: The empirical fraction of instances where labeling function \(\lambda_j\) emits a non-abstaining vote:

    \[ \operatorname{Cov}(\lambda_j) = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(\Lambda_{i, j} e 0) = rac{1}{n} \|\mathbf{\Lambda}_{:, j}\|_0 \]

  2. Total Pipeline Coverage: The proportion of instances labeled by at least one labeling function in the ensemble:

    \[ \operatorname{Cov}_{ ext{total}}( oldsymbol{\lambda}) = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}\left( \sum_{j=1}^m |\Lambda_{i, j}| > 0 ight) \]

  3. Pairwise Overlap Matrix \(\mathbf{O} \in [0, 1]^{m imes m}\): The frequency with which two labeling functions \(\lambda_j\) and \(\lambda_k\) simultaneously emit votes on the same instance:

    \[ O_{j, k} = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(\Lambda_{i, j} e 0 \ \land \ \Lambda_{i, k} e 0) \]

  4. Pairwise Conflict Matrix \(\mathbf{C} \in [0, 1]^{m imes m}\): The frequency with which two labeling functions both vote on an instance but disagree on the assigned label:

    \[ C_{j, k} = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(\Lambda_{i, j} e 0 \ \land \ \Lambda_{i, k} e 0 \ \land \ \Lambda_{i, j} e \Lambda_{i, k}) \]

  5. Empirical Validation Accuracy: Given a small held-out gold validation set \(\mathcal{D}_{ ext{val}} = \{(\mathbf{x}_k, y_k^*)\}_{k=1}^{n_v}\), the empirical precision of \(\lambda_j\) on its covered slice is:

    \[ \operatorname{Acc}_{ ext{emp}}(\lambda_j) = rac{\sum_{k=1}^{n_v} \mathbb{I}(\lambda_j(\mathbf{x}_k) = y_k^*)}{\sum_{k=1}^{n_v} \mathbb{I}(\lambda_j(\mathbf{x}_k) e 0)} \]

High conflict ratios \(C_{j, k}\) indicate decision-boundary ambiguity or contradictory heuristic definitions, providing the critical statistical leverage necessary for unsupervised generative models to infer rule reliability (Ratner et al., 2017).

docs.title: Definition 11.5.3: Generative Label Model & Latent Factor Estimation (Snorkel / Gibbs / Ising Model)
docs.text:
Let \(Y \in \{-1, +1\}\) denote the latent true binary label and \(\mathbf{\Lambda} = (\Lambda_1, \dots, \Lambda_m)^T \in \{-1, 0, +1\}^m\) denote the observed LF votes for a single instance. In data programming (Ratner et al., 2016), the joint probability distribution \(\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{\Lambda}, Y)\) is parameterized as a factor graph (Gibbs / Ising distribution):

\[ \mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{\Lambda}, Y) = \frac{1}{Z_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} \exp\left( \sum_{j=1}^m \theta_j^{\text{acc}} \Lambda_j Y + \sum_{j=1}^m \theta_j^{\text{prop}} |\Lambda_j| + \sum_{(j, k) \in \mathcal{E}} \theta_{jk}^{\text{corr}} \Lambda_j \Lambda_k \right) \]

where: - \(\theta_j^{\text{acc}} \in \mathbb{R}\) is the accuracy parameter for LF \(\lambda_j\) (governing alignment with the true label \(Y\)). - \(\theta_j^{\text{prop}} \in \mathbb{R}\) is the propensity parameter governing the baseline frequency of non-abstention. - \(\theta_{jk}^{\text{corr}} \in \mathbb{R}\) is the correlation weight across an edge set \(\mathcal{E}\) capturing statistical dependencies between heuristics. - \(Z_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) is the partition function normalizing the probability distribution:

\[ Z_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \sum_{y \in \{-1, +1\}} \sum_{\boldsymbol{\lambda} \in \{-1, 0, +1\}^m} \exp\left( \sum_{j=1}^m \theta_j^{\text{acc}} \lambda_j y + \sum_{j=1}^m \theta_j^{\text{prop}} |\lambda_j| + \sum_{(j, k) \in \mathcal{E}} \theta_{jk}^{\text{corr}} \lambda_j \lambda_k \right) \]

Unsupervised Parameter Estimation: Under conditional independence or chordal dependency graphs, parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^*\) can be estimated without access to ground-truth labels \(y^*\) by minimizing the negative marginal log-likelihood of the observed label matrix:

\[ \boldsymbol{\theta}^* = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} -\sum_{i=1}^n \log \mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{i, :}) = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} -\sum_{i=1}^n \log \left( \sum_{y \in \{-1, +1\}} \mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{i, :}, Y = y) \right) \]

Alternatively, fast matrix completion algorithms match the empirical second-order covariance of LF outputs \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{\Lambda}} = \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{\Lambda}^T \mathbf{\Lambda} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{\Lambda}} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{\Lambda}}^T\) to solve for latent accuracies in closed form or via Expectation-Maximization (Chen et al., 2020).

The model outputs soft probabilistic training labels \(\tilde{y}_i \in [0, 1]\):

\[ \tilde{y}_i = \mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^*}(Y_i = +1 \mid \mathbf{\Lambda}_{i, :}) = \frac{\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^*}(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{i, :}, Y_i = +1)}{\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^*}(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{i, :}, Y_i = +1) + \mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^*}(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{i, :}, Y_i = -1)} \]

docs.title: Definition 11.5.4: Generalization Bounds of Weakly Supervised End Models (Noise-Tolerant Loss & Sample Complexity)
docs.text:
Let \(f_{\mathbf{w}}: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a discriminative deep neural network parameterized by \(\mathbf{w}\) from hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) with empirical Rademacher complexity \(\mathcal{R}_n(\mathcal{H})\). Instead of training on unobserved ground truth labels \(y_i^*\), the end model is trained by minimizing the soft cross-entropy risk over the probabilistic labels \(\tilde{y}_i\):

\[ \hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{soft}}(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ \tilde{y}_i \log \sigma(f_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}_i)) + (1 - \tilde{y}_i) \log(1 - \sigma(f_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}_i))) \right] \]

where \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\) is the standard sigmoid function.

Theorem (Data Programming Generalization Bound, Ratner et al., 2016): Let \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{true}}(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, y^*) \sim \mathcal{D}}[\ell(f_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}), y^*)]\) denote the true risk under the clean data distribution. If the generative label model parameter estimation error satisfies \(\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^* - \boldsymbol{\theta}_0\|_2 \le \epsilon_g(m, n)\), then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over the random draw of \(n\) unlabeled training instances:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{true}}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}) - \inf_{\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{H}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{true}}(\mathbf{w}) \le \mathcal{O}\left( \mathcal{R}_n(\mathcal{H}) + \sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}} + \epsilon_g(m, n) + (1 - \operatorname{Cov}_{\text{total}}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})) \right) \]

As the unlabeled dataset size \(n \to \infty\) and rule ensemble size \(m \to \infty\), the asymptotic error of the weakly supervised end model converges to the optimal Bayes risk at rate \(\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/2})\). This proves that a deep neural model trained on noisy, programmatic weak labels asymptotically matches the performance of a model trained on expensive, fully supervised human gold labels (Ratner et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2021).

docs.title: 💻 Production-Grade Python Implementation: Pydantic Weak Supervision Pipeline
docs.text:
The following production script implements a complete Weak Supervision Pipeline. It defines strongly typed Pydantic V2 metadata schemas for labeling functions, compiles the sparse label matrix \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\), executes an unsupervised Expectation-Maximization Generative Label Model (Dawid-Skene / Snorkel formulation) to infer latent rule accuracies without gold supervision, benchmarks against naive majority voting, and verifies mathematical assertions:

import re
import numpy as np
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ConfigDict
from typing import Callable, List, Dict, Tuple, Optional

# Label Constants: Binary Sentiment (-1: Negative, +1: Positive, 0: Abstain)
ABSTAIN = 0
POSITIVE = 1
NEGATIVE = -1

class LFMetadata(BaseModel):
    """Metadata schema defining auditability attributes for a Labeling Function."""
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)
    name: str = Field(..., description="Unique human-readable identifier for the LF")
    category: str = Field(..., description="Category: Heuristic, Regex, DistantKB, or Model")
    description: str = Field(..., description="Domain justification and pattern description")
    intended_class: int = Field(..., description="Class this rule is designed to fire on (+1 or -1)")

class LabelingFunction:
    """Encapsulates executable heuristic logic with structured provenance metadata."""
    def __init__(self, metadata: LFMetadata, func: Callable[[str], int]):
        self.metadata = metadata
        self.func = func

    def __call__(self, text: str) -> int:
        return self.func(text)

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return self.metadata.name

# 1. Domain Labeling Function Implementations
def func_positive_regex(text: str) -> int:
    """Flags high-precision positive sentiment adjectives."""
    if re.search(r'\b(excellent|outstanding|superb|flawless|terrific|delightful)\b', text, re.I):
        return POSITIVE
    return ABSTAIN

def func_negative_regex(text: str) -> int:
    """Flags high-precision critical negative sentiment adjectives."""
    if re.search(r'\b(terrible|awful|horrible|defective|broken|worst|unacceptable)\b', text, re.I):
        return NEGATIVE
    return ABSTAIN

def func_short_exclamation_complaint(text: str) -> int:
    """Heuristic: short reviews with exclamation marks and negation tokens."""
    words = text.split()
    if len(words) <= 7 and "!" in text and re.search(r'\b(not|never|waste|no)\b', text, re.I):
        return NEGATIVE
    return ABSTAIN

def func_recommendation_phrase(text: str) -> int:
    """Distant phrase heuristic: explicit purchase recommendations."""
    if re.search(r'\b(highly recommend|must buy|worth every penny|five stars)\b', text, re.I):
        return POSITIVE
    return ABSTAIN

def func_noisy_overbroad_negative(text: str) -> int:
    """Intentionally noisy/overbroad heuristic flagging 'problem', 'delay', 'issue'."""
    if re.search(r'\b(problem|delay|issue|wait|cost)\b', text, re.I):
        return NEGATIVE
    return ABSTAIN

class LFMetrics(BaseModel):
    """Quality metrics for an individual labeling function."""
    coverage: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    overlaps: Dict[str, float] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    conflicts: Dict[str, float] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    inferred_accuracy: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)

class WeakSupervisionReport(BaseModel):
    """Comprehensive telemetry report for the entire weak supervision pipeline."""
    pipeline_coverage: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    mean_conflict_rate: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    lf_reports: Dict[str, LFMetrics] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    num_instances: int = Field(..., gt=0)
    num_lfs: int = Field(..., gt=0)

class WeakSupervisionPipeline:
    """Production weak supervision engine managing LF evaluation, metrics, and generative modeling."""

    def __init__(self, lfs: List[LabelingFunction]):
        self.lfs = lfs
        self.lf_names = [lf.name for lf in lfs]
        self.m = len(lfs)

    def build_label_matrix(self, texts: List[str]) -> np.ndarray:
        """Evaluates all M labeling functions over N unlabeled instances -> Lambda in {-1, 0, 1}^(N x M)."""
        n = len(texts)
        L = np.zeros((n, self.m), dtype=int)
        for i, text in enumerate(texts):
            for j, lf in enumerate(self.lfs):
                L[i, j] = lf(text)
        return L

    def compute_metrics(self, L: np.ndarray, inferred_accs: Optional[np.ndarray] = None) -> WeakSupervisionReport:
        """Computes coverage, pairwise overlap, pairwise conflict, and inferred accuracies."""
        n, m = L.shape
        non_abstain = (L != ABSTAIN).astype(float)
        covered_instances = np.sum(np.any(L != ABSTAIN, axis=1))
        pipe_cov = float(covered_instances / n)

        lf_reports = {}
        conflict_list = []

        if inferred_accs is None:
            inferred_accs = np.full(m, 0.70)

        for j in range(m):
            cov_j = float(np.mean(non_abstain[:, j]))
            overlaps_j = {}
            conflicts_j = {}

            for k in range(m):
                if j == k:
                    continue
                both = (non_abstain[:, j] * non_abstain[:, k]) > 0
                overlap_val = float(np.mean(both))
                conflict_val = float(np.mean(both & (L[:, j] != L[:, k])))
                overlaps_j[self.lf_names[k]] = round(overlap_val, 4)
                conflicts_j[self.lf_names[k]] = round(conflict_val, 4)
                if j < k:
                    conflict_list.append(conflict_val)

            lf_reports[self.lf_names[j]] = LFMetrics(
                coverage=round(cov_j, 4),
                overlaps=overlaps_j,
                conflicts=conflicts_j,
                inferred_accuracy=round(float(inferred_accs[j]), 4)
            )

        mean_conflict = float(np.mean(conflict_list)) if conflict_list else 0.0

        return WeakSupervisionReport(
            pipeline_coverage=round(pipe_cov, 4),
            mean_conflict_rate=round(mean_conflict, 4),
            lf_reports=lf_reports,
            num_instances=n,
            num_lfs=m
        )

    def majority_vote(self, L: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Baseline aggregation: unweighted sigmoid of vote sums."""
        sums = np.sum(L, axis=1)
        probs = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-sums.astype(float)))
        return probs

    def fit_generative_label_model(
        self,
        L: np.ndarray,
        max_iter: int = 50,
        tol: float = 1e-4
    ) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
        """
        Unsupervised Generative Label Model via Expectation-Maximization (Dawid-Skene / Snorkel Formulation).
        Estimates latent class prior P(Y=1) and per-LF accuracies a_j = P(L_j = Y | L_j != 0) without ground truth.
        Enforces domain heuristic bounds (a_j in [0.55, 0.98]) to ensure symmetry breaking.
        """
        n, m = L.shape
        prior_pos = 0.5
        accs = np.full(m, 0.80)

        for iteration in range(max_iter):
            old_accs = accs.copy()

            # E-step: Compute log likelihoods for latent Y = +1 and Y = -1
            log_p_pos = np.log(prior_pos) * np.ones(n)
            log_p_neg = np.log(1.0 - prior_pos) * np.ones(n)

            for j in range(m):
                p_c = accs[j]
                p_w = 1.0 - p_c
                v_pos = (L[:, j] == POSITIVE)
                v_neg = (L[:, j] == NEGATIVE)
                log_p_pos += v_pos * np.log(p_c) + v_neg * np.log(p_w)
                log_p_neg += v_pos * np.log(p_w) + v_neg * np.log(p_c)

            max_log = np.maximum(log_p_pos, log_p_neg)
            p_pos = np.exp(log_p_pos - max_log)
            p_neg = np.exp(log_p_neg - max_log)
            posteriors = p_pos / (p_pos + p_neg)

            # Abstained samples have neutral posterior
            abstained = ~np.any(L != ABSTAIN, axis=1)
            posteriors[abstained] = 0.5

            # M-step: Update prior and accuracies
            covered = np.any(L != ABSTAIN, axis=1)
            if np.sum(covered) > 0:
                prior_pos = float(np.mean(posteriors[covered]))

            for j in range(m):
                cov_j = (L[:, j] != ABSTAIN)
                v_pos = (L[:, j] == POSITIVE)
                v_neg = (L[:, j] == NEGATIVE)
                if np.sum(cov_j) > 0:
                    exp_corr = np.sum(v_pos * posteriors + v_neg * (1.0 - posteriors))
                    accs[j] = float(np.clip(exp_corr / np.sum(cov_j), 0.55, 0.98))

            if np.max(np.abs(accs - old_accs)) < tol:
                break

        return posteriors, accs

# --- Verification & Mathematical Assertions ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    lfs = [
        LabelingFunction(
            LFMetadata(
                name="lf_pos_regex",
                category="Regex",
                description="Matches strong positive sentiment adjectives",
                intended_class=POSITIVE
            ),
            func_positive_regex
        ),
        LabelingFunction(
            LFMetadata(
                name="lf_neg_regex",
                category="Regex",
                description="Matches critical negative sentiment adjectives",
                intended_class=NEGATIVE
            ),
            func_negative_regex
        ),
        LabelingFunction(
            LFMetadata(
                name="lf_short_excl",
                category="Heuristic",
                description="Detects short exclamatory complaint phrases",
                intended_class=NEGATIVE
            ),
            func_short_exclamation_complaint
        ),
        LabelingFunction(
            LFMetadata(
                name="lf_recommend",
                category="Phrase",
                description="Matches strong purchase recommendation phrases",
                intended_class=POSITIVE
            ),
            func_recommendation_phrase
        ),
        LabelingFunction(
            LFMetadata(
                name="lf_noisy_negative",
                category="Heuristic",
                description="Overbroad pattern flagging mentions of problem or delay",
                intended_class=NEGATIVE
            ),
            func_noisy_overbroad_negative
        )
    ]

    corpus = [
        "Superb display and flawless performance, highly recommend to everyone!", # 0: Pos (+1, 0, 0, +1, 0)
        "Terrible customer service, completely broken upon arrival, worst experience ever!", # 1: Neg (0, -1, 0, 0, 0)
        "Not worth the price! Waste of money!", # 2: Short complaint (0, 0, -1, 0, 0)
        "Minor delay in shipping but resolved quickly, excellent quality and must buy!", # 3: Conflicted Pos (+1, 0, 0, +1, -1)
        "Package arrived on Thursday afternoon inside a standard cardboard box.", # 4: Neutral / Abstain all
        "Unacceptable quality, defect found immediately, absolute problem!", # 5: Neg with noisy rule (0, -1, 0, 0, -1)
        "Outstanding battery life, worth every penny, zero issues encountered.", # 6: Pos (+1, 0, 0, +1, 0)
        "Horrible latency, awful UI, do not recommend.", # 7: Neg (0, -1, 0, 0, 0)
    ]

    pipeline = WeakSupervisionPipeline(lfs)
    L = pipeline.build_label_matrix(corpus)

    # Execute Generative Label Model
    posteriors, accs = pipeline.fit_generative_label_model(L)
    mv_probs = pipeline.majority_vote(L)
    report = pipeline.compute_metrics(L, accs)

    print("=== LABEL MATRIX (N=8, M=5) ===")
    print(L)
    print("\n=== INFERRED LF ACCURACIES (UNSUPERVISED) ===")
    for name, acc in zip(pipeline.lf_names, accs):
        print(f"  {name:20s}: {acc:.4f}")

    print("\n=== INSTANCE AGGREGATION COMPARISON ===")
    for idx, (doc, p_gen, p_mv) in enumerate(zip(corpus, posteriors, mv_probs)):
        print(f"Doc {idx}: P(Y=1|gen)={p_gen:.4f} | P(Y=1|mv)={p_mv:.4f} | \"{doc[:50]}...\"")

    print(f"\nPipeline Coverage: {report.pipeline_coverage * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"Mean Conflict Rate: {report.mean_conflict_rate * 100:.2f}%")

    # Mathematical Assertions
    # 1. Neutral document (Doc 4) must abstain on all LFs and receive neutral posterior 0.50
    assert np.all(L[4] == ABSTAIN), "Neutral document failed to abstain across all LFs!"
    assert posteriors[4] == 0.50, f"Abstained document must have neutral posterior 0.5, got {posteriors[4]}"

    # 2. Strong positive document (Doc 0) must have high posterior (> 0.90)
    assert posteriors[0] > 0.90, f"Doc 0 positive posterior too low: {posteriors[0]}"

    # 3. Strong negative document (Doc 1) must have low positive posterior (< 0.20)
    assert posteriors[1] < 0.20, f"Doc 1 failed negative classification: {posteriors[1]}"

    # 4. Overbroad noisy LF (lf_noisy_negative) must have lower inferred accuracy than precise regexes
    assert accs[4] < accs[0], f"Noisy LF accuracy ({accs[4]}) unexpectedly higher than precision LF ({accs[0]})"

    # 5. Pipeline coverage must be 7/8 = 87.5%
    assert report.pipeline_coverage == 0.875, f"Expected 0.875 coverage, got {report.pipeline_coverage}"

    print("\nAll Weak Supervision mathematical assertions verified successfully!")

docs.title: 🔬 Dual Industrial Case Studies: High-Impact Deployments
Case Study 1: Google Snorkel DryBell Knowledge Graph Extraction
docs.text:
Knowledge graph enrichment and entity classification across billions of web pages at Google requires training deep Transformer models over thousands of semantic relationship types. Employing human annotators to hand-label millions of web instances would cost tens of millions of dollars and introduce prohibitive human label latency (Ratner et al., 2017; Varma et al., 2019).

  1. The Weak Supervision Architecture: Google Research and Stanford deployed Snorkel DryBell across production web extraction pipelines covering dozens of internal search and assistant services (Varma et al., 2019).
  2. The Multi-Source LF Zoo: Cross-functional engineering teams authored hundreds of lightweight Python Labeling Functions wrapping internal entity dictionaries, HTML structural heuristics, legacy model ensembles, and Knowledge Graph foreign keys. Snorkel's generative model executed on distributed Apache Spark clusters, learning LF correlation structures without gold training labels.
  3. The Outcome: Snorkel DryBell trained production neural classifiers that matched or exceeded the accuracy of models trained on tens of thousands of expensive human gold labels, reducing model deployment turnaround from \(6\text{ months}\) to \(48\text{ hours}\) while achieving a \(+1.6\%\) absolute F1-score gain over human gold baselines.
Benchmark Metric Traditional Manual Hand-Labeling Google Snorkel DryBell Production Data Curation Turnaround \(12 - 24\text{ Weeks}\) \(< 48\text{ Hours}\) (\(98\%\) time reduction) Auditability & Provenance Subjective, unversioned human judgment \(100\%\) Git-versioned Python code Corpus Scale Labeled \(10,000\) hand-labeled instances \(> 10,000,000\) instances via distributed Spark F1-Score Benchmark \(84.2\%\) (Baseline human training) \(85.8\%\) (+1.6% absolute gain) Cost per Model Iteration USD 85,000 in crowd annotator labor \(< \text{USD } 500\) in cluster compute resources

docs.title: Case Study 2: Stanford Medicine Clinical Phenotyping & Radiograph AI
docs.text:
Automating clinical disease phenotyping across electronic health record (EHR) text notes and multimodal chest radiographs (MIMIC-CXR) is severely bottlenecked by physician availability. Clinical annotations require licensed radiologists or subspecialty physicians, whose billing rates range from \(\text{USD } 150\) to \(\text{USD } 350\) per hour, while HIPAA privacy regulations strictly prohibit uploading patient health information to public crowdsourcing marketplaces (Fries et al., 2021).

  1. The Ontology-Driven Weak Supervision Framework: Researchers at Stanford Medicine developed an ontology-driven weak supervision pipeline using Snorkel to label hundreds of thousands of chest radiograph reports (Fries et al., 2021).
  2. Clinical LF Zoo:
  3. UMLS / RadLex Medical Ontologies: Concept mappings identifying peripheral artery disease, pleural effusion, and cardiomegaly.
  4. NegEx Syntactic Parsers: Regular expression rules detecting negation phrases (e.g., "no evidence of consolidation", "rules out pneumonia").
  5. Lab Value Thresholds: Rule-based heuristics evaluating blood gas tests and ejection fraction percentages.
  6. The Outcome: The generative label model aggregated over 40 clinical LFs, training deep vision-language models that matched the diagnostic F1-score of expert board-certified radiologists (\(F_1 = 0.887\)), while reducing total physician annotation time by \(82.4\%\).

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & The Label Aggregation Problem
docs.text:
In programmatic weak supervision, evaluating \(M\) labeling functions across \(N\) instances produces a sparse, noisy label matrix \(\mathbf{\Lambda} \in \{-1, 0, +1\}^{N \times M}\). Simple majority voting across active LFs fails because labeling functions have unknown and widely varying accuracies, exhibit correlated errors (e.g., two regex LFs sharing common keywords), and have varying coverage (Ratner et al., 2016; Ratner et al., 2019).

The central mathematical breakthrough of modern weak supervision is the Generative Label Model: an unsupervised probabilistic factor graph that learns the true underlying accuracies \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) of each labeling function without requiring a single ground truth label, by observing cross-LF agreements and co-occurrences (Ratner et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2020). Fast covariance parameter estimation models such as FlyingSquid enable closed-form algebraic solutions over millions of samples in seconds (Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021).
