Modern dataset versioning platforms—including Data Version Control (DVC) (Pacheco et al., 2024), LakeFS (Einziger et al., 2021), and Delta Lake (Armbrust et al., 2020)—enforce four core architectural primitives: 1. Content-Addressable Storage (CAS): Payloads are identified exclusively by their cryptographic hash digest, guaranteeing universal immutability and automatic deduplication. 2. Merkle DAG Directory Trees: Snapshots are represented as hierarchical trees of hashes, enabling sub-tree reuse and logarithmic diffing. 3. Zero-Copy Branching: Development branches are isolated metadata namespaces pointing to immutable storage objects, requiring zero data duplication. 4. Content-Defined Chunking (CDC): Large continuous binary files are partitioned into variable-length chunks via rolling hashes, preserving deduplication across byte-shift mutations (Rabin, 1981; Xia et al., 2016).

docs.title: Definition 12.6.1: Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) & Cryptographic Collision Resistance
docs.text:
In Content-Addressable Storage (CAS), an arbitrary immutable data payload \(B \in \{0, 1\}^*\) is addressed strictly by its cryptographic digest \(h\) computed via a collision-resistant hash function \(\mathcal{H}: \{0, 1\}^* \to \{0, 1\}^b\) (such as SHA-256, where \(b = 256\) bits) (Merkle, 1987):

\[ h = \mathcal{H}(B) = \text{SHA-256}(B) \]

The storage layer enforces the Universal Immutability Invariant: for any two files \(B_1\) and \(B_2\), their physical storage addresses are identical if and only if their binary contents are identical:

\[ \mathcal{H}(B_1) = \mathcal{H}(B_2) \iff B_1 = B_2 \]

docs.title: Cryptographic Collision Resistance Bound
docs.text:
By the generalized Birthday Paradox, if a distributed dataset storage pool ingests \(q\) distinct binary objects, the probability of encountering at least one hash collision is bounded by:

\[ \Pr[\text{Collision}] \le \frac{q(q - 1)}{2^{b + 1}} \approx \frac{q^2}{2^{b + 1}} \]

For SHA-256 (\(b = 256\)), storing \(q = 10^{15}\) (one quadrillion) distinct dataset files yields:

\[ \Pr[\text{Collision}] \le \frac{(10^{15})^2}{2^{257}} \approx \frac{10^{30}}{2.31 \times 10^{77}} \approx 4.3 \times 10^{-48} \]

This probability is vastly lower than the rate of uncorrectable cosmic-ray-induced memory bitflips, guaranteeing that content addresses function as globally unique, immutable object identifiers.

docs.title: Definition 12.6.2: Merkle DAG Directory Trees & Canonical Manifest Invariants
docs.text:
A dataset snapshot containing \(M\) files distributed across a directory hierarchy is represented as a Merkle Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) \(\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})\) (Merkle, 1987). Leaf nodes represent raw data blobs, while interior nodes represent directory manifests.

The cryptographic digest of an interior directory node \(N_v\) having child elements \(\{c_1, c_2, \dots, c_k\}\) is computed recursively as:

\[ \mathcal{H}(N_v) = \mathcal{H}\left( \text{metadata}(N_v) \mathbin{\Vert} \bigoplus_{i=1}^k \left( \text{name}(c_i) \mathbin{\Vert} \mathcal{H}(c_i) \mathbin{\Vert} \text{size}(c_i) \right) \right) \]

where \(\|\) denotes string concatenation and \(\oplus\) denotes deterministic canonical sort ordering by filename.

docs.title: Canonical Manifest Properties
docs.text:
1. Sub-Tree Structural Sharing: If revision \(V_{k+1}\) modifies only a single file \(f \in \text{Dir}_A\), all other directories \(\text{Dir}_B, \text{Dir}_C\) retain their exact Merkle sub-tree digests:
\[ \mathcal{H}(\text{Dir}_B^{(V_{k+1})}) = \mathcal{H}(\text{Dir}_B^{(V_k)}) \]
  1. Logarithmic Diffing Complexity: Comparing two complete dataset snapshots \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) containing \(M\) files does not require scanning all \(M\) files. Traversal immediately terminates along any branch where \(\mathcal{H}(N_v^{(V_1)}) = \mathcal{H}(N_v^{(V_2)})\), reducing diffing latency from \(\mathcal{O}(M)\) down to \(\mathcal{O}(\Delta \cdot \text{depth})\), where \(\Delta\) is the number of mutated files.

docs.title: Definition 12.6.3: Storage Deduplication Ratio & Incremental Mutation Dynamics
docs.text:
Consider a sequence of \(K\) historical dataset revisions \(V_1, V_2, \dots, V_K\). Let \(\mathcal{B}(V_k)\) denote the set of content-addressed blobs required to reconstruct revision \(V_k\), and let \(|b|\) denote the byte size of blob \(b\).

The Total Logical Size of the dataset across all \(K\) versions is:

\[ S_{\text{logical}} = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{b \in \mathcal{B}(V_k)} |b| \]

The Total Physical Size stored in the CAS repository is the size of the unique set union:

\[ S_{\text{physical}} = \sum_{b \in \bigcup_{k=1}^K \mathcal{B}(V_k)} |b| \]

The Global Deduplication Efficiency Ratio \(\rho_{\text{dedup}}\) is defined as:

\[ \rho_{\text{dedup}}(V_1, \dots, V_K) = 1 - \frac{S_{\text{physical}}}{S_{\text{logical}}} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{b \in \bigcup_{k=1}^K \mathcal{B}(V_k)} |b|}{\sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{b \in \mathcal{B}(V_k)} |b|} \]

docs.title: Asymptotic Convergence under Incremental Mutations
docs.text:
Assume each revision introduces a fraction \(\delta \in (0, 1)\) of newly generated or modified data, while fraction \((1 - \delta)\) remains identical to the base version of size \(|V|\):

\[ S_{\text{physical}}(K) = |V| + (K - 1) \cdot \delta \cdot |V| \] \[ S_{\text{logical}}(K) = K \cdot |V| \]

Taking the limit as the number of revisions \(K \to \infty\):

\[ \lim_{K \to \infty} \rho_{\text{dedup}} = \lim_{K \to \infty} \left( 1 - \frac{|V| + (K - 1)\delta |V|}{K |V|} \right) = 1 - \delta \]

When \(\delta = 0.05\) (\(5\%\) mutation rate between releases), the asymptotic storage savings approach \(95\%\), proving the immense cost efficiency of content-addressable versioning over naive physical bucket copies.

docs.title: Definition 12.6.4: Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) & Rolling Rabin Fingerprint Boundaries
docs.text:
Whole-file content hashing fails on large continuous binary files (e.g., SQLite databases, uncompressed TAR archives, monolithic embedding matrices): inserting a single byte at the beginning of a \(10\text{ GB}\) file alters its entire SHA-256 hash, causing the CAS repository to re-store the entire \(10\text{ GB}\) payload.

Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) partitions a byte stream \(B = [b_0, b_1, \dots, b_{L-1}]\) into variable-length blocks using a rolling polynomial hash (Rabin Fingerprint) evaluated over a sliding window of size \(w\) (Rabin, 1981; Xia et al., 2016):

\[ R_i = \left( \sum_{j=0}^{w-1} b_{i-j} \cdot p^j \right) \pmod M \]

where \(p\) is an irreducible polynomial and \(M\) is a large prime modulus.

docs.title: Chunk Boundary Invariant
docs.text:
A chunk boundary is cut at index \(i\) if and only if the rolling fingerprint satisfies a bitmask match:

\[ R_i \equiv 0 \pmod D \]

where \(D\) is the target average chunk divisor (e.g., \(D = 8\text{ KB}\) or \(64\text{ KB}\)).

docs.title: Expected Chunk Size & Boundary Re-synchronization
docs.text:
Assuming rolling hash values are uniformly distributed over \(\mathbb{Z}_M\), the probability of placing a boundary cut at any byte position is:

\[ \Pr[\text{Cut at position } i] = \frac{1}{D} \implies \mathbb{E}[\text{Chunk Size}] = D \]

If a byte insertion of size \(\Delta x\) occurs at offset \(k\), only the single chunk spanning \([k - w, k]\) changes its boundary. Beyond that chunk, as soon as the rolling window passes through unmodified bytes, the cut condition \(R_i \equiv 0 \pmod D\) fires again at the exact same semantic boundary. The expected re-synchronization distance is bounded by:

\[ \mathbb{E}[\text{Re-sync Distance}] \le 2D \text{ bytes} \]

All subsequent chunks downstream retain their original content hashes, preserving deduplication across the remainder of the multi-gigabyte file.

Industrial Best Practice: LakeFS Branching for Zero-Copy Data Environments

When data scientists require sandboxes to test destructive cleaning pipelines on 50 TB data lakes, use LakeFS: create a copy-on-write branch (lakefs branch create dev). It spins up an isolated sandbox in 50 milliseconds with zero storage duplication, allowing safe experimentation before merging back to main (Einziger et al., 2021).

Common Pitfall / Anti-Pattern: Manual Cloud Storage Duplication

Copying entire cloud storage directories (aws s3 sync s3://prod s3://dev_test) to create development testbeds wastes thousands of dollars in cloud egress and storage fees, and loses all cryptographic lineage connections to production versions.

ACID Lakehouse Logs: Delta Lake & Apache Iceberg

While DVC and LakeFS operate primarily on file and object levels, modern Lakehouse engines (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg) track tabular mutations at the Parquet file manifest level (Armbrust et al., 2020). Each commit appends an atomic JSON transaction log entry listing added and removed Parquet files, providing instantaneous time-travel queries (SELECT * FROM table VERSION AS OF 42) without mutating base data files.

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Content-Addressable Storage & Merkle DAG Engine
docs.text:
The following typed Python program implements a complete Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) engine using Pydantic V2. It demonstrates immutable blob storage, Merkle DAG directory manifests, Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) with boundary re-synchronization, and zero-copy branching.

"""
Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) and Merkle DAG Engine.
Demonstrates cryptographic hashing, Merkle directory manifests,
Content-Defined Chunking (CDC), and zero-copy branching with Pydantic V2.
"""

from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Tuple, Set
import hashlib
import json
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


# =====================================================================
# 1. Pydantic V2 Telemetry & Manifest Models
# =====================================================================

class BlobMetadata(BaseModel):
    """Metadata describing an immutable content-addressed data blob."""
    digest: str
    size_bytes: int
    content_type: str = "application/octet-stream"


class FileManifestEntry(BaseModel):
    """Describes a single file within a versioned dataset snapshot."""
    path: str
    blob_hash: str
    size_bytes: int


class MerkleManifest(BaseModel):
    """Hierarchical snapshot manifest representing a dataset revision."""
    version_tag: str
    merkle_root: str
    parent_version: Optional[str] = None
    files: List[FileManifestEntry]
    total_logical_bytes: int


class BranchDescriptor(BaseModel):
    """Tracks a zero-copy pointer to a Merkle commit in the control plane."""
    branch_name: str
    head_merkle_root: str
    created_at_version: str


# =====================================================================
# 2. Content-Addressable Storage & Merkle DAG Engine
# =====================================================================

class ContentAddressableStorageEngine:
    """
    Simulates a production-grade Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) engine
    with Merkle DAG directory manifests, zero-copy branching, and CDC chunking.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        # Physical Blob Store: hash -> raw bytes (Immutable Data Plane)
        self.blob_store: Dict[str, bytes] = {}
        # Control Plane Manifest Catalog: version_tag -> MerkleManifest
        self.catalog: Dict[str, MerkleManifest] = {}
        # Zero-Copy Branch Table: branch_name -> BranchDescriptor
        self.branches: Dict[str, BranchDescriptor] = {}

    @staticmethod
    def sha256(data: bytes) -> str:
        """Computes collision-resistant SHA-256 digest."""
        hasher = hashlib.sha256()
        hasher.update(data)
        return hasher.hexdigest()

    def put_blob(self, payload: bytes) -> str:
        """Stores a blob immutably by its content digest."""
        digest = self.sha256(payload)
        if digest not in self.blob_store:
            self.blob_store[digest] = payload
        return digest

    def get_blob(self, digest: str) -> Optional[bytes]:
        """Retrieves raw content by cryptographic hash address."""
        return self.blob_store.get(digest)

    def commit_version(
        self,
        version_tag: str,
        file_table: Dict[str, bytes],
        parent_tag: Optional[str] = None
    ) -> MerkleManifest:
        """
        Creates a Merkle DAG directory snapshot for a collection of files.
        Stores immutable data blobs and computes the canonical Merkle root digest.
        """
        entries: List[FileManifestEntry] = []
        for path in sorted(file_table.keys()):
            raw_bytes = file_table[path]
            blob_hash = self.put_blob(raw_bytes)
            entries.append(FileManifestEntry(
                path=path,
                blob_hash=blob_hash,
                size_bytes=len(raw_bytes)
            ))

        # Compute deterministic canonical Merkle root hash
        canonical_repr = [
            {"path": e.path, "hash": e.blob_hash, "size": e.size_bytes}
            for e in entries
        ]
        manifest_bytes = json.dumps(canonical_repr, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")
        merkle_root = self.sha256(manifest_bytes)

        manifest = MerkleManifest(
            version_tag=version_tag,
            merkle_root=merkle_root,
            parent_version=parent_tag,
            files=entries,
            total_logical_bytes=sum(e.size_bytes for e in entries)
        )
        self.catalog[version_tag] = manifest
        return manifest

    def create_branch(self, branch_name: str, from_version: str) -> BranchDescriptor:
        """
        Creates an instantaneous zero-copy branch pointing to an existing Merkle root.
        Consumes 0 bytes of physical storage.
        """
        if from_version not in self.catalog:
            raise KeyError(f"Base version '{from_version}' does not exist in catalog")
        manifest = self.catalog[from_version]
        desc = BranchDescriptor(
            branch_name=branch_name,
            head_merkle_root=manifest.merkle_root,
            created_at_version=from_version
        )
        self.branches[branch_name] = desc
        return desc

    def content_defined_chunking(self, data: bytes, target_chunk_size: int = 32) -> List[bytes]:
        """
        Implements Rabin-like Content-Defined Chunking (CDC).
        Evaluates a rolling hash window; cuts boundary when hash % target_chunk_size == 0.
        """
        chunks: List[bytes] = []
        window_size = 16
        start = 0

        p = 31
        mod = 1000000007

        rolling_hash = 0
        p_pow = 1
        for _ in range(window_size - 1):
            p_pow = (p_pow * p) % mod

        for i in range(len(data)):
            byte_val = data[i]
            rolling_hash = (rolling_hash * p + byte_val) % mod

            if i >= window_size:
                old_val = data[i - window_size]
                rolling_hash = (rolling_hash - (old_val * p_pow) % mod + mod) % mod

            # Boundary cut condition with min/max chunk size bounds
            if (rolling_hash % target_chunk_size == 0 and (i - start) >= 16) or (i - start) >= 256:
                chunks.append(data[start:i + 1])
                start = i + 1

        if start < len(data):
            chunks.append(data[start:])
        return chunks

    def calculate_deduplication_ratio(self) -> float:
        """Calculates global deduplication savings: 1 - (Physical Bytes / Logical Bytes)."""
        total_logical_bytes = sum(m.total_logical_bytes for m in self.catalog.values())
        physical_unique_bytes = sum(len(b) for b in self.blob_store.values())
        if total_logical_bytes == 0:
            return 0.0
        return 1.0 - (physical_unique_bytes / total_logical_bytes)


# =====================================================================
# 3. Verification and Assertion Suite
# =====================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=" * 70)
    print("CONTENT-ADDRESSABLE STORAGE & MERKLE DAG ENGINE: RUNTIME VERIFICATION")
    print("=" * 70)

    engine = ContentAddressableStorageEngine()

    # 1. Commit Version 1.0.0: 3 synthetic data partitions (~6.8 MB total)
    p_train = b"TRAIN_TENSORS_NUMERICAL_DATA_BATCH_001_CHUNK_ALPHA" * 50000
    p_labels = b"GROUND_TRUTH_LABELS_ANNOTATION_CLASS_IDS_V1" * 50000
    p_embeds = b"LATENT_EMBEDDING_VECTORS_FLOAT32_SPACE_REPR" * 50000

    v1_files = {
        "data/features.bin": p_train,
        "data/labels.bin": p_labels,
        "data/embeddings.bin": p_embeds
    }
    m1 = engine.commit_version("v1.0.0", v1_files)
    print(f"Committed v1.0.0 | Merkle Root: {m1.merkle_root[:16]}... | Logical: {m1.total_logical_bytes:,} bytes")

    # 2. Commit Version 2.0.0: Only labels are mutated (fine-grained label correction)
    p_labels_v2 = b"GROUND_TRUTH_LABELS_ANNOTATION_CLASS_IDS_V2_CORRECTED" * 50000
    v2_files = {
        "data/features.bin": p_train,   # Identical payload
        "data/labels.bin": p_labels_v2,  # Mutated payload
        "data/embeddings.bin": p_embeds  # Identical payload
    }
    m2 = engine.commit_version("v2.0.0", v2_files, parent_tag="v1.0.0")
    print(f"Committed v2.0.0 | Merkle Root: {m2.merkle_root[:16]}... | Logical: {m2.total_logical_bytes:,} bytes")

    # 3. Invariant Checks
    assert m1.merkle_root != m2.merkle_root, "Merkle roots must detect mutations!"
    assert len(engine.blob_store) == 4, f"Expected exactly 4 unique physical blobs, found {len(engine.blob_store)}"

    # Check shared blob hashes
    f1_map = {f.path: f.blob_hash for f in m1.files}
    f2_map = {f.path: f.blob_hash for f in m2.files}
    assert f1_map["data/features.bin"] == f2_map["data/features.bin"], "Unchanged file must share exact blob address"
    assert f1_map["data/embeddings.bin"] == f2_map["data/embeddings.bin"], "Unchanged file must share exact blob address"
    assert f1_map["data/labels.bin"] != f2_map["data/labels.bin"], "Mutated file must receive distinct blob address"

    # 4. Zero-Copy Branching Verification
    branch = engine.create_branch("feature/experimental-cleaning", from_version="v2.0.0")
    assert branch.head_merkle_root == m2.merkle_root, "Branch must instantaneously point to head Merkle root"
    print(f"Created Zero-Copy Branch '{branch.branch_name}' -> points to {branch.head_merkle_root[:16]}...")

    # 5. Deduplication Efficiency Calculation
    rho = engine.calculate_deduplication_ratio()
    print(f"Global Deduplication Ratio rho_dedup: {rho * 100:.2f}%")
    assert 0.30 <= rho <= 0.45, f"Expected 30-45% storage savings, got {rho:.2f}"

    # 6. Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) Boundary Re-synchronization Check
    base_stream = b"UNIFORM_DATA_PAYLOAD_TOKEN_ABCDEFGHIJ_1234567890_" * 50
    modified_stream = b"PREFIX_INSERTION_" + base_stream

    base_chunks = engine.content_defined_chunking(base_stream, target_chunk_size=32)
    mod_chunks = engine.content_defined_chunking(modified_stream, target_chunk_size=32)

    # Check that chunks re-synchronize after shift
    base_hashes = {engine.sha256(c) for c in base_chunks}
    mod_hashes = {engine.sha256(c) for c in mod_chunks}
    common_hashes = base_hashes.intersection(mod_hashes)
    assert len(common_hashes) > 0, "CDC must re-synchronize chunk boundaries after byte insertion!"
    print(f"CDC Verification: Re-synchronized {len(common_hashes)} identical chunk digests despite byte shift!")

    print("\n✓ ALL PRODUCTION ENGINE INVARIANTS VERIFIED!")

docs.title: 🔬 Interactive Laboratory Workbench (SIMULATOR 12.6)

docs.title: 1. The Multi-Modal Volume Dilemma
docs.text:
A single 20-second driving clip recorded across 5 LiDAR units and 5 high-resolution cameras consumes \(2.4\text{ GB}\) of raw binary payloads. A 1,000-hour multi-sensor training corpus exceeds \(430\text{ Terabytes}\).

Computer vision annotation teams continuously refine labels: fixing 3D bounding box dimensions, annotating occluded pedestrians, or adding HD vector map lane topologies. While the raw sensory tensors remain 100% immutable, each annotation sprint generates a new dataset release. Under naive bucket duplication (aws s3 sync s3://v1 s3://v2), creating 200 benchmark iterations would require \(200 \times 430\text{ TB} = 86\text{ Petabytes}\) of duplicate cloud storage, costing over USD 1.9 million per year in AWS S3 Standard storage fees.

docs.title: 2. The Content-Addressable Storage Resolution
docs.text: The engineering team deployed Data Version Control (DVC) (Pacheco et al., 2024) backed by S3 Content-Addressable Storage: - Decoupled Control and Data Planes: The \(430\text{ TB}\) of raw sensor binaries were ingested once into S3 CAS, addressed by SHA-256 digests. - Micro-Manifest Versioning: Each new annotation release committed only a 5 MB JSON file containing bounding box coordinates and content hashes linking back to the immutable sensor frames. - Fast Local Checkouts: GPU training nodes utilized DVC hardlinks (dvc config cache.type hardlink), enabling workers to switch between 100 GB training splits in under 2 seconds without duplicating local NVMe disk blocks.

docs.title: 3. Quantitative Results & Cost Reductions
docs.text:
• Deduplication Efficiency: Reached a \(99.8\%\) storage deduplication ratio across 200 distinct experimental benchmark releases.
  • Annual Cloud Savings: Eliminated over USD 480,000 per year in redundant cloud object storage and data transfer fees.
Architectural Dimension Naive S3 Bucket Sync DVC Content-Addressable Storage Physical Storage (200 Versions) \(86\text{ Petabytes}\) (linear duplication) \(431\text{ Terabytes}\) (\(99.8\%\) deduplication) Version Creation Time \(8 - 14\text{ hours}\) (network copy) \(< 2\text{ seconds}\) (metadata commit) Workspace Checkout Latency \(45\text{ minutes}\) (full network download) \(< 2\text{ seconds}\) (local OS hardlinks) Data-to-Code Lineage Broken manual spreadsheets Deterministic Git commit cryptographic hash

docs.title: 1. The Production Data Validation Hazard
docs.text: Validating complex SQL transformations, schema migrations, and deduplication logic on toy datasets rarely uncovers edge-case bugs. However, testing directly on production data lakes risks corrupting active analytics tables. Traditionally, organizations created staging environments by cloning production buckets—a process requiring \(6+\) hours to copy \(500\text{ TB}\) of data, costing thousands of dollars in egress and storage.

docs.title: 2. The LakeFS Zero-Copy Branching Architecture
docs.text: By deploying LakeFS (Einziger et al., 2021) on top of S3 object storage: - Graveler SSTable Metadata Trees: LakeFS manages file manifests using immutable, sorted-string table (SSTable) key-value trees. A branch is simply an isolated pointer to a root metadata commit. - Copy-on-Write Isolation: Creating a branch (lakefs branch create dev) takes 42 milliseconds and duplicates zero bytes of S3 data. Data engineers execute destructive ETL pipelines on dev. Any modified files are written as new objects in S3; unchanged files continue referencing the shared production blobs. - Atomic Pre-Commit Hooks & Merges: Automated data quality checks run on the branch. If validation tests pass, merging dev into main is an atomic metadata operation taking under 1 second, guaranteeing zero downtime or dirty reads for downstream consumers.

docs.title: 3. Quantitative Operational Impact
docs.text:
• Environment Provisioning Time: Dropped from \(6\text{ hours}\) down to \(42\text{ milliseconds}\).
  • Staging Infrastructure Cost: Reduced physical staging storage duplication costs from \(\$11,500\text{/month}\) to \(\$0\).
System Metric Traditional S3 Bucket Staging LakeFS Zero-Copy Metadata Branching Branch Creation Duration \(6\text{ hours}\) (bulk 500 TB transfer) \(42\text{ milliseconds}\) (metadata pointer) Duplicate Storage Overhead \(500\text{ TB}\) duplicate storage \(0\text{ bytes}\) (Copy-on-Write diffs only) Merge Atomicity Non-atomic (partial overwrite risk) Atomic commit update (\(< 1\text{ second}\)) Rollback Capability Disaster recovery restore (\(12+\text{ hrs}\)) Instant rollback (lakefs revert HEAD)

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment 1: Asymptotic Deduplication Ratio across Iterative Releases

A deep learning dataset of base size \(|V| = 200\text{ GB}\) undergoes iterative weekly revisions. Each revision modifies or introduces exactly fraction \(\delta = 0.08\) (\(8\%\)) of new content, while the remaining \(92\%\) is identical to previous versions.

  1. Calculate the exact physical storage required in Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) after \(K = 10\) and \(K = 50\) releases, compared to a naive bucket copy approach.
  2. Determine the deduplication ratio \(\rho_{\text{dedup}}\) for \(K = 10\) and \(K = 50\).
  3. State the asymptotic deduplication efficiency as \(K \to \infty\).
Reveal Detailed Solution

Step 1: Compute Storage Volumes (Definition 12.6.3) - Base size: \(|V| = 200\text{ GB}\) - Mutation rate: \(\delta = 0.08\)

Naive Bucket Copy: $\(S_{\text{naive}}(K) = K \cdot |V|\)$ - For \(K = 10\): \(S_{\text{naive}}(10) = 10 \times 200\text{ GB} = 2,000\text{ GB} = 2.0\text{ TB}\). - For \(K = 50\): \(S_{\text{naive}}(50) = 50 \times 200\text{ GB} = 10,000\text{ GB} = 10.0\text{ TB}\).

CAS Content-Addressable Storage: $\(S_{\text{physical}}(K) = |V| + (K - 1) \cdot \delta \cdot |V| = |V| \cdot [1 + (K - 1)\delta]\)$ - For \(K = 10\): $\(S_{\text{physical}}(10) = 200 \times [1 + (10 - 1) \times 0.08] = 200 \times [1 + 0.72] = 200 \times 1.72 = 344\text{ GB}\)$ - For \(K = 50\): $\(S_{\text{physical}}(50) = 200 \times [1 + (50 - 1) \times 0.08] = 200 \times [1 + 3.92] = 200 \times 4.92 = 984\text{ GB} \approx 0.984\text{ TB}\)$

Step 2: Calculate Deduplication Efficiency \(\rho_{\text{dedup}}\) $\(\rho_{\text{dedup}}(K) = 1 - \frac{S_{\text{physical}}(K)}{S_{\text{naive}}(K)}\)$ - For \(K = 10\): $\(\rho_{\text{dedup}}(10) = 1 - \frac{344\text{ GB}}{2,000\text{ GB}} = 1 - 0.172 = 0.828 = 82.8\%\)$ - For \(K = 50\): $\(\rho_{\text{dedup}}(50) = 1 - \frac{984\text{ GB}}{10,000\text{ GB}} = 1 - 0.0984 = 0.9016 = 90.16\%\)$

Step 3: Asymptotic Efficiency $\(\lim_{K \to \infty} \rho_{\text{dedup}} = 1 - \delta = 1 - 0.08 = 0.920 = 92.0\%\)$ Conclusion: Under CAS, physical storage grows linearly at only \(16\text{ GB/week}\) instead of \(200\text{ GB/week}\). After 50 weeks, CAS saves over \(9\text{ TB}\) (\(90.16\%\)) of cloud storage.

Self-Assessment 2: Content-Defined Chunking Boundary Re-synchronization Distance

A \(5\text{ GB}\) binary matrix file is partitioned using Content-Defined Chunking with target average chunk size \(D = 64\text{ KB} = 65,536\text{ bytes}\) and sliding window \(w = 48\text{ bytes}\).

A developer inserts a \(100\text{ byte}\) metadata header at offset 0 of the file.

  1. Explain why fixed-size chunking (\(64\text{ KB}\) fixed intervals) suffers \(0\%\) deduplication across the entire remaining \(5\text{ GB}\) file.
  2. Under Rabin Content-Defined Chunking, what is the probability that chunk boundaries re-synchronize within a distance of \(X = 3D = 192\text{ KB}\) from the insertion point?
Reveal Detailed Solution

Step 1: Fixed-Size Chunking Failure Analysis In fixed-size chunking, chunk boundaries occur at rigid byte offsets: \(0, 65536, 131072, \dots\).

Inserting 100 bytes at byte 0 shifts every single subsequent byte in the file by +100 bytes: $\(\text{Chunk } 1 \to [100, 65635], \quad \text{Chunk } 2 \to [65636, 131171], \dots\)$ Because cryptographic hashes (SHA-256) exhibit the avalanche effect, shifting inputs by 100 bytes changes 100% of the chunk boundary contents. Consequently, every single chunk hash across the entire 5 GB file changes, resulting in \(0\%\) deduplication and re-uploading all 5 GB.

Step 2: CDC Boundary Re-synchronization Probability (Definition 12.6.4) In Rabin CDC, cut boundaries are content-dependent, occurring whenever the rolling hash satisfies \(R_i \equiv 0 \pmod D\).

Once the sliding window moves past the 100-byte insertion (at offset \(100 + w = 148\)), the byte sequence seen by the rolling window is identical to the original un-shifted file.

At each byte position \(i \ge 148\), the probability of firing a boundary cut is \(p = \frac{1}{D}\). The probability of NOT firing a boundary cut in a span of \(k\) bytes is: $\(\Pr[\text{No cut in } k \text{ bytes}] = \left(1 - \frac{1}{D}\right)^k\)$ For \(k = 3D = 3 \times 65,536 = 196,608\text{ bytes}\), using the exponential approximation \((1 - 1/D)^D \approx e^{-1}\): $\(\Pr[\text{No cut in } 3D \text{ bytes}] \approx e^{-3} \approx 0.0498 = 4.98\%\)$

Therefore, the probability that at least one boundary cut occurs (re-synchronizing the stream) within \(3D\) bytes is: $\(\Pr[\text{Re-sync within } 3D] = 1 - e^{-3} \approx 1 - 0.0498 = 0.9502 = 95.02\%\)$

Conclusion: With over \(95\%\) probability, the stream re-aligns within \(192\text{ KB}\). Only the first chunk is modified; the remaining \(4.9998\text{ GB}\) (\(> 99.99\%\)) of chunks retain identical cryptographic hashes and are deduplicated with zero network transfer.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & Theoretical Foundations
docs.text:
While dataset versioning provides indispensable guarantees for model provenance, auditability, and experimentation reproducibility (Sculley et al., 2015), real-world production deployments confront severe engineering and regulatory headwinds. High-velocity streaming ingestion—frequently buffered by distributed logs like Apache Kafka (Wang et al., 2015) and processed via distributed analytics frameworks like Apache Spark (Zaharia et al., 2016)—creates millions of discrete micro-batch files. This phenomenon, known as the small-file problem, cripples analytical query engines, degrades distributed filesystems (Shvachko et al., 2010), and inflates cloud object storage API transaction costs (Armbrust et al., 2020).

Simultaneously, privacy and compliance frameworks—most notably the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Article 17 ("Right to be Forgotten"), the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), and HIPAA de-identification rules (Villaronga et al., 2018; Politou et al., 2018)—directly contradict the immutable append-only foundation of Content-Addressable Storage (CAS). When an individual exercises their legal right to data erasure, purging their records from historical, cryptographically signed dataset releases imposes catastrophic write amplification and storage rewriting overhead (Hermann & Balso, 2017).

To balance these conflicting demands, modern data lakehouse architectures decouple logical row deletions from physical data rewrites via Deletion Vectors, consolidate streaming micro-batches through Bin-Packing Compaction, and apply Automated Retention Lifecycle Tiers to prune unreferenced orphan snapshots.

docs.title: Definition 12.7.1: Small-File Query Latency Degradation & HTTP Overhead
docs.text:
Let an analytical dataset of total data volume \(V\) be partitioned across \(N\) distinct physical objects \(\{f_1, f_2, \dots, f_N\}\) stored in a cloud object store (e.g., AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage). Accessing any individual object over HTTPS imposes a fixed network round-trip handshake and metadata resolution latency \(t_{\text{req}} \in [15\text{ ms}, 40\text{ ms}]\) (Armbrust et al., 2020).

Given an aggregate client-to-storage network streaming bandwidth \(B_{\text{stream}}\), the total query scan duration \(T_{\text{scan}}\) across \(N\) files is:

\[ T_{\text{scan}} = \sum_{i=1}^N \left( t_{\text{req}} + \frac{S_i}{B_{\text{stream}}} \right) = N \cdot t_{\text{req}} + \frac{V}{B_{\text{stream}}} \]

where \(S_i\) is the byte size of file \(i\), and \(V = \sum_{i=1}^N S_i\).

docs.title: Overhead Ratio & Asymptotic Collapse
docs.text:
Let \(\bar{S} = V / N\) denote the average file size. The fraction of total query wall-clock time consumed purely by HTTP handshake and metadata overhead \(\Phi_{\text{overhead}}\) is:

\[ \Phi_{\text{overhead}} = \frac{N \cdot t_{\text{req}}}{N \cdot t_{\text{req}} + \frac{V}{B_{\text{stream}}}} = \frac{t_{\text{req}}}{t_{\text{req}} + \frac{\bar{S}}{B_{\text{stream}}}} \]

As the streaming ingestion frequency increases and file size shrinks (\(\bar{S} \to 0\)):

\[ \lim_{\bar{S} \to 0} \Phi_{\text{overhead}} = 1.0 \quad (100\% \text{ latency spent on connection handshakes}) \]

For example, scanning \(V = 100\text{ GB}\) stored as \(N = 100,000\) micro-files of \(1\text{ MB}\) each with \(t_{\text{req}} = 25\text{ ms}\) and \(B_{\text{stream}} = 1\text{ GB/s}\) yields: - Pure data transfer time: \(100\text{ GB} / 1\text{ GB/s} = 100\text{ seconds}\). - Connection overhead time: \(100,000 \times 0.025\text{ s} = 2,500\text{ seconds } (\approx 41.6\text{ minutes})\). - Overhead ratio: \(\Phi_{\text{overhead}} = 2500 / 2600 \approx 96.15\%\).

docs.title: Definition 12.7.2: Bin-Packing Compaction Speedup & Optimal Target Sizing
docs.text:
Bin-packing compaction coalesces \(N_{\text{small}}\) fragmented micro-files into \(M = \lceil V / S_{\text{target}} \rceil\) consolidated columnar segments, where \(S_{\text{target}} \gg \bar{S}\).

The theoretical query scan acceleration factor \(\mathcal{S}_{\text{compaction}}\) achieved by compaction is:

\[ \mathcal{S}_{\text{compaction}} = \frac{T_{\text{scan, uncompacted}}}{T_{\text{scan, compacted}}} = \frac{N_{\text{small}} \cdot t_{\text{req}} + \frac{V}{B_{\text{stream}}}}{\left\lceil \frac{V}{S_{\text{target}}} \right\rceil \cdot t_{\text{req}} + \frac{V}{B_{\text{stream}}}} \]

docs.title: Optimal Target Segment Sizing (\(S_{\text{target}}^*\))
docs.text:
The choice of \(S_{\text{target}}\) represents a fundamental trade-off: 1. Lower Bound (\(S_{\text{target}} \ge 128\text{ MB}\)): Large enough to amortize \(t_{\text{req}}\) to \(< 1\%\) of total scan time and maximize Parquet row-group dictionary encoding and vectorized SIMD decoding (Armbrust et al., 2020). 2. Upper Bound (\(S_{\text{target}} \le 512\text{ MB} - 1\text{ GB}\)): Small enough to allow granular predicate pushdown pruning (skipping entire blocks via min/max zone maps) and fit within single-core CPU executor memory without triggering garbage collection thrashing.

Consolidating \(100,000\) micro-files (\(100\text{ GB}\)) into \(M = 400\) blocks of \(S_{\text{target}} = 256\text{ MB}\) slashes connection overhead from \(2,500\text{ s}\) down to \(10\text{ s}\), delivering an empirical end-to-end speedup of:

\[ \mathcal{S}_{\text{compaction}} = \frac{2500 + 100}{10 + 100} = \frac{2600}{110} \approx 23.64\times \]

docs.title: Definition 12.7.3: Object Storage API Cost Explosion Model
docs.text:
Cloud object storage financial pricing models charge independently for raw persistent byte volume and transactional HTTP request verbs: - \(C_{\text{storage}}\): Cost per gigabyte-month (e.g., \(\text{USD } 0.023 / \text{GB-month}\) for AWS S3 Standard). - \(C_{\text{PUT}}\): Cost per write transaction (e.g., \(\text{USD } 0.005 / 1,000 \text{ requests} = \text{USD } 5 \times 10^{-6} / \text{req}\)). - \(C_{\text{GET}}\): Cost per read transaction (e.g., \(\text{USD } 0.0004 / 1,000 \text{ requests} = \text{USD } 4 \times 10^{-7} / \text{req}\)).

Let an ingestion pipeline ingest total volume \(\lambda_{\text{ingest}}\) GB per month divided into micro-files of size \(S_{\text{micro}}\) MB. Let the dataset be queried \(Q\) times per month, where each query executes a full-dataset scan across all \(N\) files. The total monthly cloud storage bill \(C_{\text{monthly}}\) is:

\[ C_{\text{monthly}} = C_{\text{storage}} \cdot V + C_{\text{PUT}} \cdot \left( \frac{\lambda_{\text{ingest}} \times 1024}{S_{\text{micro}}} \right) + C_{\text{GET}} \cdot \left( Q \cdot \frac{V \times 1024}{S_{\text{micro}}} \right) \]

docs.title: The Transaction Cost Inflection Point
docs.text:
Transactional request fees surpass static byte storage costs when:

\[ C_{\text{PUT}} \cdot \left( \frac{\lambda_{\text{ingest}} \times 1024}{S_{\text{micro}}} \right) + C_{\text{GET}} \cdot \left( Q \cdot \frac{V \times 1024}{S_{\text{micro}}} \right) > C_{\text{storage}} \cdot V \]

When file sizes shrink below \(100\text{ KB}\) (\(S_{\text{micro}} < 0.1\text{ MB}\)), transactional HTTP GET and PUT request charges routinely exceed static byte storage expenses by over \(300\%\) (Hermann & Balso, 2017).

docs.title: Definition 12.7.4: Compliance Erasure Write Amplification & Deletion Vector Amortization
docs.text: Under data privacy regulations such as GDPR Article 17 ("Right to Erasure") and CCPA, a data subject may demand the immediate, verifiable excision of their records \(R_{\text{target}}\) from an organization's dataset archives (Villaronga et al., 2018; Politou et al., 2018).

docs.title: Synchronous File Rewrite Amplification
docs.text:
Because cloud object storage files and Content-Addressable Storage blobs are strictly immutable, in-place deletion is impossible. In a naive versioning architecture, purging a single record of size \(S_{\text{record}}\) requires reading the entire containing file of size \(S_{\text{file}}\), filtering out the record in memory, and re-serializing a new physical file version. The immediate Erasure Write Amplification Factor \(\Omega_{\text{GDPR}}\) is:

\[ \Omega_{\text{GDPR}} = \frac{S_{\text{file}}}{S_{\text{record}}} \]

For a \(500\text{-byte}\) user record residing in a \(256\text{ MB}\) Parquet block:

\[ \Omega_{\text{GDPR}} = \frac{256 \times 1024 \times 1024\text{ bytes}}{500\text{ bytes}} \approx 536,871\times \]

Rewriting \(256\text{ MB}\) of data across cloud storage to purge \(500\text{ bytes}\) is computationally unsustainable when processing thousands of user revocation notices monthly.

docs.title: Deletion Vector Bitmap Amortization
docs.text:
Modern Lakehouse formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg) decouple logical deletion from physical file rewriting through Deletion Vectors (Armbrust et al., 2020). An erasure request writes a compressed Roaring Bitmap entry \(\mathbf{b}_{\text{del}}\) of size \(S_{\text{bitmap}} \approx 64\text{ bytes}\) to the transaction log, masking row offset \(i\):

\[ \Omega_{\text{bitmap}} = \frac{S_{\text{bitmap}}}{S_{\text{record}}} = \frac{64\text{ bytes}}{500\text{ bytes}} = 0.128 \ll 1.0 \]

Analytical query engines apply the bitmap as an in-memory bitmask during vectorized Parquet scanning. Physical file rewrites are deferred to scheduled bi-monthly compaction maintenance windows, amortizing the write amplification across all accumulated batch mutations:

\[ \bar{\Omega}_{\text{amortized}} = 1 + \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{K_{\text{del}}} S_{\text{record}}^{(j)}}{S_{\text{file}}} \approx 1.05 - 1.15\times \]

Industrial Best Practice: Automated Garbage Collection and Retention Tiers

In high-velocity machine learning teams, automated pipelines spawn hundreds of experimental snapshots weekly. Establish automated Lifecycle Garbage Collection (GC) policies: prune unreferenced intermediate staging commits older than 14 days, while permanently locking signed, production-tagged benchmark releases (v1.0-gold) (Sculley et al., 2015).

Common Pitfall / Anti-Pattern: Incomplete Artifact Pinning in Reproducibility Claims

Claiming a model is reproducible by committing model weights and training code to Git while leaving the training dataset un-pinned is invalid. If upstream data lakes undergo partition compaction, row deletion, or late-arriving streaming insertions, re-running the training pipeline will produce divergent model weights.

Cryptographic Shredding for Historical Immutable Backups

When data subject records reside in historical, immutable, write-once-read-many (WORM) compliant archives, physical rewriting is mathematically or legally prohibited. Organizations implement Cryptographic Shredding: each user's sensitive features are encrypted with an individual Data Encryption Key (DEK). To comply with erasure requests, the organization permanently destroys the user's specific DEK, rendering their historical data ciphertext irreversibly unrecoverable (Villaronga et al., 2018).

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Dataset Compactor & Compliance Engine
docs.text:
The following typed Python program implements a production-grade Dataset Compaction & Compliance Erasure Engine using Pydantic V2. It demonstrates streaming micro-batch ingestion, bin-packing compaction, query scan latency benchmarking, AWS S3 financial cost modeling, and GDPR tombstone deletion vectors.

"""
Dataset Compaction & Compliance Erasure Engine.
Demonstrates small-file bin-packing, query latency modeling, S3 transaction cost analysis,
and GDPR deletion vector tombstones with Pydantic V2.
"""

from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Tuple, Any
import math
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


# =====================================================================
# 1. Pydantic V2 Telemetry & Cost Models
# =====================================================================

class MicrobatchFile(BaseModel):
    """Represents an uncompacted micro-batch file in cloud object storage."""
    file_id: str
    size_mb: float
    row_count: int


class CompactedBlock(BaseModel):
    """Represents a consolidated, bin-packed columnar Parquet segment."""
    block_id: str
    size_mb: float
    row_count: int
    constituent_file_count: int


class TombstoneRecord(BaseModel):
    """Represents a soft-deletion tombstone vector entry for compliance erasure."""
    record_uuid: str
    block_id: str
    row_index: int
    is_purged_physically: bool = False


class S3CostReport(BaseModel):
    """Monthly cloud object storage financial cost model breakdown."""
    total_volume_gb: float
    storage_cost_usd: float
    put_request_cost_usd: float
    get_request_cost_usd: float
    total_monthly_usd: float
    api_to_storage_ratio: float


# =====================================================================
# 2. Core Compaction & Compliance Engine Implementation
# =====================================================================

class DatasetCompactionAndComplianceEngine:
    """
    Simulates production Lakehouse file compaction (Delta/Iceberg bin-packing),
    query scan latency models, S3 transaction cost models, and GDPR tombstone vectors.
    """

    def __init__(self, t_req_sec: float = 0.025, network_gb_sec: float = 1.0):
        self.t_req = t_req_sec  # 25 ms per S3 GET metadata & handshake
        self.network_bandwidth = network_gb_sec  # 1.0 GB/s network throughput
        self.uncompacted_files: List[MicrobatchFile] = []
        self.compacted_blocks: List[CompactedBlock] = []
        self.tombstone_registry: Dict[str, TombstoneRecord] = {}

    def load_streaming_microbatches(self, count: int, size_mb: float, rows_per_file: int = 1000):
        """Simulates ingestion of high-frequency streaming micro-batch files."""
        self.uncompacted_files = [
            MicrobatchFile(
                file_id=f"part_{i:06d}.parquet",
                size_mb=size_mb,
                row_count=rows_per_file
            )
            for i in range(count)
        ]

    def calculate_scan_latency(self, use_compacted: bool = False) -> float:
        """
        Calculates total query scan duration:
        T_scan = N * t_req + V / B_stream
        """
        if use_compacted:
            num_files = len(self.compacted_blocks)
            total_vol_mb = sum(b.size_mb for b in self.compacted_blocks)
        else:
            num_files = len(self.uncompacted_files)
            total_vol_mb = sum(f.size_mb for f in self.uncompacted_files)

        total_vol_gb = total_vol_mb / 1024.0
        transfer_time = total_vol_gb / self.network_bandwidth
        overhead_time = num_files * self.t_req
        return overhead_time + transfer_time

    def compact_files(self, target_size_mb: float = 256.0) -> List[CompactedBlock]:
        """
        Bin-packs small micro-batch files into target-sized consolidated columnar blocks.
        """
        total_vol_mb = sum(f.size_mb for f in self.uncompacted_files)
        total_rows = sum(f.row_count for f in self.uncompacted_files)
        num_blocks = math.ceil(total_vol_mb / target_size_mb)

        self.compacted_blocks = []
        files_per_block = math.ceil(len(self.uncompacted_files) / max(1, num_blocks))

        for b_idx in range(num_blocks):
            allocated_mb = min(target_size_mb, total_vol_mb - (b_idx * target_size_mb))
            block_rows = min(total_rows // num_blocks, total_rows)
            self.compacted_blocks.append(CompactedBlock(
                block_id=f"compacted_seg_{b_idx:04d}.parquet",
                size_mb=allocated_mb,
                row_count=block_rows,
                constituent_file_count=files_per_block
            ))
        return self.compacted_blocks

    def calculate_monthly_s3_cost(
        self,
        daily_queries: int = 100,
        monthly_ingest_gb: float = 500.0,
        is_compacted: bool = False
    ) -> S3CostReport:
        """
        Models AWS S3 Standard pricing:
        - Storage: USD 0.023 / GB-month
        - PUT requests: USD 0.005 / 1,000 requests (USD 5e-6 / req)
        - GET requests: USD 0.0004 / 1,000 requests (USD 4e-7 / req)
        """
        c_storage_unit = 0.023
        c_put_unit = 0.000005
        c_get_unit = 0.0000004

        if is_compacted and self.compacted_blocks:
            file_count = len(self.compacted_blocks)
        else:
            file_count = max(1, len(self.uncompacted_files))

        total_gb = monthly_ingest_gb
        storage_cost = total_gb * c_storage_unit
        # Each ingested micro-file incurred 1 PUT
        put_cost = len(self.uncompacted_files) * c_put_unit
        # Each query scans all files in the partition
        monthly_gets = daily_queries * 30 * file_count
        get_cost = monthly_gets * c_get_unit

        total_monthly = storage_cost + put_cost + get_cost
        api_ratio = (put_cost + get_cost) / max(0.001, storage_cost)

        return S3CostReport(
            total_volume_gb=round(total_gb, 2),
            storage_cost_usd=round(storage_cost, 2),
            put_request_cost_usd=round(put_cost, 2),
            get_request_cost_usd=round(get_cost, 2),
            total_monthly_usd=round(total_monthly, 2),
            api_to_storage_ratio=round(api_ratio, 2)
        )

    def execute_compliance_erasure(
        self,
        record_uuid: str,
        target_block_id: str,
        row_offset: int,
        use_deletion_vector: bool = True
    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """
        Compares synchronous physical rewriting vs. Delta Lake deletion vector tombstones.
        """
        block_bytes = 256 * 1024 * 1024  # 256 MB Parquet block
        record_bytes = 500               # 500 bytes user record

        if use_deletion_vector:
            # Soft delete: append 64-byte Roaring Bitmap entry to transaction log
            tombstone = TombstoneRecord(
                record_uuid=record_uuid,
                block_id=target_block_id,
                row_index=row_offset,
                is_purged_physically=False
            )
            self.tombstone_registry[record_uuid] = tombstone
            bytes_written = 64
            write_amplification = bytes_written / record_bytes
            latency_ms = 1.2
            method = "Deletion Vector Bitmap (Deferred)"
        else:
            # Synchronous rewrite: must re-write the entire 256 MB file to delete 500 bytes
            bytes_written = block_bytes
            write_amplification = block_bytes / record_bytes
            latency_ms = 4500.0
            method = "Synchronous File Rewrite (Naive)"

        return {
            "record_uuid": record_uuid,
            "method": method,
            "bytes_written": bytes_written,
            "write_amplification": round(write_amplification, 2),
            "latency_ms": latency_ms
        }


# =====================================================================
# 3. Verification & Assertion Suite
# =====================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=" * 70)
    print("DATASET COMPACTION & COMPLIANCE ENGINE: VERIFICATION RUN")
    print("=" * 70)

    engine = DatasetCompactionAndComplianceEngine(t_req_sec=0.025, network_gb_sec=1.0)

    # 1. Ingest 10,000 small streaming files of 1 MB each (Total Volume = 10,000 MB = ~9.76 GB)
    engine.load_streaming_microbatches(count=10000, size_mb=1.0)
    uncompacted_latency = engine.calculate_scan_latency(use_compacted=False)
    print(f"Uncompacted Scan Latency (10,000 files): {uncompacted_latency:.2f} seconds")
    assert 255.0 <= uncompacted_latency <= 265.0, "Uncompacted scan latency calculation mismatch"

    # 2. Compact files into 256 MB segments
    compacted_blocks = engine.compact_files(target_size_mb=256.0)
    print(f"Compacted into {len(compacted_blocks)} Parquet segments (Target: 256 MB)")
    assert len(compacted_blocks) == 40, f"Expected 40 compacted blocks, got {len(compacted_blocks)}"

    compacted_latency = engine.calculate_scan_latency(use_compacted=True)
    print(f"Compacted Scan Latency (40 blocks):       {compacted_latency:.2f} seconds")
    assert 10.0 <= compacted_latency <= 12.0, "Compacted scan latency calculation mismatch"

    speedup = uncompacted_latency / compacted_latency
    print(f"Compaction Query Speedup:                {speedup:.2f}x")
    assert speedup > 20.0, f"Expected >20x speedup, got {speedup:.2f}x"

    # 3. Monthly S3 Cost Model Verification
    cost_uncompacted = engine.calculate_monthly_s3_cost(daily_queries=100, is_compacted=False)
    cost_compacted = engine.calculate_monthly_s3_cost(daily_queries=100, is_compacted=True)
    print(f"Uncompacted S3 Monthly Cost:             USD {cost_uncompacted.total_monthly_usd}")
    print(f"Compacted S3 Monthly Cost:               USD {cost_compacted.total_monthly_usd}")
    print(f"Uncompacted API / Storage Ratio:         {cost_uncompacted.api_to_storage_ratio:.2f}x")
    assert cost_uncompacted.get_request_cost_usd > cost_compacted.get_request_cost_usd * 200

    # 4. Compliance Erasure & Write Amplification Verification
    res_sync = engine.execute_compliance_erasure("pat_90210", "compacted_seg_0001.parquet", 120, use_deletion_vector=False)
    res_tomb = engine.execute_compliance_erasure("pat_90210", "compacted_seg_0001.parquet", 120, use_deletion_vector=True)

    print(f"Sync Rewrite Amplification:              {res_sync['write_amplification']:,.1f}x (Bytes: {res_sync['bytes_written']:,})")
    print(f"Deletion Vector Amplification:           {res_tomb['write_amplification']:.2f}x (Bytes: {res_tomb['bytes_written']:,})")
    assert res_sync["write_amplification"] > 500000, "Sync write amplification must exceed 500,000x"
    assert res_tomb["write_amplification"] < 1.0, "Tombstone write amplification must be under 1x"

    print("\n✓ ALL PRODUCTION ENGINE INVARIANTS VERIFIED!")

docs.title: 1. The Compliance Conflict & Naive Failure
docs.text:
Under HIPAA de-identification standards and GDPR Article 17, when a patient revokes research consent, all their associated clinical records must be excised across all historical training splits.

Initially, the health platform executed naive synchronous Parquet rewriting: whenever an erasure request arrived, a Spark job scanned the \(80\text{ TB}\) lake, identified the target patient UUID, and re-wrote every containing \(256\text{ MB}\) Parquet block. After receiving 45 consent revocations in a single month, continuous background I/O thrashing halted active model training runs, and monthly cloud rewriting bills spiked by \(\text{USD } 72,000\).

docs.title: 2. The Architectural Resolution
docs.text: The platform transitioned to Delta Lake Deletion Vectors (Armbrust et al., 2020) combined with Cryptographic Shredding (Villaronga et al., 2018): - Sub-Second Soft Deletions: Erasure requests append a 64-byte Roaring Bitmap to the Delta transaction log, masking patient records without touching physical Parquet storage. - Per-Subject Key Shredding: Highly sensitive genomic features are encrypted with patient-specific Data Encryption Keys (DEKs). Upon revocation, destroying the patient's individual DEK renders all historical ciphertext permanently indecipherable across immutable historical backups. - Consolidated Maintenance: Physical block rewriting is deferred to an automated bi-monthly batch compaction job, consolidating hundreds of accumulated revocations into a single pass.

docs.title: 3. Quantitative Results & Operational Savings
docs.text:
• Write Amplification Reduction: Immediate write amplification collapsed from \(536,871\times\) down to \(0.13\times\) (an amortized \(1.15\times\) during batch vacuum).
  • Financial Cost Savings: Cloud rewriting expenses dropped from \(\text{USD } 72,000\text{/month}\) down to under \(\text{USD } 4,300\text{/month}\)—a \(94\%\) expenditure reduction.
Architectural Metric Naive Synchronous Rewriting Deletion Vectors & Cryptographic Shredding Immediate Write Amplification \(536,871\times\) (\(256\text{ MB}\) per record) \(0.13\times\) (\(64\text{ bytes}\) bitmap append) Erasure Execution Latency \(45 - 90\text{ minutes}\) (full Spark scan) \(< 2\text{ seconds}\) (metadata log commit) Monthly Cloud Rewriting Cost \(\text{USD } 72,000\text{/month}\) \(< \text{USD } 4,300\text{/month}\) (\(94\%\) savings) Historical Backup Compliance Violates immutable WORM archives Cryptographic shredding permanently invalidates ciphertext

docs.title: 1. The Small-File Operational Breakdown
docs.text: Kafka ingestion pipelines wrote streaming sensor telemetry in 1-minute micro-batches of \(200\text{ KB}\) each to S3. Over several months, individual partition directories accumulated over \(1.5\text{ Million}\) tiny Parquet objects. - Query Planning Stalls: Distributed query engines (Presto, Spark SQL) spent \(45\text{ minutes}\) just executing LIST and HEAD S3 requests before reading a single data byte. - Transaction Billing Explosion: Monthly AWS S3 GET and LIST request charges surged to \(\text{USD } 85,000\text{/month}\), eclipsing the actual byte storage cost by over \(320\%\).

docs.title: 2. The Compaction & Lifecycle Architecture
docs.text: Uber engineered an automated background compaction and lifecycle manager (Hermann & Balso, 2017): - Hierarchical Bin-Packing: Micro-batch files are continuously bin-packed into \(256\text{ MB}\) columnar Parquet files with synchronized min/max zone map indices. - Transactional Table Commit: Compaction processes commit consolidated files via ACID metadata swaps, preventing reader queries from observing transient duplicates. - Automated Lifecycle Sweeps: Staging directories apply a 14-day retention rule, automatically vacuuming unreferenced orphan snapshots.

docs.title: 3. Quantitative Operational Impact
docs.text:
• Feature Query Latency: Query planning durations plummeted from \(45\text{ minutes}\) down to \(1.8\text{ seconds}\)—a \(1,500\times\) acceleration.
  • Request Cost Reduction: Monthly object storage transaction fees fell from \(\text{USD } 85,000\) to \(\text{USD } 10,200\)—an \(88\%\) reduction.

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment 1: Inode Table Exhaustion Analysis and POSIX Scaling Limits

A computer vision machine learning team stores \(100\text{ Million}\) small JPEG images (\(15\text{ KB}\) average size) on an on-premises Linux server using an EXT4 filesystem with default formatting parameters (\(1\text{ inode per } 16\text{ KB}\) of disk space, total storage capacity \(2\text{ TB}\)).

  1. Calculate the total byte volume consumed by the images.
  2. Explain why the operating system suddenly throws No space left on device errors when saving image 100,000,001, even though the disk reports over \(500\text{ GB}\) of free storage space.
  3. How does packaging images into container formats (e.g., WebDataset TAR archives or Apache Parquet blocks) resolve this issue?
Reveal Detailed Solution

Step 1: Compute Total Byte Volume $\(V_{\text{bytes}} = 100,000,000 \times 15\text{ KB} = 1,500,000,000\text{ KB} \approx 1.5\text{ Terabytes}\)$ On a \(2.0\text{ TB}\) disk, \(2.0 - 1.5 = 0.5\text{ TB} = 500\text{ GB}\) of physical disk space remains completely unwritten.

Step 2: Diagnose Inode Exhaustion In traditional POSIX Linux filesystems (EXT4), every physical file and directory requires an entry in the pre-allocated filesystem inode table. The total number of inodes created during filesystem formatting is: $\(N_{\text{inodes}} = \frac{\text{Total Capacity}}{\text{Inode Ratio}} = \frac{2 \times 10^{12}\text{ bytes}}{16,384\text{ bytes/inode}} \approx 122,070,312\text{ inodes}\)$ When factoring in directory structures, metadata files, and temporary OS files, all \(122\text{ Million}\) inodes are exhausted once the 100 million image files are written. The Linux kernel returns ENOSPC (No space left on device) whenever the inode table is saturated, regardless of available byte capacity.

Step 3: Architectural Resolution Packaging images into contiguous container files (e.g., WebDataset TAR archives containing 10,000 images each or 256 MB Parquet blocks) reduces the physical filesystem file count from \(100,000,000\) down to \(10,000\) files. This consumes only \(10,000\) inodes, eliminating filesystem metadata exhaustion while accelerating sequential I/O by orders of magnitude.

Self-Assessment 2: Calculating Exact Monthly S3 Savings from Compaction Bin-Packing

A real-time IoT feature lake ingests \(\lambda_{\text{ingest}} = 1,000\text{ GB}\) of Parquet telemetry monthly in \(S_{\text{micro}} = 200\text{ KB}\) micro-batch files (\(S_{\text{micro}} \approx 0.1953\text{ MB}\)). The dataset is queried \(Q = 200\) times per month by analytical training pipelines.

Using the S3 Cost Model (Definition 12.7.3) with: - \(C_{\text{storage}} = \text{USD } 0.023 / \text{GB-month}\) - \(C_{\text{PUT}} = \text{USD } 0.005 / 1,000\text{ requests}\) (\(\text{USD } 5 \times 10^{-6}/\text{req}\)) - \(C_{\text{GET}} = \text{USD } 0.0004 / 1,000\text{ requests}\) (\(\text{USD } 4 \times 10^{-7}/\text{req}\))

  1. Calculate the monthly bill under uncompacted streaming.
  2. Calculate the monthly bill if an automated compactor consolidates files into \(S_{\text{target}} = 256\text{ MB}\) blocks immediately after ingestion.
Reveal Detailed Solution

Step 1: Uncompacted Monthly S3 Cost - Total File Count: $\(N_{\text{uncomp}} = \frac{1,000\text{ GB} \times 1,024\text{ MB/GB}}{0.1953125\text{ MB/file}} = 5,242,880\text{ files}\)$ - Static Storage Cost: $\(C_{\text{storage}} = 1,000\text{ GB} \times \text{USD } 0.023 = \text{USD } 23.00\)$ - Ingestion PUT Request Cost: $\(C_{\text{PUT}} = 5,242,880 \times \text{USD } 5 \times 10^{-6} = \text{USD } 26.21\)$ - Query GET Request Cost (\(Q = 200\) queries across all files): $\(N_{\text{GET}} = 200 \times 5,242,880 = 1,048,576,000\text{ GET requests}\)$ $\(C_{\text{GET}} = 1,048,576,000 \times \text{USD } 4 \times 10^{-7} = \text{USD } 419.43\)$ - Total Uncompacted Monthly Bill: $\(C_{\text{total, uncomp}} = 23.00 + 26.21 + 419.43 = \text{USD } 468.64\)$ Notice that GET query requests account for \(\frac{419.43}{468.64} \approx 89.5\%\) of the total cloud bill!

Step 2: Compacted Monthly S3 Cost (\(S_{\text{target}} = 256\text{ MB}\)) - Consolidated Block Count: $\(N_{\text{compacted}} = \frac{1,000\text{ GB} \times 1,024\text{ MB/GB}}{256\text{ MB}} = 4,000\text{ blocks}\)$ - Static Storage Cost: \(\text{USD } 23.00\) - Ingestion PUT Cost: \(\text{USD } 26.21\) (assuming micro-batches still ingested, or compacted in memory) - Compaction Write PUTs: \(4,000 \times \text{USD } 5 \times 10^{-6} \approx \text{USD } 0.02\) - Query GET Request Cost (\(Q = 200\) queries across \(4,000\) blocks): $\(N_{\text{GET, comp}} = 200 \times 4,000 = 800,000\text{ GET requests}\)$ $\(C_{\text{GET, comp}} = 800,000 \times \text{USD } 4 \times 10^{-7} = \text{USD } 0.32\)$ - Total Compacted Monthly Bill: $\(C_{\text{total, comp}} = 23.00 + 26.21 + 0.02 + 0.32 = \text{USD } 49.55\)$

Conclusion: Automated compaction slashes monthly GET request costs from \(\text{USD } 419.43\) to \(\text{USD } 0.32\) (\(99.9\%\) reduction), reducing the total monthly object storage bill from \(\text{USD } 468.64\) down to \(\text{USD } 49.55\)—saving \(\text{USD } 419.09\text{/month}\) (\(89.4\%\) overall savings) while accelerating queries by \(> 20\times\).

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & Theoretical Foundations
docs.text:
In modern production machine learning, an inference checkpoint or analytical dashboard is rarely derived from a single static input file. Instead, it represents the terminal state of an intricate, multi-stage computational DAG involving distributed web crawls, schema normalizations, streaming deduplication filters, join aggregations, feature embeddings, and distributed hyperparameter training (Herschel et al., 2017).

Data Lineage (or Data Provenance) establishes a formal, mathematically verifiable record capturing the origin, derivation history, and custody chain of every data artifact throughout its operational lifecycle (Moreau et al., 2011). By uniting Why-, How-, and Where-provenance models (Buneman et al., 2001; Cheney et al., 2009) with automated data quality assertions (Schelter et al., 2018) across MLOps orchestration pipelines (Kreuzberger et al., 2023), lineage engines turn opaque black-box model failures into deterministic root-cause isolation.

Modern provenance engines classify lineage metadata across three foundational dimensions (Buneman et al., 2001; Cheney et al., 2009): 1. Why-Provenance: Identifies the exact subset of upstream input tuples or dataset partitions that witnessed and contributed to the existence of an output tuple. 2. How-Provenance: Encodes the algebraic derivation formula explaining how input elements were filtered, projected, joined, and aggregated to synthesize the output (Green et al., 2007). 3. Where-Provenance: Pinpoints the exact physical storage address, byte offset, or source database attribute from which an output scalar value was copied verbatim.

docs.title: Definition 12.8.1: The W3C PROV-O Bipartite Provenance Graph Model
docs.text:
Conformant with the Open Provenance Model (OPM) and the W3C PROV-O specification (Moreau et al., 2011), a dataset lineage catalog is formally modeled as a labeled directed acyclic graph \(G = (V, E)\) partitioned into three disjoint vertex sets:

\[ V = \mathcal{E} \cup \mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{G}, \quad \mathcal{E} \cap \mathcal{A} = \emptyset, \quad \mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{G} = \emptyset \]

where: - \(\mathcal{E}\) is the set of Entities (physical datasets, partitioned tables, Parquet files, schemas, or trained model checkpoints). - \(\mathcal{A}\) is the set of Activities (deterministic transformation jobs, Spark SQL stages, feature extractions, or training runs). - \(\mathcal{G}\) is the set of Agents (authenticated users, Kubernetes service accounts, or CI/CD runners responsible for execution).

The directed edge set \(E \subseteq V \times V\) encodes causal dependencies strictly across four typed provenance relations: 1. \(\text{used} \subseteq \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{E}\): An execution activity \(a \in \mathcal{A}\) consumed entity \(e \in \mathcal{E}\). 2. \(\text{wasGeneratedBy} \subseteq \mathcal{E} \times \mathcal{A}\): An output entity \(e' \in \mathcal{E}\) was materialized by activity \(a \in \mathcal{A}\). 3. \(\text{wasDerivedFrom} \subseteq \mathcal{E} \times \mathcal{E}\): Direct artifact transformation dependency summarizing \(e' \leftarrow a \leftarrow e\). 4. \(\text{wasAssociatedWith} \subseteq \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{G}\): Operational attribution linking job \(a\) to responsible agent \(g\).

docs.title: Strict Temporal Acyclicity Invariant
docs.text:
Because every execution activity transitions forward in physical wall-clock time (\(t_{\text{generate}} > t_{\text{consume}}\)), the causal lineage graph \(G\) is strictly acyclic:

\[ \forall v \in V, \quad (v \to^+ v) \notin E^+ \]

docs.title: Definition 12.8.2: Transitive Closure via Nilpotent Adjacency Matrices
docs.text:
Let the graph \(G = (V, E)\) have \(|V| = n\) vertices indexed \(\{1, \dots, n\}\). Define the binary directed causal dependency adjacency matrix \(A \in \{0, 1\}^{n \times n}\) where \(A_{ij} = 1\) if vertex \(v_j\) directly depends on or was generated using vertex \(v_i\).

Because \(G\) is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with maximum finite topological path depth \(L < n\), the matrix \(A\) is strictly nilpotent:

\[ A^L = \mathbf{0} \]

Consequently, the Neumann geometric matrix series converges exactly in finite steps:

\[ R = (I - A)^{-1} = \sum_{m=0}^{L-1} A^m = I + A + A^2 + \dots + A^{L-1} \]

The boolean normalization of \(R\) defines the Transitive Reachability Matrix. For any target artifact \(v_k \in V\):

  1. Upstream Ancestry: The complete causal ancestor sub-graph producing \(v_k\) corresponds to non-zero entries in column \(k\):
\[ \text{Ancestry}(v_k) = \left\{ v_i \in V \;\middle|\; \left[ (I - A)^{-1} \right]_{ik} > 0 \right\} \]
  1. Downstream Descendants (Blast Radius): The complete downstream impact sub-graph affected by \(v_k\) corresponds to non-zero entries in row \(k\):
\[ \text{Descendants}(v_k) = \left\{ v_j \in V \;\middle|\; \left[ (I - A)^{-1} \right]_{kj} > 0 \right\} \]

docs.title: Definition 12.8.3: Provenance Semiring Polynomials (How-Provenance)
docs.text:
While binary reachability answers which sources contributed to a dataset, How-provenance models how individual input records mathematically combine (Green et al., 2007). Annotate each base input tuple \(t_i\) with a formal provenance token \(x_i \in X\). Let \(( \mathbb{N}[X], +, \cdot, 0, 1 )\) denote the commutative provenance semiring of polynomials with natural number coefficients over variables \(X\):

  1. Selection / Filtering (\(\sigma_P\)): Preserves the provenance polynomial of tuples satisfying predicate \(P\), mapping failing tuples to additive identity \(0\).
  2. Union / Projection (\(\cup, \Pi\)): Combines alternative derivations of identical output tuples via polynomial addition (\(+\)):
\[ \text{Prov}(t_{\text{out}}) = \text{Prov}(t_1) + \text{Prov}(t_2) \]
  1. Relational Join (\(\bowtie\)): Combines paired tuples across tables via polynomial multiplication (\(\cdot\)):
\[ \text{Prov}(t_1 \bowtie t_2) = \text{Prov}(t_1) \cdot \text{Prov}(t_2) \]

docs.title: Algebraic Derivation Example
docs.text:
Suppose an output feature tuple \(t^*\) carries provenance polynomial:

\[ P(t^*) = 2 \cdot x_1 \cdot x_2 + x_3^2 \]

This single compact expression proves that \(t^*\) was synthesized either by joining source record \(x_1\) with \(x_2\) (occurring via 2 distinct join paths), OR by a self-join on source record \(x_3\). Setting \(x_1 = 0\) immediately evaluates whether deleting source tuple \(x_1\) causes \(t^*\) to disappear (\(P(t^*) = x_3^2 \neq 0 \implies\) \(t^*\) survives via alternate lineage path \(x_3\)).

docs.title: Definition 12.8.4: Poisoning Impact Ratio (PIR) & Lineage Storage Scaling
docs.text:
When an upstream ingestion error, silent schema drift, or adversarial data poisoning attack compromises source entity \(v^* \in \mathcal{E}\) (Ikeda et al., 2011), engineers compute the Poisoning Impact Ratio (PIR) to quantify the exact blast radius across deployed machine learning models \(\mathcal{E}_{\text{models}} \subset \mathcal{E}\):

\[ \text{PIR}(v^*) = \frac{\left| \text{Descendants}(v^*) \cap \mathcal{E}_{\text{models}} \right|}{\left| \mathcal{E}_{\text{models}} \right|} \in [0, 1] \]

If \(\text{PIR}(v^*) = 0.75\), exactly \(75\%\) of all serving models inherit corrupted state from \(v^*\) and must be automatically quarantined, rolled back, and retrained.

docs.title: Fine-Grained vs. Coarse-Grained Storage Complexity
docs.text:
Consider a dataset with \(N\) individual rows processed through a pipeline of \(T\) transformation operators across \(P\) physical partitions (\(P \ll N\)) and \(C\) schema columns (\(C \ll N\)):

  1. Fine-Grained Row-Level Provenance: Recording per-row edge transformations generates linear storage inflation proportional to dataset volume:
\[ \mathcal{S}_{\text{row-lineage}} = \mathcal{O}(N \cdot T) \]

For \(N = 10^9\) rows and \(T = 10\) stages, tracking \(10^{10}\) provenance edges routinely consumes \(10\times\) more storage than the raw dataset itself.

  1. Coarse-Grained Partition & Column-Level Provenance: Production platforms track transformations at the partition and column AST boundary:
\[ \mathcal{S}_{\text{coarse}} = \mathcal{O}(P \cdot T + C \cdot T) \]

Because \(P \approx 10^3\) and \(C \approx 10^2\) while \(N \approx 10^9\), coarse-grained lineage slashes metadata storage footprints by six orders of magnitude (\(10^6\times\)) while retaining full root-cause observability (Ikeda et al., 2011).

Industrial Best Practice: OpenLineage Telemetry Integration

Instrument distributed compute pipelines (Apache Spark, Airflow, dbt, Flink) with the vendor-neutral OpenLineage standard. Every task execution automatically emits structured JSON RunEvent pulses detailing input dataset URIs, column-level SQL AST transformation plans, code Git SHAs, and output schemas directly to centralized metadata catalogs (Marquez, DataHub).

Common Pitfall / Anti-Pattern: Column-Level Lineage Blindness

Recording exclusively table-level lineage (raw_users \(\to\) training_features) is insufficient for high-velocity MLOps debugging. If a credit-risk classifier exhibits sudden score degradation, engineers require Column-Level Lineage to immediately isolate which exact transformation (CASE WHEN income > 0...) or upstream attribute type-cast corrupted the derived debt_ratio feature.

Cryptographic Provenance Checksums in Regulated Industries

In financial trading and healthcare diagnostics, provenance metadata must be tamper-evident. Production pipelines bind every inference prediction to a composite SHA-256 provenance tuple: (input_data_merkle_root, git_commit_hash, docker_image_digest, random_seed), enabling deterministic bitwise replay years after deployment (Kreuzberger et al., 2023).

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: W3C PROV-O Lineage & Blast Radius Engine
docs.text:
The following typed Python program implements a complete W3C PROV-O Data Lineage Provenance Engine using Pydantic V2. It models bipartite provenance graphs, computes nilpotent adjacency matrix transitive reachability, isolates upstream ancestry chains, quantifies the Poisoning Impact Ratio (PIR), and tracks column-level AST transformations.

"""
W3C PROV-O Data Lineage & Provenance Engine.
Implements bipartite provenance DAGs, transitive matrix reachability,
Poisoning Impact Ratio (PIR) blast radius analysis, and column AST lineage
using Pydantic V2.
"""

from typing import Dict, List, Set, Tuple, Optional, Any
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


# =====================================================================
# 1. Pydantic V2 Telemetry & Provenance Models
# =====================================================================

class ProvenanceNode(BaseModel):
    """Represents a W3C PROV-O Entity, Activity, Agent, or Model Checkpoint."""
    node_id: str
    node_type: str  # 'entity', 'activity', 'agent', 'model'
    content_hash: str = "sha256:000000"


class ProvenanceEdge(BaseModel):
    """Represents a directed dependency relationship in the provenance DAG."""
    source_id: str
    target_id: str
    predicate: str  # 'used', 'wasGeneratedBy', 'wasDerivedFrom', 'wasAssociatedWith'


class ColumnLineageMapping(BaseModel):
    """Tracks attribute-level AST SQL/ETL dependencies."""
    target_table: str
    target_column: str
    source_columns: List[str]
    expression: str


class BlastRadiusReport(BaseModel):
    """Quantifies downstream blast radius and Poisoning Impact Ratio (PIR)."""
    corrupted_source: str
    affected_nodes: List[str]
    compromised_models: List[str]
    total_production_models: int
    poisoning_impact_ratio: float


# =====================================================================
# 2. W3C PROV-O Data Lineage Provenance Engine
# =====================================================================

class DataLineageProvenanceEngine:
    """
    Implements a formal DAG for W3C PROV-O provenance tracking,
    nilpotent adjacency matrix closure, column-level AST lineage, and PIR analysis.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.nodes: List[ProvenanceNode] = []
        self.node_to_idx: Dict[str, int] = {}
        self.edges: List[ProvenanceEdge] = []
        self.column_mappings: Dict[str, ColumnLineageMapping] = {}

    def add_node(self, node_id: str, node_type: str, content_hash: str = "sha256:default"):
        if node_id not in self.node_to_idx:
            idx = len(self.nodes)
            self.nodes.append(ProvenanceNode(
                node_id=node_id,
                node_type=node_type,
                content_hash=content_hash
            ))
            self.node_to_idx[node_id] = idx

    def add_edge(self, source_id: str, target_id: str, predicate: str = "wasDerivedFrom"):
        """Adds directed causal edge: source_id -> target_id."""
        if source_id not in self.node_to_idx or target_id not in self.node_to_idx:
            raise KeyError(f"Both nodes '{source_id}' and '{target_id}' must exist in DAG.")
        self.edges.append(ProvenanceEdge(
            source_id=source_id,
            target_id=target_id,
            predicate=predicate
        ))

    def add_column_lineage(self, target_table: str, target_col: str, source_cols: List[str], expr: str):
        key = f"{target_table}.{target_col}"
        self.column_mappings[key] = ColumnLineageMapping(
            target_table=target_table,
            target_column=target_col,
            source_columns=source_cols,
            expression=expr
        )

    def _multiply_bool_matrices(self, A: List[List[int]], B: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
        """Boolean matrix multiplication for DAG transitive reachability."""
        n = len(A)
        C = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        for i in range(n):
            for k in range(n):
                if A[i][k] == 1:
                    for j in range(n):
                        if B[k][j] == 1:
                            C[i][j] = 1
        return C

    def compute_transitive_reachability(self) -> List[List[int]]:
        """
        Computes transitive closure using Neumann series: (I - A)^-1 = I + A + A^2 + ...
        Converges in <= |V| steps due to DAG acyclicity (nilpotent adjacency matrix).
        """
        n = len(self.nodes)
        adj = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        for e in self.edges:
            u = self.node_to_idx[e.source_id]
            v = self.node_to_idx[e.target_id]
            adj[u][v] = 1

        reach = [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
        curr_power = [row[:] for row in adj]

        for _ in range(n):
            has_edges = False
            for i in range(n):
                for j in range(n):
                    if curr_power[i][j] > 0:
                        reach[i][j] = 1
                        has_edges = True
            if not has_edges:
                break
            curr_power = self._multiply_bool_matrices(curr_power, adj)

        return reach

    def get_upstream_ancestry(self, target_node_id: str) -> Set[str]:
        """Returns all causal upstream ancestors contributing to target_node_id."""
        reach = self.compute_transitive_reachability()
        t_idx = self.node_to_idx[target_node_id]
        ancestors: Set[str] = set()
        for i in range(len(self.nodes)):
            if reach[i][t_idx] == 1 and i != t_idx:
                ancestors.add(self.nodes[i].node_id)
        return ancestors

    def compute_poisoning_impact_ratio(self, corrupted_node_id: str) -> BlastRadiusReport:
        """
        Evaluates PIR: proportion of deployed production models compromised
        if corrupted_node_id contains poisoned records or schema defects.
        """
        reach = self.compute_transitive_reachability()
        c_idx = self.node_to_idx[corrupted_node_id]

        descendant_ids: List[str] = []
        for j in range(len(self.nodes)):
            if reach[c_idx][j] == 1:
                descendant_ids.append(self.nodes[j].node_id)

        all_models = [n.node_id for n in self.nodes if n.node_type == "model"]
        compromised_models = [m for m in all_models if m in descendant_ids]

        pir = len(compromised_models) / len(all_models) if all_models else 0.0

        return BlastRadiusReport(
            corrupted_source=corrupted_node_id,
            affected_nodes=descendant_ids,
            compromised_models=compromised_models,
            total_production_models=len(all_models),
            poisoning_impact_ratio=round(pir, 4)
        )


# =====================================================================
# 3. Verification & Assertion Suite
# =====================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=" * 70)
    print("W3C PROV-O DATA LINEAGE ENGINE: RUNTIME VERIFICATION")
    print("=" * 70)

    lineage = DataLineageProvenanceEngine()

    # 1. Construct Bipartite Provenance DAG (Entities, Activities, Models)
    lineage.add_node("raw_crawler_data", "entity", "sha256:1a9f0b")
    lineage.add_node("partner_feed_data", "entity", "sha256:8c2e11")
    lineage.add_node("cleaning_pipeline", "activity", "git:a1b2c3d")
    lineage.add_node("feature_embeddings", "entity", "sha256:9e3d1a")
    lineage.add_node("recommendation_model", "model", "sha256:f20a6c")
    lineage.add_node("fraud_detection_model", "model", "sha256:e44b91")
    lineage.add_node("isolated_nlp_model", "model", "sha256:7d1022")

    lineage.add_edge("raw_crawler_data", "cleaning_pipeline", "used")
    lineage.add_edge("cleaning_pipeline", "feature_embeddings", "wasGeneratedBy")
    lineage.add_edge("feature_embeddings", "recommendation_model", "used")
    lineage.add_edge("feature_embeddings", "fraud_detection_model", "used")
    lineage.add_edge("partner_feed_data", "isolated_nlp_model", "used")

    # 2. Verify Transitive Reachability Matrix
    reach = lineage.compute_transitive_reachability()
    raw_idx = lineage.node_to_idx["raw_crawler_data"]
    rec_idx = lineage.node_to_idx["recommendation_model"]
    nlp_idx = lineage.node_to_idx["isolated_nlp_model"]

    assert reach[raw_idx][rec_idx] == 1, "Recommendation model must depend on raw_crawler_data!"
    assert reach[raw_idx][nlp_idx] == 0, "Isolated NLP model must NOT depend on raw_crawler_data!"

    # 3. Verify Upstream Ancestry Trace
    rec_ancestors = lineage.get_upstream_ancestry("recommendation_model")
    print(f"Upstream Ancestry of 'recommendation_model': {sorted(list(rec_ancestors))}")
    assert rec_ancestors == {"raw_crawler_data", "cleaning_pipeline", "feature_embeddings"}

    # 4. Evaluate Poisoning Impact Ratio (PIR)
    report = lineage.compute_poisoning_impact_ratio("raw_crawler_data")
    print(f"Blast Radius PIR: {report.poisoning_impact_ratio * 100:.2f}% ({len(report.compromised_models)}/{report.total_production_models} models)")
    print(f"Compromised Models: {report.compromised_models}")
    assert abs(report.poisoning_impact_ratio - (2.0 / 3.0)) < 1e-3, "PIR must equal 66.7%"

    # 5. Column-Level AST Lineage Verification
    lineage.add_column_lineage(
        target_table="user_risk_features",
        target_col="debt_ratio",
        source_cols=["raw_users.income", "raw_users.debt"],
        expr="(income / NULLIF(debt, 0))"
    )
    col_map = lineage.column_mappings["user_risk_features.debt_ratio"]
    assert "raw_users.debt" in col_map.source_columns
    print(f"Column AST Lineage Verified: {col_map.target_table}.{col_map.target_column} <- {col_map.source_columns}")

    print("\n✓ ALL PROVENANCE & LINEAGE INVARIANTS VERIFIED!")
