docs.title: Exercise 1: Anatomy of a DOI, Handle Resolution & Schema.org JSON-LD Structured Search Indexing
docs.text:
A biomedical research consortium releases a multi-omics dataset with persistent identifier doi:10.5281/zenodo.7891234.

  1. Explain the exact mechanism by which a global Handle resolver resolves 10.5281/zenodo.7891234 to an active landing page URL, and why hard-coded HTTP URLs violate FAIR Principle F1 (Wilkinson et al., 2016).
  2. Write a minimal, valid Schema.org JSON-LD metadata block that Google Dataset Search (Brickley et al., 2019) can crawl to index this repository with license, DOI, temporal coverage, and author affiliations.
  3. Compute the semantic completeness \(\mathcal{C}_{\text{meta}}\) under the vector space formulation of Definition 13.3.1 assuming equal weights (\(w_k = \frac{1}{8}\)) across the 8 standard dimensions if the manifest lacks demographic distributions (\(m_5 = 0\)) and sensor calibrations (\(m_6 = 0\)), while all other 6 dimensions score \(1.0\).
Reveal Complete Step-by-Step Solution

Step 1: Handle Resolution Protocol vs. Hard-Coded URLs

A Digital Object Identifier (DOI) is a specific implementation of the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI) Handle System.

  • The prefix 10.5281 identifies the specific DOI registration agency and allocator (in this case, CERN / Zenodo under DataCite).
  • The suffix zenodo.7891234 identifies the unique dataset artifact within that namespace.

When an automated client queries https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7891234: 1. The client performs an HTTP GET request to the global proxy server at doi.org. 2. The proxy queries the distributed Handle registry via TCP port 2641 to retrieve the authoritative metadata record associated with 10.5281/zenodo.7891234. 3. The Handle server returns an HTTP 302 / 303 Redirect containing the current target URL (e.g., https://zenodo.org/records/7891234).

Hard-coded HTTP URLs (https://lab.university.edu/~drsmith/data.csv) violate FAIR Principle F1 because institutional server migrations, domain lapses, and file path reorganizations cause inevitable hyperlink rot. By decoupling the immutable persistent identifier (10.5281/...) from the physical storage location, data custodians can update the redirect target in the Handle registry without breaking existing citations in published literature.

Step 2: Valid Schema.org JSON-LD Structured Metadata

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org/",
  "@type": "Dataset",
  "name": "Single-Cell Multi-Omics Immune Response Benchmark",
  "description": "Single-cell RNA sequencing and surface protein profiles of peripheral blood mononuclear cells under viral stimulation.",
  "identifier": [
    "https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7891234",
    "doi:10.5281/zenodo.7891234"
  ],
  "url": "https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7891234",
  "license": "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/",
  "temporalCoverage": "2022-01-15/2023-11-30",
  "creator": {
    "@type": "Organization",
    "name": "Global Multi-Omics Consortium",
    "sameAs": "https://ror.org/03vek6s52"
  },
  "distribution": [
    {
      "@type": "DataDownload",
      "encodingFormat": "application/x-parquet",
      "contentUrl": "https://zenodo.org/records/7891234/files/pbmc_multiomics.parquet"
    }
  ]
}

Step 3: Calculating Semantic Completeness \(\mathcal{C}_{\text{meta}}\)

Given equal weighting across \(K = 8\) dimensions:

\[w_k = \frac{1}{8} = 0.125, \quad \forall k \in \{1, \dots, 8\}\]

The documentation vector is:

\[\mathbf{m}(\mathcal{D}) = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0)^\top\]

Applying Definition 13.3.1:

\[\mathcal{C}_{\text{meta}}(\mathcal{D}) = \sum_{k=1}^8 w_k m_k = 6 \times (0.125 \times 1.0) + 2 \times (0.125 \times 0.0) = 0.750\]

The dataset achieves a semantic completeness index of \(0.750\) (or 75%), failing typical production compliance gates requiring \(\mathcal{C}_{\text{meta}} \ge 0.850\).

docs.title: Exercise 2: CROISSANT Field Extraction & 1-WL Isomorphism Hash Invariance
docs.text:
Consider an enterprise data engineering pipeline evaluating two candidate metadata schemas \(\mathcal{G}_1\) and \(\mathcal{G}_2\) representing an image classification dataset.

In \(\mathcal{G}_1\), a blank node \(B_1\) is labeled _:b1 and points via predicate cr:extract to sc:image. In \(\mathcal{G}_2\), the same blank node is serialized in a different JSON-LD order with label _:b99.

  1. Prove why a naïve cryptographic string hash of the raw JSON-LD documents \( ext{SHA256}( ext{JSON}_1) eq ext{SHA256}( ext{JSON}_2)\) fails, and demonstrate how the 1-WL Graph Hashing Algorithm guarantees \(\mathcal{H}_{ ext{WL}}(\mathcal{G}_1) = \mathcal{H}_{ ext{WL}}(\mathcal{G}_2)\).
  2. If an adversary silently modifies the predicate from dct:license with value CC-BY-4.0 to dct:license with value CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial restriction), explain mathematically how the color refinement step in Definition 13.3.3 propagates this change to the terminal canonical hash.
Reveal Complete Step-by-Step Solution

Step 1: Naïve Text Hashing vs. 1-WL Graph Hash Invariance

A cryptographic string hash function treats a document as a 1-dimensional sequence of ASCII / UTF-8 bytes:

\[ ext{Hash}_{ ext{text}}(\mathcal{M}) = ext{SHA256}(b_1 b_2 \dots b_N)\]

In RDF and JSON-LD, the following transformations preserve semantic equivalence: 1. Key-value ordering permutation within JSON objects ({"@id": "...", "@type": "..."} vs. {"@type": "...", "@id": "..."}). 2. Blank node identifier skolemization (_:b1 vs. _:b99). 3. Insignificant whitespace and indentation variations.

Because byte streams differ under any key reordering or blank node renaming:

\[ ext{SHA256}( ext{JSON}_1) eq ext{SHA256}( ext{JSON}_2)\]

In contrast, the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman (1-WL) graph hashing algorithm operates over graph topological structure: - At iteration \(\ell = 0\), both blank nodes \(B_1\) and \(B_99\) initialize their base colors purely based on node type (type(v) = BlankNode), completely stripping the arbitrary local identifier strings _:b1 and _:b99. - At iteration \(\ell = 1\), both nodes collect their relational neighborhoods: \(M^{(1)}(B_1) = ext{sort}\left( \left\{ ( ext{"cr:extract"}, c^{(0)}( ext{sc:image})), ( ext{"dcat:distribution"}, c^{(0)}(\mathcal{D})) ight\} ight)\) and \(M^{(1)}(B_{99}) = ext{sort}\left( \left\{ ( ext{"cr:extract"}, c^{(0)}( ext{sc:image})), ( ext{"dcat:distribution"}, c^{(0)}(\mathcal{D})) ight\} ight)\). - Because the sorted neighborhood multisets are identical: \(c^{(1)}(B_1) = ext{SHA256}\left( c^{(0)}(B_1) \parallel ext{Serialize}(M^{(1)}(B_1)) ight) = c^{(1)}(B_{99})\). - Since all vertices across \(\mathcal{G}_1\) and \(\mathcal{G}_2\) yield identical color multisets, sorting the multisets produces bitwise identical digests: \(\mathcal{H}_{ ext{WL}}(\mathcal{G}_1) = \mathcal{H}_{ ext{WL}}(\mathcal{G}_2)\).

Step 2: Tamper Propagation Under Predicate Mutation

Suppose the license node target is mutated from \(O_1 = ext{"CC-BY-4.0"}\) to \(O_2 = ext{"CC-BY-NC-4.0"}\).

  1. Base Label Divergence (\(\ell = 0\)): \(c^{(0)}(O_1) = ext{SHA256}( ext{"CC-BY-4.0"}) eq ext{SHA256}( ext{"CC-BY-NC-4.0"}) = c^{(0)}(O_2)\).
  2. Refinement Propagation to Dataset Node (\(\ell = 1\)): Let \(v_{\mathcal{D}}\) be the central dataset node. Its neighborhood multiset includes the license triple: \(M^{(1)}(v_{\mathcal{D}})_{\mathcal{G}_1} = \left\{ \dots, ( ext{"dct:license"}, c^{(0)}(O_1)) ight\}\) and \(M^{(1)}(v_{\mathcal{D}})_{\mathcal{G}_2} = \left\{ \dots, ( ext{"dct:license"}, c^{(0)}(O_2)) ight\}\). Because \(c^{(0)}(O_1) eq c^{(0)}(O_2)\), the multisets differ: \(M^{(1)}(v_{\mathcal{D}})_{\mathcal{G}_1} eq M^{(1)}(v_{\mathcal{D}})_{\mathcal{G}_2} \implies c^{(1)}(v_{\mathcal{D}})_{\mathcal{G}_1} eq c^{(1)}(v_{\mathcal{D}})_{\mathcal{G}_2}\).
  3. Avalanche Effect on Canonical Hash: The sorted multiset of terminal colors for \(\mathcal{G}_1\) contains at least two differing elements compared to \(\mathcal{G}_2\) (\(c(O)\) and \(c(v_{\mathcal{D}})\)). By the avalanche property of cryptographic hashing: \(\mathcal{H}_{ ext{WL}}(\mathcal{G}_1) eq \mathcal{H}_{ ext{WL}}(\mathcal{G}_2)\). The probability of a hash collision under SHA-256 is negligible (\(\le 2^{-256}\)), rendering silent metadata modification instantly detectable by downstream automated compliance checkers (Abiteboul, 1997).

docs.title: The Operationalization of FAIR: Beyond Aspirational Manifestos
docs.text:
In 2016, a consortium of international researchers and data stewards formulated the FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management: Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability (Wilkinson et al., 2016). While widely celebrated, early adoptions frequently treated FAIR as a subjective checklist or a qualitative aspiration. In modern dataset engineering, FAIR must be operationalized as an executable, multi-criteria mathematical specification (Jacobsen et al., 2020; Mons et al., 2017).

A central insight of rigorous data stewardship is that FAIR applies equally to data payload (\(\mathcal{D}\)) and metadata descriptions (\(\mathcal{M}\)), but their lifecycles are decoupled. Furthermore, FAIR is emphatically not synonymous with Open Data: a highly confidential clinical dataset containing protected health information can achieve 100% FAIR compliance if its access restrictions are governed by automated, standardized, and machine-actionable authorization protocols (Jacobsen et al., 2020).

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        THE CANONICAL 15 ATOMIC FACETS OF FAIR DATA                                |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| FINDABLE (F)             | ACCESSIBLE (A)          | INTEROPERABLE (I)       | REUSABLE (R)               |
| - F1: Global Unique PID  | - A1: Open Std Protocol | - I1: Formal Knowledge  | - R1: Plural Attributes    |
| - F2: Rich Metadata      |   * A1.1: Free/Standard | - I2: FAIR Vocabularies | - R1.1: Clear SPDX License |
| - F3: Explicit PID Link  |   * A1.2: Auth Support  | - I3: Qualified Links   | - R1.2: Detailed Provenance|
| - F4: Searchable Index   | - A2: Tombstone Record  |                         | - R1.3: Community Standard |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: Mathematical Formulations of FAIR Data Principles
docs.text: To evaluate and audit compliance systematically, we formulate four formal mathematical definitions governing metric tensors, searchability distributions, protocol longevity invariants, and reusability decay rates.

docs.title: Definition 13.4.1: The 15 FAIR Facets & Multi-Criteria Maturity Metric Tensor
docs.text:
Let a digital research object \(\mathcal{R} = (\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{M})\) consist of a dataset payload \(\mathcal{D}\) and its associated metadata manifest \(\mathcal{M}\). The compliance of \(\mathcal{R}\) is evaluated against the 15 atomic sub-principles defined by Wilkinson et al. (2016), partitioned across four cardinal pillars \(\mathcal{P} = \{\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{I}, \mathbf{R}\}\):

\[\boldsymbol{\mu}(\mathcal{R}) = \left( \mu_{F_1}, \dots, \mu_{F_4}, \mu_{A_{1.1}}, \mu_{A_{1.2}}, \mu_{A_2}, \mu_{I_1}, \mu_{I_2}, \mu_{I_3}, \mu_{R_1}, \mu_{R_{1.1}}, \mu_{R_{1.2}}, \mu_{R_{1.3}} \right)^\top \in [0, 1]^{15}\]

where each coordinate \(\mu_i(\mathcal{R}) \in [0, 1]\) represents the audited compliance score of facet \(i\).

For each cardinal pillar \(p \in \mathcal{P}\), the intra-pillar mean compliance \(\bar{\mu}_p\) is:

\[\bar{\mu}_p = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}_p|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_p} \mu_i(\mathcal{R})\]

While a linear weighted combination yields a baseline maturity index:

\[\Phi_{\text{linear}}(\mathcal{R}) = \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}} w_p \bar{\mu}_p, \quad \text{where } \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}} w_p = 1, \; w_p > 0\]

linear aggregation violates the foundational Non-Compensatory Axiom of Data Stewardship: high semantic interoperability cannot compensate for complete inaccessibility. If a dataset is inaccessible (\(\bar{\mu}_A = 0\)), its real-world scientific utility is zero.

To enforce non-compensability, we formulate the Strict FAIR Maturity Metric \(\Phi_{\text{strict}}(\mathcal{R})\) using a generalized Hölder / Cobb-Douglas harmonic aggregation with penalty exponent \(\rho > 0\):

\[\Phi_{\text{strict}}(\mathcal{R}) = \left( \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}} \beta_p \cdot (\bar{\mu}_p + \epsilon)^{-\rho} \right)^{-1/\rho}\]

where \(\sum_{p} \beta_p = 1\), \(\beta_p > 0\), and \(\epsilon > 0\) is a stability regularization constant. As the penalty exponent \(\rho \to \infty\), the aggregation converges to the strict Leontief bottleneck:

\[\lim_{\rho \to \infty} \Phi_{\text{strict}}(\mathcal{R}) = \min_{p \in \{\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{I}, \mathbf{R}\}} \bar{\mu}_p\]

guaranteeing that any systemic failure in an individual pillar decisively gates the overall certification of the dataset (Jacobsen et al., 2020; Wang & Strong, 1996).

docs.title: Definition 13.4.2: Findability Searchability Index & Semantic Triplet Recall
docs.text:
Findability dictates that digital resources can be discovered by both human investigators and autonomous computational agents. Let \(\mathcal{Q}\) represent the distribution of natural language and SPARQL semantic search queries issued over a research domain.

Let \(\mathbf{e}(q) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\mathbf{e}(\mathcal{M}) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) represent the normalized semantic embeddings of query \(q\) and metadata manifest \(\mathcal{M}\) in a shared representation space. We define the Semantic Findability Retrieval Score \(\mathcal{S}_{\text{find}}(\mathcal{R}, q)\):

\[\mathcal{S}_{\text{find}}(\mathcal{R}, q) = \sigma\left( \langle \mathbf{e}(q), \mathbf{e}(\mathcal{M}) \rangle + \gamma_{\text{PID}} \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{PID}_{\text{valid}}(\mathcal{R})) + \gamma_{\text{idx}} \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{Indexed}(\mathcal{R}, \mathcal{I}_{\text{cat}})) \right)\]

where \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\) is the sigmoid activation, \(\gamma_{\text{PID}} > 0\) is the persistent identifier incentive bonus, \(\gamma_{\text{idx}} > 0\) is the indexed repository bonus, and \(\mathbb{I}(\cdot)\) is the indicator function.

docs.title: Theorem 13.4.1 (Findability Lower Bound):
docs.text:
If a dataset lacks an indexed catalog registration (\(\mathbb{I}(\text{Indexed}) = 0\)) and lacks a resolvable PID (\(\mathbb{I}(\text{PID}) = 0\)), then under standard cosine embeddings \(\langle \mathbf{e}(q), \mathbf{e}(\mathcal{M}) \rangle \le 1.0\):

\[\mathcal{S}_{\text{find}}(\mathcal{R}, q) \le \sigma(1.0) \approx 0.731\]

Whereas an indexed, PID-endowed manifest with identical textual content achieves:

\[\mathcal{S}_{\text{find}}(\mathcal{R}, q) \ge \sigma(1.0 + \gamma_{\text{PID}} + \gamma_{\text{idx}}) \ge 0.952 \quad (\text{for } \gamma_{\text{PID}} = 1.0, \gamma_{\text{idx}} = 1.0)\]

This explains why unindexed local files become functionally invisible to automated discovery crawlers (Brickley et al., 2019; Wilkinson et al., 2016).

docs.title: Definition 13.4.3: Accessibility Protocol Invariants & The A2 Tombstone Invariant
docs.text:
Accessibility mandates that data and metadata are retrievable using their identifier via open, standardized communications protocols (\(A_1\)), allowing for authentication and authorization where necessary (\(A_{1.2}\)).

Crucially, Principle \(A_2\) dictates that:

\[\text{Metadata are accessible, even when the data are no longer available.}\]

Let \(T_{\text{data}}\) be the active physical hosting lifespan of dataset payload \(\mathcal{D}\), and let \(T_{\text{meta}}\) be the archival lifespan of metadata manifest \(\mathcal{M}\). The FAIR Accessibility Longevity Invariant requires:

\[T_{\text{meta}} \gg T_{\text{data}}, \quad \text{with } \lim_{t \to \infty} P\left( \text{Resolvable}(\mathcal{M}_t) \right) = 1\]

When a dataset payload \(\mathcal{D}\) is decommissioned—due to cloud storage costs, physical media deprecation, privacy redactions, or GDPR "Right to be Forgotten" mandates—the server must never return an HTTP 404 Not Found. Instead, the endpoint must return an HTTP 410 Gone containing a cryptographically signed Tombstone Manifest \(\mathcal{M}_{\text{tombstone}}\):

\[\mathcal{M}_{\text{tombstone}} = \left( \text{DOI}, t_{\text{retract}}, \text{Reason}, \mathcal{H}_{\text{SHA256}}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{retired}}), \text{ContactURI} \right)\]

This ensures that downstream literature citing the DOI can verify historical provenance and validate cryptographic digests without silent link breakage (Jacobsen et al., 2020; Stodden et al., 2016).

docs.title: Definition 13.4.4: Semantic Interoperability Ontology Alignment & Reusability Decay
docs.text:
Interoperability requires knowledge representations using formal, accessible, and broadly applicable ontologies (\(I_1\)), vocabularies that themselves follow FAIR (\(I_2\)), and qualified cross-references (\(I_3\)). Reusability requires plural relevant attributes (\(R_1\)), clear SPDX licenses (\(R_{1.1}\)), detailed provenance (\(R_{1.2}\)), and domain standards (\(R_{1.3}\)).

Following the landmark empirical study by Vines et al. (2014) and quality economics by Wang & Strong (1996), uncurated datasets suffer exponential reusability decay over time:

\[\mathcal{R}_{\text{decay}}(t) = \mathcal{R}_0 \cdot e^{-\lambda t}\]

where \(\mathcal{R}_0 = 1.0\) is initial reusability and \(\lambda > 0\) is the decay constant. In uncurated, non-FAIR datasets, Vines et al. (2014) measured an annual decay rate of \(\lambda_0 \approx 0.170 \text{ year}^{-1}\), yielding a half-life of:

\[t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln(2)}{\lambda_0} \approx \frac{0.6931}{0.170} \approx 4.08 \text{ years}\]

Under comprehensive FAIR stewardship (\(\Phi_{\text{strict}} \ge 0.90\)), persistent PIDs prevent URL rot, standardized ontologies eliminate semantic drift, and machine-readable licenses remove legal ambiguity. The effective decay constant scales inversely with the strict FAIR index:

\[\lambda_{\text{FAIR}} = \lambda_0 \cdot \left( 1 - \Phi_{\text{strict}}(\mathcal{R}) \right) + \lambda_{\text{floor}}\]

where \(\lambda_{\text{floor}} \approx 0.015 \text{ year}^{-1}\) represents unavoidable semantic drift in domain ontologies. For a FAIR-certified dataset with \(\Phi_{\text{strict}} = 0.95\):

\[\lambda_{\text{FAIR}} = 0.170 \times (1 - 0.95) + 0.015 = 0.0085 + 0.015 = 0.0235 \text{ year}^{-1}\]

yielding an extended functional half-life of:

\[t_{1/2}^{\text{FAIR}} = \frac{\ln(2)}{0.0235} \approx 29.5 \text{ years}\]

representing a 7.2-fold increase in scientific and commercial durability (Vines et al., 2014; Wilkinson et al., 2016).

docs.title: 💻 Runnable Executable Python Implementation
docs.text:
The following production-grade implementation, FAIRComplianceAssessmentEngine, provides complete mathematical validation and auditing for the FAIR Guiding Principles. It implements: 1. Pydantic V2 models for all 15 atomic FAIR facets, digital resources, and HTTP 410 tombstone records. 2. Exact calculation of intra-pillar compliance \(\bar{\mu}_p\), linear index \(\Phi_{\text{linear}}\), and non-compensatory harmonic index \(\Phi_{\text{strict}}\). 3. Automated generation and verification of RFC-compliant HTTP 410 Tombstone manifests for retired payloads. 4. Vines exponential reusability decay simulations over multi-decade horizons.

"""
FAIRComplianceAssessmentEngine: Production-grade validation and mathematical auditing
for the 15 atomic FAIR Guiding Principles, non-compensatory harmonic scoring,
and RFC-compliant HTTP 410 Tombstone longevity invariants.
"""

from __future__ import annotations
import math
import hashlib
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Set, Tuple, Any
from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator, model_validator


class FAIRPillar(str, Enum):
    FINDABLE = "Findable"
    ACCESSIBLE = "Accessible"
    INTEROPERABLE = "Interoperable"
    REUSABLE = "Reusable"


class FAIRFacetID(str, Enum):
    F1 = "F1_Persistent_Identifier"
    F2 = "F2_Rich_Metadata"
    F3 = "F3_Metadata_Includes_PID"
    F4 = "F4_Searchable_Registry"
    A1_1 = "A1_1_Open_Protocol"
    A1_2 = "A1_2_Auth_Protocol"
    A2 = "A2_Metadata_Longevity"
    I1 = "I1_Knowledge_Representation"
    I2 = "I2_FAIR_Vocabularies"
    I3 = "I3_Qualified_References"
    R1 = "R1_Plural_Attributes"
    R1_1 = "R1_1_Clear_SPDX_License"
    R1_2 = "R1_2_Detailed_Provenance"
    R1_3 = "R1_3_Community_Standards"


class FAIRFacetScore(BaseModel):
    facet: FAIRFacetID
    pillar: FAIRPillar
    compliance: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0, description="Compliance score in [0.0, 1.0]")
    weight: float = Field(default=1.0, gt=0.0, description="Intra-pillar importance weight")
    evidence: str = Field(..., min_length=1)


class DigitalResourceManifest(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(..., min_length=1)
    doi: Optional[str] = None
    access_url: Optional[str] = None
    license_spdx: Optional[str] = None
    ontology_uris: List[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    has_tombstone_policy: bool = False
    is_indexed_in_search: bool = False
    is_payload_active: bool = True
    payload_sha256: Optional[str] = None


class TombstoneRecord(BaseModel):
    doi: str
    retirement_timestamp: str
    retirement_reason: str
    original_payload_sha256: str
    metadata_archive_url: str
    custodian_contact: str
    http_status_code: int = 410

    @field_validator("http_status_code")
    @classmethod
    def verify_http_410(cls, v: int) -> int:
        if v != 410:
            raise ValueError(f"Tombstone must return HTTP 410 Gone under FAIR A2, got {v}")
        return v


class FAIRAuditReport(BaseModel):
    resource_name: str
    pillar_means: Dict[FAIRPillar, float]
    phi_linear: float
    phi_strict: float
    is_certified: bool
    reusability_half_life_years: float
    diagnostics: List[str]


class FAIRComplianceAssessmentEngine:
    """
    Mathematical engine implementing Definitions 13.4.1 through 13.4.4.
    """

    def __init__(self, rho_penalty: float = 2.0, epsilon: float = 1e-6):
        self.rho = rho_penalty
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.pillar_weights: Dict[FAIRPillar, float] = {
            FAIRPillar.FINDABLE: 0.25,
            FAIRPillar.ACCESSIBLE: 0.25,
            FAIRPillar.INTEROPERABLE: 0.25,
            FAIRPillar.REUSABLE: 0.25,
        }

    def evaluate_resource(
        self, resource: DigitalResourceManifest
    ) -> List[FAIRFacetScore]:
        """
        Audits a digital resource against the 15 atomic FAIR facets.
        """
        scores: List[FAIRFacetScore] = []

        # --- FINDABLE (F1 - F4) ---
        has_doi = bool(resource.doi and resource.doi.startswith("10."))
        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.F1,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.FINDABLE,
                compliance=1.0 if has_doi else 0.1,
                evidence="Valid global DOI registered with DataCite/Crossref" if has_doi else "Lacks persistent identifier",
            )
        )

        has_rich_meta = len(resource.ontology_uris) >= 2
        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.F2,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.FINDABLE,
                compliance=0.95 if has_rich_meta else 0.3,
                evidence="Rich metadata with structured schema mappings" if has_rich_meta else "Sparse metadata attributes",
            )
        )

        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.F3,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.FINDABLE,
                compliance=1.0 if has_doi else 0.2,
                evidence="Metadata record explicitly cites primary PID",
            )
        )

        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.F4,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.FINDABLE,
                compliance=1.0 if resource.is_indexed_in_search else 0.15,
                evidence="Indexed in Google Dataset Search / Zenodo / Dataverse" if resource.is_indexed_in_search else "Unindexed dark dataset",
            )
        )

        # --- ACCESSIBLE (A1.1, A1.2, A2) ---
        has_open_proto = bool(resource.access_url and resource.access_url.startswith(("https://", "sftp://")))
        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.A1_1,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.ACCESSIBLE,
                compliance=1.0 if has_open_proto else 0.0,
                evidence="Standard HTTPS/REST endpoint" if has_open_proto else "Proprietary or non-standard protocol",
            )
        )

        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.A1_2,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.ACCESSIBLE,
                compliance=1.0,  # Open or standard OAuth2/eRA authentication supported
                evidence="Standard OAuth2 / Token authentication supported",
            )
        )

        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.A2,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.ACCESSIBLE,
                compliance=1.0 if resource.has_tombstone_policy else 0.0,
                evidence="Automated HTTP 410 Tombstone Policy registered" if resource.has_tombstone_policy else "Risk of HTTP 404 URL rot",
            )
        )

        # --- INTEROPERABLE (I1, I2, I3) ---
        has_ontologies = len(resource.ontology_uris) > 0
        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.I1,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.INTEROPERABLE,
                compliance=0.92 if has_ontologies else 0.2,
                evidence="RDF / Schema.org formal knowledge representation",
            )
        )

        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.I2,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.INTEROPERABLE,
                compliance=0.88 if has_ontologies else 0.1,
                evidence="Controlled vocabularies conform to FAIR ontologies",
            )
        )

        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.I3,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.INTEROPERABLE,
                compliance=0.85,
                evidence="Qualified cross-references to external ontology concepts",
            )
        )

        # --- REUSABLE (R1, R1.1, R1.2, R1.3) ---
        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.R1,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.REUSABLE,
                compliance=0.90,
                evidence="Comprehensive domain-specific attribute attributes",
            )
        )

        valid_spdx = {"CC-BY-4.0", "CC-BY-SA-4.0", "CC0-1.0", "MIT", "Apache-2.0"}
        has_license = bool(resource.license_spdx and resource.license_spdx in valid_spdx)
        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.R1_1,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.REUSABLE,
                compliance=1.0 if has_license else 0.0,
                evidence=f"Standard SPDX open license: {resource.license_spdx}" if has_license else "Missing or non-standard license",
            )
        )

        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.R1_2,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.REUSABLE,
                compliance=0.88,
                evidence="Detailed PROV-O machine-readable provenance trace",
            )
        )

        scores.append(
            FAIRFacetScore(
                facet=FAIRFacetID.R1_3,
                pillar=FAIRPillar.REUSABLE,
                compliance=0.92,
                evidence="Complies with W3C and domain-specific community schemas",
            )
        )

        return scores

    def compute_maturity_metrics(
        self, scores: List[FAIRFacetScore]
    ) -> Tuple[Dict[FAIRPillar, float], float, float]:
        """
        Computes intra-pillar means, linear maturity Phi_linear,
        and non-compensatory harmonic maturity Phi_strict.
        """
        pillar_groups: Dict[FAIRPillar, List[float]] = {p: [] for p in FAIRPillar}
        for s in scores:
            pillar_groups[s.pillar].append(s.compliance)

        pillar_means: Dict[FAIRPillar, float] = {}
        for p, vals in pillar_groups.items():
            pillar_means[p] = sum(vals) / len(vals) if vals else 0.0

        # Linear aggregation
        phi_linear = sum(self.pillar_weights[p] * pillar_means[p] for p in FAIRPillar)

        # Non-compensatory harmonic aggregation: ( sum beta_p * (mu_p + eps)^(-rho) )^(-1/rho)
        harmonic_sum = sum(
            self.pillar_weights[p] * ((pillar_means[p] + self.epsilon) ** (-self.rho))
            for p in FAIRPillar
        )
        phi_strict = (harmonic_sum) ** (-1.0 / self.rho)

        return pillar_means, phi_linear, phi_strict

    def simulate_reusability_half_life(self, phi_strict: float) -> float:
        """
        Calculates functional reusability half-life (years) under Vines decay formulation:
        lambda = lambda_0 * (1 - Phi_strict) + lambda_floor
        """
        lambda_0 = 0.170  # Annual uncurated decay (Vines et al., 2014)
        lambda_floor = 0.015  # Unavoidable domain ontology evolution
        effective_lambda = lambda_0 * (1.0 - min(1.0, phi_strict)) + lambda_floor
        half_life_years = math.log(2.0) / effective_lambda
        return half_life_years

    def generate_tombstone(
        self, resource: DigitalResourceManifest, reason: str, custodian: str
    ) -> TombstoneRecord:
        """
        Generates an RFC-compliant HTTP 410 Tombstone record under FAIR A2.
        """
        if not resource.doi:
            raise ValueError("Cannot generate tombstone for a resource lacking a permanent DOI.")

        payload_hash = resource.payload_sha256 or hashlib.sha256(b"dummy_payload").hexdigest()
        return TombstoneRecord(
            doi=resource.doi,
            retirement_timestamp="2026-11-13T08:00:00Z",
            retirement_reason=reason,
            original_payload_sha256=payload_hash,
            metadata_archive_url=f"https://zenodo.org/records/tombstone/{resource.doi.replace('/', '_')}",
            custodian_contact=custodian,
            http_status_code=410,
        )

    def run_full_audit(
        self, resource: DigitalResourceManifest, min_strict_threshold: float = 0.80
    ) -> FAIRAuditReport:
        """
        Executes end-to-end evaluation, checking certification criteria and diagnosing deficits.
        """
        scores = self.evaluate_resource(resource)
        pillar_means, phi_linear, phi_strict = self.compute_maturity_metrics(scores)
        half_life = self.simulate_reusability_half_life(phi_strict)

        diagnostics: List[str] = []
        for p, mean in pillar_means.items():
            if mean < 0.70:
                diagnostics.append(f"Pillar {p.value} has critical deficit: {mean:.3f} < 0.700")

        if phi_strict < min_strict_threshold:
            diagnostics.append(f"Strict index {phi_strict:.3f} below certification gate {min_strict_threshold:.3f}")

        is_certified = (phi_strict >= min_strict_threshold) and all(m >= 0.70 for m in pillar_means.values())

        return FAIRAuditReport(
            resource_name=resource.name,
            pillar_means=pillar_means,
            phi_linear=phi_linear,
            phi_strict=phi_strict,
            is_certified=is_certified,
            reusability_half_life_years=half_life,
            diagnostics=diagnostics,
        )


# =====================================================================
# Verification and Mathematical Invariant Assertions
# =====================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":
    engine = FAIRComplianceAssessmentEngine(rho_penalty=2.0)

    # 1. Evaluate a Gold-Standard FAIR Certified Resource
    gold_resource = DigitalResourceManifest(
        name="GlobalMarineMicrobiomeReference",
        doi="10.5281/zenodo.9482104",
        access_url="https://zenodo.org/records/9482104",
        license_spdx="CC-BY-4.0",
        ontology_uris=["https://schema.org/Dataset", "http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/"],
        has_tombstone_policy=True,
        is_indexed_in_search=True,
        is_payload_active=True,
        payload_sha256="4f8a3c89b211e041da567a9821ef3209841fba098231efbca120938475281902",
    )

    gold_report = engine.run_full_audit(gold_resource)
    print(f"--- GOLD RESOURCE AUDIT ---")
    print(f"Linear Maturity (Phi_linear): {gold_report.phi_linear:.4f}")
    print(f"Strict Maturity (Phi_strict): {gold_report.phi_strict:.4f}")
    print(f"Reusability Half-Life:        {gold_report.reusability_half_life_years:.1f} years")
    print(f"Certified:                    {gold_report.is_certified}")

    assert gold_report.is_certified, "Gold standard resource must pass certification"
    assert gold_report.phi_strict > 0.85, "Strict maturity must exceed 0.85"
    assert gold_report.reusability_half_life_years > 25.0, "FAIR half-life must exceed 25 years"

    # 2. Evaluate a Broken Resource (Compensatory vs Non-Compensatory Test)
    # Resource has perfect F, I, R but is completely inaccessible (A = 0)
    broken_resource = DigitalResourceManifest(
        name="LockedProprietarySilo",
        doi="10.5281/zenodo.0000000",
        access_url=None,  # No open protocol
        license_spdx="CC-BY-4.0",
        ontology_uris=["https://schema.org/Dataset"],
        has_tombstone_policy=False,  # No A2 tombstone
        is_indexed_in_search=True,
    )

    broken_report = engine.run_full_audit(broken_resource)
    print(f"\n--- BROKEN ACCESSIBILITY RESOURCE ---")
    print(f"Linear Maturity (Phi_linear): {broken_report.phi_linear:.4f}")
    print(f"Strict Maturity (Phi_strict): {broken_report.phi_strict:.4f}")
    print(f"Certified:                    {broken_report.is_certified}")

    # Theorem verification: Linear score appears acceptable (~0.7), but Strict score collapses!
    assert broken_report.phi_linear > 0.65, "Linear score misleadingly masks collapse"
    assert broken_report.phi_strict < 0.40, "Non-compensatory metric must penalize pillar collapse"
    assert not broken_report.is_certified, "Broken resource must fail certification"

    # 3. Test HTTP 410 Tombstone Generation under FAIR A2
    tombstone = engine.generate_tombstone(
        resource=gold_resource,
        reason="Biological specimens depleted; physical payload retracted to cold storage",
        custodian="data-steward@marine-consortium.org",
    )
    print(f"\n--- HTTP 410 TOMBSTONE RECORD ---")
    print(f"Status:   HTTP {tombstone.http_status_code} Gone")
    print(f"DOI:      {tombstone.doi}")
    print(f"Reason:   {tombstone.retirement_reason}")
    print(f"SHA-256:  {tombstone.original_payload_sha256[:16]}...")
    assert tombstone.http_status_code == 410, "Tombstone must return HTTP 410"

    print("\n[SUCCESS] All FAIR mathematical invariants and assertions verified successfully.")

docs.title: Case Study 1: Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) & Darwin Core Archive
docs.text:
The Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) is an international open data infrastructure funding ecological and climate research. GBIF aggregates over 2.4 billion species occurrence records from more than 2,000 publishing institutions across 150 nations (Wilkinson et al., 2016; Mons et al., 2017).

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        GBIF DARWIN CORE ARCHIVE (DwC-A) FEDERATION ARCHITECTURE                   |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Institution / Museum   | Native Schema      | DwC-A Mapper (I1)   | GBIF Central Ingest (F1-F4)   |
+------------------------+--------------------+---------------------+-------------------------------+
| Natural History London | Custom SQL Server  | DwC Taxon & Event   | Mint Dynamic Query DOI        |
| Smithsonian NMNH       | EMu Relational DB  | DwC Occurrence Core | W3C RDF Graph Canonical Hash  |
| Australian Herbarium   | BioCASt XML Export | Darwin Core XML/ZIP | Schema.org JSON-LD Crawl Index|
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| RESULT: 2.4 Billion heterogeneous biodiversity records unified into an autonomous FAIR ecosystem. |
| Global ecological researchers download reproducible query snapshots cited via permanent DOIs.   |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: FAIR Implementation Mechanisms:
docs.text:
1. Findability (\(F_1, F_4\)): When an ecological investigator filters an ad-hoc slice (e.g., all Apis mellifera occurrences in North America between 2010 and 2024), GBIF dynamically mints a query-specific Digital Object Identifier (DOI) through DataCite. The snapshot payload and its query AST are permanently archived.
  2. Interoperability (\(I_1, I_3\)): All participant museums export data using the Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) standard, anchoring scientific names to the GBIF Taxonomic Backbone. Synonyms are resolved deterministically across historical Latin nomenclatures without manual human intervention.
  3. Reusability (\(R_{1.1}, R_{1.2}\)): All occurrences enforce explicit machine-readable Creative Commons licenses (CC0, CC-BY, or CC-BY-NC). Datasets lacking clear SPDX identifiers are blocked at the ingestion gateway.

docs.title: Case Study 2: Genomic Data Commons (NCI GDC) & Controlled Access Tiering
docs.text:
A frequent misconception in data management is that the FAIR principles require open, public access for all files. The National Cancer Institute's Genomic Data Commons (GDC) manages multiple petabytes of high-throughput DNA and RNA sequencing data from clinical trials (TCGA, TARGET) while maintaining 100% FAIR compliance (Jacobsen et al., 2020; Boettiger, 2015).

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|               GENOMIC DATA COMMONS: TWO-TIER FAIR ACCESSIBILITY ARCHITECTURE                      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Security Tier         | Data Payload Assets                 | FAIR Facet Compliance               |
+-----------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| Tier 1: Open Access   | • High-level somatic mutations      | • F1-F4: Public DataCite DOIs       |
| (Unauthenticated)     | • Normalized gene expression values | • A1.1: Public HTTPS REST API       |
|                       | • Demographic summary tables        | • I1: Schema.org / NCIt ontologies  |
|                       | • Clinical metadata manifests       | • R1.1: Open Government Work license|
+-----------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| Tier 2: Controlled    | • Raw sequencing reads (FASTQ)      | • A1.2: Standard dbGaP Auth Protocol|
| (Authenticated)       | • Aligned BAM/CRAM files            | • eRA Commons cryptographic token   |
|                       | • Germline variant calls (VCF)      | • Machine-actionable access requests|
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: Operationalizing Principle \(A_{1.2}\):
docs.text: Under FAIR Principle \(A_{1.2}\), access to sensitive data must be governed by an open, standardized communications protocol that supports authentication and authorization. GDC fulfills this by: 1. Publishing all patient metadata, clinical phenotypes, and somatic mutation summaries on public, unauthenticated REST endpoints (\(A_1\)). 2. Requiring an automated OAuth2 token exchange linked to the NIH eRA Commons and dbGaP authorization service for germline sequences (\(A_{1.2}\)). 3. When clinical trials end and patient consent expires, the GDC automated archival system retracts raw sequencing files while maintaining the metadata endpoint with an HTTP 410 Gone Tombstone Record (\(A_2\)), ensuring that published cancer genomics papers maintain immutable scientific citation records.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Calculating Strict vs. Linear FAIR Maturity under Single-Pillar Failure
docs.text:
An autonomous data crawler audits an institutional biomedical archive containing 5,000 legacy clinical datasets. The automated audit reveals the following pillar compliance means: - \(\bar{\mu}_F = 0.96\) (High findability with DataCite DOIs) - \(\bar{\mu}_I = 0.92\) (Mapped to SNOMED-CT and Schema.org) - \(\bar{\mu}_R = 0.90\) (Clear CC-BY-4.0 licenses and PROV-O records) - \(\bar{\mu}_A = 0.05\) (The university storage SAN decommissioned the physical FTP servers, returning unhandled connection timeouts)

  1. Compute the linear maturity index \(\Phi_{\text{linear}}\) assuming equal pillar weights (\(w_p = 0.25\)).
  2. Compute the strict non-compensatory harmonic index \(\Phi_{\text{strict}}\) under penalty exponent \(\rho = 2.0\) with stability constant \(\epsilon = 10^{-6}\).
  3. Analyze the policy implications of using \(\Phi_{\text{linear}}\) versus \(\Phi_{\text{strict}}\) for enterprise repository certification.
Reveal Complete Step-by-Step Solution

Step 1: Calculating Linear FAIR Maturity \(\Phi_{\text{linear}}\)

Under equal weights \(w_p = 0.25\):

\[\Phi_{\text{linear}} = \sum_{p \in \{\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{I}, \mathbf{R}\}} w_p \bar{\mu}_p = 0.25 \times (0.96 + 0.05 + 0.92 + 0.90)\] \[\Phi_{\text{linear}} = 0.25 \times 2.83 = 0.7075 \quad (70.8\%)\]

Step 2: Calculating Strict Non-Compensatory Maturity \(\Phi_{\text{strict}}\)

Under Definition 13.4.1 with \(\rho = 2.0\), \(\beta_p = 0.25\), and \(\bar{\mu}_A = 0.05\):

\[\Phi_{\text{strict}} = \left( \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}} \beta_p \cdot (\bar{\mu}_p + \epsilon)^{-\rho} \right)^{-1/\rho} = \left( 0.25 \left[ (0.96)^{-2} + (0.05)^{-2} + (0.92)^{-2} + (0.90)^{-2} \right] \right)^{-1/2}\]

Computing each term: - \((0.96)^{-2} \approx 1.085\) - \((0.05)^{-2} = \frac{1}{0.0025} = 400.000\) - \((0.92)^{-2} \approx 1.181\) - \((0.90)^{-2} \approx 1.235\)

Summing the terms:

\[\sum = 1.085 + 400.000 + 1.181 + 1.235 = 403.501\]

Multiplying by weight \(\beta = 0.25\):

\[\text{Weighted Sum} = 0.25 \times 403.501 = 100.875\]

Taking the inverse exponent \(-1/2\):

\[\Phi_{\text{strict}} = (100.875)^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{100.875}} \approx \frac{1}{10.0437} \approx 0.0996 \quad (9.96\%)\]

Step 3: Policy Implications Analysis

  • Linear Metric Failure: Under \(\Phi_{\text{linear}}\), the archive scores 70.8%, achieving a passing "Silver" certification tier in many naïve repository evaluation schemes. However, researchers downloading the data face complete failure because the underlying files do not exist. Linear averaging permits high scores in metadata documentation to mask a total operational catastrophe.
  • Strict Metric Integrity: Under \(\Phi_{\text{strict}}\), the score collapses to 9.96%, reflecting the real-world reality that an inaccessible dataset has virtually zero functional utility. Non-compensatory harmonic evaluation prevents deceptive reporting and guarantees that certification gates block compromised archives.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Implementing an RFC-Compliant HTTP 410 Tombstone Manifest under FAIR \(A_2\)
docs.text:
A high-energy physics laboratory retires a 50-terabyte raw detector run (doi:10.5281/zenodo.4891024) due to tape media obsolescence, while retaining processed summary n-tuples.

  1. Explain the architectural error of returning an HTTP 404 Not Found versus an HTTP 410 Gone for retired datasets citing scientific literature.
  2. Construct the exact JSON-LD payload that the persistent identifier resolver must return when querying https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4891024 post-retirement, fulfilling FAIR Principle \(A_2\).
  3. Using the Vines decay formulation (\(\lambda_{\text{FAIR}} = \lambda_0 (1 - \Phi) + \lambda_{\text{floor}}\)), calculate the half-life of a dataset with \(\Phi_{\text{strict}} = 0.95\) versus \(\Phi_{\text{strict}} = 0.30\) assuming \(\lambda_0 = 0.170 \text{ yr}^{-1}\) and \(\lambda_{\text{floor}} = 0.015 \text{ yr}^{-1}\).
Reveal Complete Step-by-Step Solution

Step 1: HTTP 404 Not Found vs. HTTP 410 Gone

  • HTTP 404 Not Found indicates a transient or indeterminate condition: the server does not know whether the resource never existed, whether the URL was mistyped, or whether a routing error occurred. Web crawlers and automated verification agents interpret a 404 as broken link rot, and search engines eventually purge the URL from indexes.
  • HTTP 410 Gone is an authoritative, permanent status code defined in RFC 9110. It informs client agents that the target resource was intentionally removed, that no forwarding address exists, and that the removal is permanent. Under FAIR Principle \(A_2\), returning HTTP 410 accompanied by a machine-readable tombstone preserves citation integrity in scientific literature by proving that the cited DOI was valid and historically authentic.

Step 3: Calculating Functional Half-Life under Vines Formulation

The effective decay constant is given by:

\[\lambda = \lambda_0 (1 - \Phi) + \lambda_{\text{floor}}\]

For \(\Phi_{\text{strict}} = 0.95\) (FAIR Certified):

\[\lambda_{\text{high}} = 0.170 \times (1 - 0.95) + 0.015 = 0.170 \times 0.05 + 0.015 = 0.0085 + 0.015 = 0.0235 \text{ year}^{-1}\] \[t_{1/2}^{\text{high}} = \frac{\ln(2)}{\lambda_{\text{high}}} = \frac{0.69315}{0.0235} \approx 29.5 \text{ years}\]

For \(\Phi_{\text{strict}} = 0.30\) (Neglected / Non-FAIR):

\[\lambda_{\text{low}} = 0.170 \times (1 - 0.30) + 0.015 = 0.170 \times 0.70 + 0.015 = 0.1190 + 0.015 = 0.1340 \text{ year}^{-1}\] \[t_{1/2}^{\text{low}} = \frac{\ln(2)}{\lambda_{\text{low}}} = \frac{0.69315}{0.1340} \approx 5.17 \text{ years}\]

FAIR certification extends the functional half-life of scientific data from 5.2 years to 29.5 years—a 5.7-fold increase in research longevity.

docs.title: The Duality of Openness and Quality in Scientific Machine Learning
docs.text:
The open science movement has democratized artificial intelligence by providing global access to foundational training corpora, clinical cohorts, and scientific benchmarks. However, open access without rigorous quality verification and cryptographic provenance creates catastrophic systemic vulnerabilities (Wang & Strong, 1996; Schelter et al., 2018). When open datasets circulate across internet mirrors and community repositories, unversioned transformations, silent label corruptions, and missing sensor calibrations propagate downstream undetected (Sculley et al., 2015).

Provenance tracking is the formal mathematical discipline that reconstructs the causal chain of custody: where did data originate, who collected it, what computational transformations altered it, and what downstream artifacts depend upon it? (Moreau et al., 2011; Missier et al., 2013). Without machine-actionable provenance, modern data systems become vulnerable to cascading data poisoning, irreproducible experimental findings, and legal non-compliance (Baggerly & Coombes, 2009).

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        THE DUALITY OF OPENNESS AND PROVENANCE GOVERNANCE                          |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| UNMANAGED OPEN REPOSITORY         | MANAGED PROVENANCE PIPELINE (W3C PROV-O)                      |
| - Unversioned CSV/Tar drops       | - Directed Acyclic Multigraph of Entities, Activities, Agents |
| - Unknown upstream cleaning code  | - Causal Upstream Ancestry Reachability Cones                 |
| - Silent label corruption spreads | - Quantified Downstream Contamination Blast Radius            |
| - Untracked data leakage & drift  | - Cryptographic Merkle Lineage (H(v) = SHA256(Payload || H(u)))|
| - Off-by-one errors fatal         | - Enforced Temporal Consistency (t_gen <= t_start <= t_end)   |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: Mathematical Formulations of Dataset Quality & Provenance
docs.text: To model data transformation pipelines rigorously, we formulate four foundational mathematical definitions governing directed acyclic provenance multigraphs, causal error propagation, Merkle lineage immutability, and temporal consistency invariants.

docs.title: Definition 13.5.1: The W3C PROV Provenance Directed Acyclic Graph (PROV-DAG) & Causal Reachability Cone
docs.text:
Formally, a dataset provenance trace is modeled as a directed, edge-labeled bipartite multigraph conforming to the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) PROV specification (Moreau et al., 2011; Missier et al., 2013):

\[\mathcal{G}_{\text{prov}} = \left( \mathcal{V}_{\text{nodes}}, \mathcal{E}_{\text{edges}}, \tau \right)\]

where the vertex set \(\mathcal{V}_{\text{nodes}}\) is partitioned into three disjoint canonical classes:

\[\mathcal{V}_{\text{nodes}} = \mathcal{E}\text{ntity} \;\dot{\cup}\; \mathcal{A}\text{ctivity} \;\dot{\cup}\; \mathcal{A}\text{gent}\]
  1. Entities (\(\mathcal{E}\text{ntity}\)): Physical or digital data artifacts, file shards, feature tensors, and model weights (e.g., raw_data.csv, normalized_tokens.parquet).
  2. Activities (\(\mathcal{A}\text{ctivity}\)): Dynamic computational processes, data transformation jobs, and model training runs occurring over finite time intervals (e.g., clean_text(), train_resnet()).
  3. Agents (\(\mathcal{A}\text{gent}\)): Autonomous actors, human investigators, or automated CI/CD runners bearing responsibility (e.g., DataCurator_Alice, GitHubActions_Runner).

The directed edges \(\mathcal{E}_{\text{edges}}\) encode causal dependencies: - \(\text{wasGeneratedBy} \subset \mathcal{E}\text{ntity} \times \mathcal{A}\text{ctivity}\) - \(\text{used} \subset \mathcal{A}\text{ctivity} \times \mathcal{E}\text{ntity}\) - \(\text{wasDerivedFrom} \subset \mathcal{E}\text{ntity} \times \mathcal{E}\text{ntity}\) - \(\text{wasAssociatedWith} \subset \mathcal{A}\text{ctivity} \times \mathcal{A}\text{gent}\) - \(\text{wasAttributedTo} \subset \mathcal{E}\text{ntity} \times \mathcal{A}\text{gent}\)

For any target entity \(e \in \mathcal{E}\text{ntity}\), we define its Upstream Provenance Ancestry Cone \(\mathcal{A}_{\text{up}}(e)\) as the set of all causal ancestors reachable via backward edge traversal:

\[\mathcal{A}_{\text{up}}(e) = \left\{ u \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{nodes}} \;\middle|\; u \rightsquigarrow e \text{ in } \mathcal{G}_{\text{prov}} \right\}\]

Conversely, if an entity \(e\) is discovered to be corrupted, poisoned, or revoked under GDPR consent mandates, its Downstream Contamination Blast Radius \(\mathcal{B}_{\text{down}}(e)\) is the topological transitive closure of all affected descendants:

\[\mathcal{B}_{\text{down}}(e) = \left\{ v \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{nodes}} \;\middle|\; e \rightsquigarrow v \text{ in } \mathcal{G}_{\text{prov}} \right\}\]

Computing \(\mathcal{B}_{\text{down}}(e)\) enables targeted, minimal-cost invalidation and retraining, eliminating the catastrophic need to tear down unaffected pipeline partitions (Moreau et al., 2011).

docs.title: Definition 13.5.2: Causal Quality Attenuation & Error Propagation Bounds
docs.text:
Let each entity \(e \in \mathcal{E}\text{ntity}\) possess an audited quality metric \(Q(e) \in [0, 1]\) measuring composite data integrity (e.g., signal-to-noise ratio, label fidelity, or completeness Wang & Strong, 1996).

When an activity \(a \in \mathcal{A}\text{ctivity}\) consumes input entities \(\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}\) via \(\text{used}\) edges to generate an output entity \(e_{\text{out}}\) via \(\text{wasGeneratedBy}\), the transformation is governed by an intrinsic activity fidelity \(\eta_a \in (0, 1]\) and an additive noise injection parameter \(\xi_a \ge 0\):

\[Q(e_{\text{out}}) = \eta_a \cdot \min_{i=1,\dots,k} Q(e_i) - \xi_a\]

docs.title: Theorem 13.5.1 (Upstream Quality Attenuation Bound):
docs.text:
Consider a composite data processing pipeline forming a linear causal provenance path \(\pi = (e_0, a_1, e_1, a_2, \dots, a_L, e_L)\) of topological depth \(L\). The terminal entity quality \(Q(e_L)\) is strictly bounded by:

\[Q(e_L) \le Q(e_0) \cdot \prod_{j=1}^L \eta_{a_j} - \sum_{j=1}^L \xi_{a_j} \prod_{m=j+1}^L \eta_{a_m}\]

docs.title: Proof:
docs.text:
By induction on pipeline depth \(L\). For \(L = 1\), \(Q(e_1) = \eta_{a_1} Q(e_0) - \xi_{a_1}\), matching the theorem. Assuming the hypothesis holds for depth \(L - 1\):

\[Q(e_{L-1}) \le Q(e_0) \prod_{j=1}^{L-1} \eta_{a_j} - \sum_{j=1}^{L-1} \xi_{a_j} \prod_{m=j+1}^{L-1} \eta_{a_m}\]

Applying activity \(a_L\):

\[Q(e_L) = \eta_{a_L} Q(e_{L-1}) - \xi_{a_L} \le \eta_{a_L} \left( Q(e_0) \prod_{j=1}^{L-1} \eta_{a_j} - \sum_{j=1}^{L-1} \xi_{a_j} \prod_{m=j+1}^{L-1} \eta_{a_m} \right) - \xi_{a_L}\]

Distributing \(\eta_{a_L}\) yields the terminal expression. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Corollary 13.5.1 (Exponential Quality Decay):
docs.text:
If all pipeline activities have identical fidelity \(\eta \in (0, 1)\) and zero additive noise (\(\xi = 0\)), then as pipeline depth \(L \to \infty\):

\[\lim_{L \to \infty} Q(e_L) = Q(e_0) \cdot \lim_{L \to \infty} \eta^L = 0\]

This proves that unmonitored multi-step preprocessing pipelines inevitably destroy data fidelity unless intermediate activities incorporate active quality restoration filters (\(\eta \ge 1.0\)) (Wang & Strong, 1996; Schelter et al., 2018).

docs.title: Definition 13.5.3: Cryptographic Lineage Merkelization & Git-Tree Invariance
docs.text:
To guarantee immutability against retroactive tampering or silent bit rot in distributed open science repositories, the provenance DAG is mapped to a Directed Acyclic Merkle Graph (DAMG) (Boettiger, 2015; Stodden et al., 2016).

Each node \(v \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{nodes}}\) is assigned a cryptographic content identifier \(\mathcal{H}(v)\) recursively defined as:

\[\mathcal{H}(v) = \text{SHA256}\left( \text{Payload}(v) \parallel \text{sort}\left( \left\{ (p, \mathcal{H}(u)) \;\middle|\; (u, p, v) \in \mathcal{E}_{\text{edges}} \right\} \right) \right)\]

where \(\text{Payload}(v)\) is the byte content of entity \(v\) (or the serialized deterministic execution environment of activity \(v\)), and the incoming parent hashes are sorted lexicographically to preserve isomorphism invariance.

docs.title: Theorem 13.5.2 (Cryptographic Tamper-Evidence):
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{prov}}\) be a Merkle lineage graph. If any upstream raw dataset \(e_0\) or intermediate processing script \(a_k\) undergoes an unrecorded modification of even a single byte:

\[\Delta \text{Payload}(e_0) \neq 0 \implies \mathcal{H}(e_L)' \neq \mathcal{H}(e_L) \quad \text{with probability } 1 - 2^{-256}\]

Under the collision-resistance property of SHA-256, finding two distinct dataset pipelines that produce the same terminal model digest is computationally intractable, providing an unbroken cryptographic chain of custody (Boettiger, 2015).

docs.title: Definition 13.5.4: W3C PROV-O Constraint Satisfaction & Temporal Consistency Invariants
docs.text:
In open science, invalid provenance graphs often introduce subtle temporal paradoxes—such as models training on test data that was collected months later, or activities referencing data before it was generated. Formally, a valid W3C PROV trace must satisfy three first-order logic temporal constraints (Moreau et al., 2011; Missier et al., 2013):

  1. Generation-Usage Ordering Constraint: An activity cannot consume an entity before that entity was physically or digitally generated:

    \[\forall a \in \mathcal{A}, e \in \mathcal{E}: (a, \text{used}, e) \in \mathcal{E}_{\text{edges}} \implies t_{\text{gen}}(e) \le t_{\text{start}}(a)\]

  2. Activity Lifetime Invariant: The start of an activity must precede or equal its completion timestamp:

    \[\forall a \in \mathcal{A}: t_{\text{start}}(a) \le t_{\text{end}}(a)\]

  3. Generation-Invalidation Invariant: An entity must be generated before it is invalidated, and cannot be used after invalidation:

    \[\forall e \in \mathcal{E}: t_{\text{gen}}(e) \le t_{\text{inval}}(e) \quad \text{and} \quad \forall (a, \text{used}, e): t_{\text{end}}(a) \le t_{\text{inval}}(e)\]

Any provenance graph violating these constraints possesses a Temporal Inconsistency Deficit \(\Omega_{\text{temporal}} > 0\). In machine learning pipelines, temporal violations are the primary symptom of catastrophic look-ahead bias and covariate leakage, invalidating empirical performance claims (Sculley et al., 2015).

docs.title: 💻 Runnable Executable Python Implementation
docs.text:
The following production-grade implementation, DatasetQualityProvenanceEngine, provides complete mathematical validation for dataset provenance and quality tracking. It implements: 1. Pydantic V2 models for W3C PROV entities, activities, agents, and causal relations. 2. Exact calculation of Upstream Ancestry Cones \(\mathcal{A}_{\text{up}}\) and Downstream Blast Radii \(\mathcal{B}_{\text{down}}\) using breadth-first search. 3. Causal Quality Attenuation tracking implementing Theorem 13.5.1. 4. Cryptographic Merkle lineage hash cascade generation. 5. First-order logic temporal consistency validation and look-ahead paradox detection.

"""
DatasetQualityProvenanceEngine: Production-grade validation and mathematical auditing
for W3C PROV-O multigraphs, causal blast radius bounds, Merkle lineage hashing,
and temporal consistency invariants.
"""

from __future__ import annotations
import math
import hashlib
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Set, Tuple, Any
from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator, model_validator


class PROVNodeType(str, Enum):
    ENTITY = "Entity"
    ACTIVITY = "Activity"
    AGENT = "Agent"


class PROVEdgeType(str, Enum):
    WAS_GENERATED_BY = "wasGeneratedBy"  # Entity -> Activity
    USED = "used"                          # Activity -> Entity
    WAS_DERIVED_FROM = "wasDerivedFrom"  # Entity -> Entity
    WAS_ASSOCIATED_WITH = "wasAssociatedWith"  # Activity -> Agent
    WAS_ATTRIBUTED_TO = "wasAttributedTo"  # Entity -> Agent


class PROVNode(BaseModel):
    node_id: str = Field(..., min_length=1)
    node_type: PROVNodeType
    payload_hash: str = Field(..., min_length=8, description="Cryptographic SHA-256 of contents/env")
    quality_score: float = Field(default=1.0, ge=0.0, le=1.0, description="Quality metric Q in [0, 1]")
    t_start: Optional[float] = Field(default=None, description="Start timestamp (epoch seconds)")
    t_end: Optional[float] = Field(default=None, description="End / generation timestamp (epoch seconds)")


class PROVEdge(BaseModel):
    source_id: str = Field(..., min_length=1)
    target_id: str = Field(..., min_length=1)
    edge_type: PROVEdgeType
    activity_fidelity: float = Field(default=1.0, ge=0.0, le=1.0, description="Activity fidelity eta")
    noise_injection: float = Field(default=0.0, ge=0.0, description="Additive noise xi")


class BlastRadiusReport(BaseModel):
    corrupted_entity_id: str
    upstream_ancestry_size: int
    upstream_ancestry_nodes: List[str]
    blast_radius_size: int
    blast_radius_nodes: List[str]
    affected_models: List[str]
    terminal_quality: float


class DatasetQualityProvenanceEngine:
    """
    Mathematical engine implementing Definitions 13.5.1 through 13.5.4.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.nodes: Dict[str, PROVNode] = {}
        self.edges_out: Dict[str, List[PROVEdge]] = {}
        self.edges_in: Dict[str, List[PROVEdge]] = {}

    def add_node(self, node: PROVNode) -> None:
        self.nodes[node.node_id] = node
        self.edges_out.setdefault(node.node_id, [])
        self.edges_in.setdefault(node.node_id, [])

    def add_edge(self, edge: PROVEdge) -> None:
        if edge.source_id not in self.nodes or edge.target_id not in self.nodes:
            raise ValueError(f"Edge endpoints ({edge.source_id} -> {edge.target_id}) must exist in graph.")
        self.edges_out[edge.source_id].append(edge)
        self.edges_in[edge.target_id].append(edge)

    def compute_reachability_cones(self, target_id: str) -> Tuple[Set[str], Set[str]]:
        """
        Computes the Upstream Ancestry Cone A_up and Downstream Blast Radius B_down.
        """
        if target_id not in self.nodes:
            raise KeyError(f"Target node '{target_id}' not found.")

        # 1. Upstream Ancestry Cone (traverse edges_in)
        ancestry: Set[str] = set()
        queue = [target_id]
        while queue:
            curr = queue.pop(0)
            for edge in self.edges_in.get(curr, []):
                parent = edge.source_id
                if parent not in ancestry:
                    ancestry.add(parent)
                    queue.append(parent)

        # 2. Downstream Blast Radius (traverse edges_out)
        blast_radius: Set[str] = set()
        queue = [target_id]
        while queue:
            curr = queue.pop(0)
            for edge in self.edges_out.get(curr, []):
                child = edge.target_id
                if child not in blast_radius:
                    blast_radius.add(child)
                    queue.append(child)

        return ancestry, blast_radius

    def compute_quality_propagation(self, path: List[str]) -> float:
        """
        Evaluates Theorem 13.5.1 along a causal sequence of entities and activities.
        path: [e_0, a_1, e_1, a_2, ..., e_L]
        """
        if not path or path[0] not in self.nodes:
            raise ValueError("Invalid path sequence.")

        curr_quality = self.nodes[path[0]].quality_score

        for i in range(1, len(path)):
            prev_node = path[i - 1]
            curr_node = path[i]

            # Find edge
            matching_edges = [
                e for e in self.edges_out.get(prev_node, []) if e.target_id == curr_node
            ]
            if not matching_edges:
                raise ValueError(f"No direct edge found between {prev_node} and {curr_node}")

            edge = matching_edges[0]
            # Q_out = eta * Q_in - xi
            curr_quality = max(0.0, edge.activity_fidelity * curr_quality - edge.noise_injection)

        return curr_quality

    def compute_merkle_lineage_hash(self, target_id: str) -> str:
        """
        Recursively calculates the cryptographic Merkle content digest H(v).
        H(v) = SHA256( Payload(v) || sort( (pred, H(parent)) ) )
        """
        if target_id not in self.nodes:
            raise KeyError(f"Node '{target_id}' not found.")

        visited: Dict[str, str] = {}

        def dfs(node_id: str) -> str:
            if node_id in visited:
                return visited[node_id]

            parent_hashes: List[str] = []
            for edge in self.edges_in.get(node_id, []):
                parent_id = edge.source_id
                h_parent = dfs(parent_id)
                parent_hashes.append(f"{edge.edge_type.value}:{h_parent}")

            parent_hashes.sort()
            node_payload = self.nodes[node_id].payload_hash
            block = node_payload + "|" + "|".join(parent_hashes)
            digest = hashlib.sha256(block.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
            visited[node_id] = digest
            return digest

        return dfs(target_id)

    def validate_temporal_consistency(self) -> Tuple[bool, List[str]]:
        """
        Enforces Definition 13.5.4 first-order logic temporal constraints:
        1. Generation-Usage: t_gen(e) <= t_start(a) for (a, used, e)
        2. Activity Lifetime: t_start(a) <= t_end(a)
        """
        violations: List[str] = []

        for node in self.nodes.values():
            if node.node_type == PROVNodeType.ACTIVITY:
                if node.t_start is not None and node.t_end is not None:
                    if node.t_start > node.t_end:
                        violations.append(
                            f"Activity '{node.node_id}' has negative lifetime: start ({node.t_start}) > end ({node.t_end})"
                        )

        for edges in self.edges_out.values():
            for e in edges:
                src = self.nodes[e.source_id]
                tgt = self.nodes[e.target_id]

                # (Activity used Entity): Entity must be generated before Activity starts
                if e.edge_type == PROVEdgeType.USED:
                    # src is Activity, tgt is Entity
                    if tgt.t_end is not None and src.t_start is not None:
                        if tgt.t_end > src.t_start:
                            violations.append(
                                f"Look-ahead violation: Activity '{src.node_id}' used entity '{tgt.node_id}' before generation! (t_gen={tgt.t_end} > t_start={src.t_start})"
                            )

        is_valid = len(violations) == 0
        return is_valid, violations

    def generate_blast_radius_report(self, corrupted_entity_id: str) -> BlastRadiusReport:
        ancestry, blast_radius = self.compute_reachability_cones(corrupted_entity_id)
        affected_models = [
            nid for nid in blast_radius
            if self.nodes[nid].node_type == PROVNodeType.ENTITY and "model" in nid.lower()
        ]

        return BlastRadiusReport(
            corrupted_entity_id=corrupted_entity_id,
            upstream_ancestry_size=len(ancestry),
            upstream_ancestry_nodes=sorted(list(ancestry)),
            blast_radius_size=len(blast_radius),
            blast_radius_nodes=sorted(list(blast_radius)),
            affected_models=affected_models,
            terminal_quality=self.nodes[corrupted_entity_id].quality_score,
        )


# =====================================================================
# Verification and Mathematical Invariant Assertions
# =====================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":
    engine = DatasetQualityProvenanceEngine()

    # 1. Build an End-to-End Machine Learning Provenance DAG
    # Agents
    engine.add_node(PROVNode(node_id="Agent_LabTeam", node_type=PROVNodeType.AGENT, payload_hash="hash_lab_01"))

    # Stage 0: Raw Dataset
    engine.add_node(
        PROVNode(
            node_id="Entity_RawSensors",
            node_type=PROVNodeType.ENTITY,
            payload_hash="sha256_raw_sensors_v1",
            quality_score=0.98,
            t_start=100.0,
            t_end=150.0,
        )
    )

    # Stage 1: Cleaning Activity
    engine.add_node(
        PROVNode(
            node_id="Activity_Clean",
            node_type=PROVNodeType.ACTIVITY,
            payload_hash="sha256_script_clean_py",
            t_start=160.0,
            t_end=200.0,
        )
    )
    engine.add_edge(PROVEdge(source_id="Activity_Clean", target_id="Entity_RawSensors", edge_type=PROVEdgeType.USED))

    # Stage 1 Output: Cleaned Tokens
    engine.add_node(
        PROVNode(
            node_id="Entity_CleanTokens",
            node_type=PROVNodeType.ENTITY,
            payload_hash="sha256_clean_tokens_v1",
            quality_score=0.95,
            t_start=160.0,
            t_end=200.0,
        )
    )
    engine.add_edge(
        PROVEdge(
            source_id="Entity_CleanTokens",
            target_id="Activity_Clean",
            edge_type=PROVEdgeType.WAS_GENERATED_BY,
            activity_fidelity=0.97,
            noise_injection=0.01,
        )
    )

    # Stage 2: Training Activity
    engine.add_node(
        PROVNode(
            node_id="Activity_TrainModel",
            node_type=PROVNodeType.ACTIVITY,
            payload_hash="sha256_script_train_py",
            t_start=210.0,
            t_end=350.0,
        )
    )
    engine.add_edge(PROVEdge(source_id="Activity_TrainModel", target_id="Entity_CleanTokens", edge_type=PROVEdgeType.USED))

    # Stage 2 Output: Trained Weights
    engine.add_node(
        PROVNode(
            node_id="Entity_ModelWeights",
            node_type=PROVNodeType.ENTITY,
            payload_hash="sha256_model_weights_final",
            quality_score=0.91,
            t_start=210.0,
            t_end=350.0,
        )
    )
    engine.add_edge(
        PROVEdge(
            source_id="Entity_ModelWeights",
            target_id="Activity_TrainModel",
            edge_type=PROVEdgeType.WAS_GENERATED_BY,
            activity_fidelity=0.96,
            noise_injection=0.02,
        )
    )

    # 2. Test Reachability Cones
    ancestry, blast_radius = engine.compute_reachability_cones("Entity_CleanTokens")
    print(f"CleanTokens Ancestry Size: {len(ancestry)} (Expected >= 2)")
    print(f"CleanTokens Blast Radius Size: {len(blast_radius)} (Expected >= 2)")

    assert "Entity_RawSensors" in ancestry, "Raw sensors must be in upstream ancestry"
    assert "Entity_ModelWeights" in blast_radius, "Model weights must be in downstream blast radius"

    # 3. Test Causal Blast Radius Report
    report = engine.generate_blast_radius_report("Entity_RawSensors")
    print(f"\n--- BLAST RADIUS REPORT FOR RAW SENSORS ---")
    print(f"Affected Nodes Count: {report.blast_radius_size}")
    print(f"Affected Models:      {report.affected_models}")
    assert "Entity_ModelWeights" in report.affected_models, "Model must be flagged in blast radius"

    # 4. Test Cryptographic Merkle Lineage Invariance
    root_hash_initial = engine.compute_merkle_lineage_hash("Entity_ModelWeights")
    print(f"\nInitial Merkle Lineage Hash: {root_hash_initial}")

    # Perturb raw sensor payload (tampering test)
    engine.nodes["Entity_RawSensors"].payload_hash = "sha256_raw_sensors_TAMPERED"
    root_hash_tampered = engine.compute_merkle_lineage_hash("Entity_ModelWeights")
    print(f"Tampered Merkle Lineage Hash: {root_hash_tampered}")

    assert root_hash_initial != root_hash_tampered, "Merkle root must change under upstream perturbation!"

    # 5. Test Temporal Consistency Validation
    is_valid, violations = engine.validate_temporal_consistency()
    print(f"\nTemporal Validation Status: {'VALID' if is_valid else 'VIOLATIONS'}")
    assert is_valid, f"Graph should be temporally consistent, got violations: {violations}"

    # Inject Look-Ahead Leakage Paradox (Activity starts before entity generated)
    engine.nodes["Activity_Clean"].t_start = 120.0  # Before Entity_RawSensors t_end=150.0
    is_valid_paradox, violations_paradox = engine.validate_temporal_consistency()
    print(f"Paradox Injected Status: {'VALID' if is_valid_paradox else 'PARADOX CAUGHT'}")
    print(f"Violations Logged: {violations_paradox}")
    assert not is_valid_paradox, "Engine must catch look-ahead temporal paradox!"

    print("\n[SUCCESS] All quality and provenance mathematical assertions passed.")

docs.title: Case Study 1: The Duke University Oncology Clinical Trial Retraction
docs.text:
In 2006, researchers at Duke University led by Anil Potti published landmark papers in Nature Medicine and the New England Journal of Medicine, claiming that genomic microarray expression profiles could predict patient sensitivity to specific chemotherapy regimens with over 90% accuracy. Based on these findings, Duke launched three major clinical trials assigning cancer patients to toxic chemotherapy drugs.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        THE DUKE ONCOLOGY PROVENANCE COLLAPSE                                      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Forensic Investigators: Keith Baggerly & Kevin Coombes (MD Anderson Biostatisticians, 2009)     |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| FAILURE DISCOVERED: Off-By-One Spreadsheet Row Offset Swapped Drug Sensitivity Labels            |
| • Forensic investigation required > 1,500 hours of manual "data archaeology"                      |
| • Undocumented Excel scripts shifted gene rows by one index relative to patient drug responses    |
| • Sensitivity and resistance labels were completely inverted for multiple clinical compounds      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| SYSTEMIC OUTCOME: 10 Major Papers Retracted | Clinical Trials Halted | Criminal Lawsuits Filed    |
| Proved that scientific reproducibility without machine-actionable provenance is a fatal liability.|
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: Forensic Findings & Provenance Failure (Baggerly & Coombes, 2009):
docs.text:
1. Unversioned Ad-Hoc Scripts: The Duke laboratory maintained no Git version control, no data hashing, and no recorded pipeline logs. Spreadsheets were manually manipulated and passed between graduate students via email.
  2. The Off-By-One Shift: Baggerly and Coombes discovered that a simple copy-paste error shifted the microarray expression matrix down by one row relative to the patient outcome column. The algorithm was effectively learning noise, and in several drug panels, recommending therapies that were toxic to non-responders.
  3. The Provenance Invariant Solution: Under Definition 13.5.3 (Cryptographic Lineage Merkelization), every transformation script and raw shard produces a deterministic Merkle root. A single row permutation alters the cryptographic hash \(\mathcal{H}(v)\), halting automated CI/CD deployment before clinical trials can begin (Baggerly & Coombes, 2009; Stodden et al., 2016).

docs.title: Operationalizing Causal Blast Radius at Scale:
docs.text: When automated quality linters identify that an upstream web crawl contained contaminated benchmark solutions (e.g., leaked GSM8K or HumanEval evaluation sets), discarding the entire pre-training corpus is economically prohibitive. By implementing the W3C PROV-O reachability model (Definition 13.5.1): 1. The contaminated URL domain is registered as a tainted Entity node \(e_{\text{tainted}}\). 2. The blast radius engine computes \(\mathcal{B}_{\text{down}}(e_{\text{tainted}})\), isolating the exact \(14\) Parquet token shards that ingested documents from that domain. 3. Engineers surgically filter the affected token shards and apply continuous checkpoint rollback or targeted weight unlearning, saving millions of dollars in compute while preserving model integrity (Sculley et al., 2015; Boettiger, 2015).
