docs.title: 1. Historical Bias (World-to-Data Divergence)
docs.text:
Historical bias occurs when the data-generation process accurately and faithfully reflects existing socio-economic disparities, systemic prejudices, or historical inequities:

\[\Pr_{\text{world}}(Y = 1 \mid A = 0) \neq \Pr_{\text{world}}(Y = 1 \mid A = 1)\]

Even if sampling, measurement, and annotation are mathematically perfect, an empirical risk minimizer optimizes for historical status-quo reproduction rather than normative equity.

docs.title: 2. Sampling Selection Bias & Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW)
docs.text:
Selection bias occurs when the probability of an observation being selected into the training dataset (\(S = 1\)) is conditionally dependent on the features \(\mathbf{X}\) or protected attribute \(A\):

\[\Pr(S = 1 \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}, A = a) \neq \Pr(S = 1)\]

Let \(\pi(\mathbf{x}, a) = \Pr(S = 1 \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}, A = a) > 0\) denote the propensity of selection. The empirical distribution of sampled data \(P_{\text{sample}}(\mathbf{X})\) diverges from the population \(P_{\text{pop}}(\mathbf{X})\).

To recover unbiased population estimates of any target parameter \(\mu_Y = \mathbb{E}[Y]\), we apply the Horvitz-Thompson Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) Estimator:

\[\hat{\mu}_{\text{HT}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{S_i Y_i}{\pi(\mathbf{X}_i, A_i)}\]

docs.title: Unbiasedness Proof of Horvitz-Thompson IPW
docs.text:
Taking the expectation over the joint distribution of \((S, \mathbf{X}, A, Y)\):

\[\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}_{\text{HT}}] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{S_i Y_i}{\pi(\mathbf{X}_i, A_i)} \right] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}, A, Y} \left[ \frac{\mathbb{E}[S_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i, A_i, Y_i] Y_i}{\pi(\mathbf{X}_i, A_i)} \right]\]

Under the missing-at-random (MAR) assumption, \(\mathbb{E}[S_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i, A_i, Y_i] = \Pr(S_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{X}_i, A_i) = \pi(\mathbf{X}_i, A_i)\):

\[\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}_{\text{HT}}] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}, A, Y} \left[ \frac{\pi(\mathbf{X}_i, A_i) Y_i}{\pi(\mathbf{X}_i, A_i)} \right] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}[Y_i] = \mu_Y \quad \blacksquare\]

In practice, the self-normalized Hajek Estimator is preferred due to reduced finite-sample variance:

\[\hat{\mu}_{\text{Hajek}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{S_i Y_i}{\pi(\mathbf{X}_i, A_i)}}{\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{S_i}{\pi(\mathbf{X}_i, A_i)}}\]

docs.title: 3. Measurement Error: Classical vs. Differential Attenuation
docs.text: When predictors \(\mathbf{X}\) are recorded through physical sensors, survey instruments, or administrative databases, measurement noise distorts the relationship with target \(Y\).

docs.title: Classical Measurement Error & Regression Dilution (Attenuation Bias)
docs.text:
Let true predictor \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_X^2)\) be unobservable. Instead, we observe \(X^* = X + u\), where \(u \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)\) is zero-mean noise independent of \(X\) and regression disturbance \(\epsilon\). The true underlying data-generating process is:

\[Y = \beta X + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\epsilon^2)\]

When Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regresses \(Y\) onto the noisy measurement \(X^*\), the estimated slope is:

\[\hat{\beta} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X^*, Y)}{\text{Var}(X^*)} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X + u, \beta X + \epsilon)}{\text{Var}(X + u)}\]

Because \(u \perp X\), \(u \perp \epsilon\), and \(X \perp \epsilon\):

\[\text{Cov}(X + u, \beta X + \epsilon) = \beta \text{Cov}(X, X) + \text{Cov}(X, \epsilon) + \beta \text{Cov}(u, X) + \text{Cov}(u, \epsilon) = \beta \sigma_X^2\] \[\text{Var}(X + u) = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_u^2\]

Substituting gives the classical attenuation formula:

\[\hat{\beta} = \beta \cdot \left( \frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_u^2} \right) = \beta \cdot \lambda_{\text{rel}}\]

where \(\lambda_{\text{rel}} = \frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_u^2} \in (0, 1]\) is the reliability ratio. The estimated relationship is strictly attenuated (shrunk towards zero).

docs.title: Differential Measurement Error Across Demographic Groups
docs.text:
In socio-technical systems, measurement error is rarely classical; sensor accuracy depends directly on demographic attributes \(A\):

\[\sigma_{u \mid A = 0}^2 \gg \sigma_{u \mid A = 1}^2\]

Consequently, group-specific reliability ratios diverge:

\[\lambda_0 = \frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_{u \mid A = 0}^2} \ll \lambda_1 = \frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_{u \mid A = 1}^2} \approx 1.0\]
  • For privileged Group 1, the model recovers \(\hat{\beta}_1 \approx \beta\).
  • For unprivileged Group 0, the model estimates \(\hat{\beta}_0 = \beta \cdot \lambda_0 \ll \beta\).

[!WARNING] The Algorithmic Consequence of Differential Attenuation: An automated scoring system will perceive the feature \(X\) as substantially less predictive or reliable for Group 0. In multi-feature models, the estimator will discard or downweight \(X\) for Group 0 in favor of spurious demographic correlates, driving predictive inequality [Obermeyer2019].

docs.title: 4. Proxy Label Bias & The Obermeyer Health Disparity
docs.text:
Proxy label bias occurs when the true target concept \(Y^*\) is unobservable or legally restricted, forcing engineers to substitute an accessible operational proxy \(\tilde{Y}\):

\[\tilde{Y} = g(Y^*, A) + \eta\]

In 2019, Obermeyer et al. uncovered a massive commercial healthcare algorithm affecting \(>200\) million patients [Obermeyer2019]: - Target Concept: True healthcare need \(Y^*\) (number of active chronic conditions, severity of heart failure, diabetes). - Engineered Proxy: Total healthcare annual costs \(\tilde{Y}\). - Structural Distortion: Due to unequal access to healthcare, insurance disparities, and discriminatory physician utilization patterns, less money was historically spent on Black patients relative to White patients at identical illness levels: $\(\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y} \mid Y^* = y, A = \text{Black}] < \mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y} \mid Y^* = y, A = \text{White}]\)$ - Result: To qualify for specialized high-risk care management programs (threshold \(\tilde{Y} > \tau\)), Black patients had to be significantly sicker than White patients. Remedying the proxy label bias boosted the proportion of Black patients enrolled from \(17.7\%\) to \(46.5\%\).

docs.title: 5. Aggregation Bias & Simpson's Reversal in Loss Minimization
docs.text:
Aggregation bias occurs when a single model is fitted across heterogeneous sub-populations where the true underlying conditional mapping varies by group:

\[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathbf{X}, A = 0] \neq \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathbf{X}, A = 1]\]

Consider two groups where within each group, feature \(X\) has a positive effect on outcome \(Y\) (\(\beta_0 > 0, \beta_1 > 0\)). If group centroids are offset such that the group with higher \(X\) has lower baseline intercept, a global pooled regression can produce a negative overall slope:

\[\hat{\beta}_{\text{pooled}} = \frac{\sum_{i} (X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sum_{i} (X_i - \bar{X})^2} < 0\]

Fitting a pooled estimator minimizes average population risk, sacrificing the minority subgroup whose local conditional relationship is completely reversed by aggregate loss optimization.

docs.title: 6. Intersectional Under-Representation & Gender Shades
docs.text:
Representation bias scales exponentially worse across intersectional demographic identities [Buolamwini2018]. Let demographic attributes be decomposed into independent dimensions (e.g., gender \(G \in \{M, F\}\), skin phenotype \(P \in \{L, D\}\)). If collection achieves marginal balance:

\[\Pr(G = F) = 0.50, \quad \Pr(P = D) = 0.50\]

Convenience sampling often severely depletes the intersectional slice:

\[\Pr(G = F, P = D) \ll 0.25\]

In the landmark Gender Shades study by Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru [Buolamwini2018], commercial facial classification APIs achieved \(>99\%\) accuracy on lighter males, but error rates exploded to \(34.7\%\) on darker females.

[!TIP] Industrial Best Practice: Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al., 2021) & Model Cards (Mitchell et al., 2019) Accompany every production dataset with a standardized Datasheet for Datasets and downstream Model Card. Document explicit answers to: 1. Motivation: For what purpose was the dataset created? Who funded it? 2. Composition: What do the instances represent? Are protected attributes recorded? Are sensitive sub-populations oversampled or underrepresented? 3. Collection Process: What sampling mechanism was deployed? Was consent obtained? 4. Pre-processing: What cleaning, imputation, or filtering operations were executed?

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation & Pydantic V2 Verification Suite
docs.text:
Below is an executable Python suite with Pydantic V2 validating the three key quantitative dataset bias phenomena: 1. Sampling Selection Bias & Horvitz-Thompson Recovery: Verifies unbiased population mean recovery via inverse probability weighting. 2. Measurement Error Attenuation: Verifies the closed-form reliability ratio \(\lambda = \frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_u^2}\) against empirical regression dilution. 3. Proxy Label Bias (Obermeyer Simulation): Demonstrates how substituting healthcare cost for clinical illness severely undercounts the health needs of minority patients.

# test_ch7_p2_pydantic.py
# Production Implementation & Pydantic V2 Verification Suite for Lesson 7.2

from typing import Dict, List, Any
import numpy as np
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class SamplingBiasAudit(BaseModel):
    true_population_mean: float = Field(..., description="True population mean mu_Y")
    biased_sample_mean: float = Field(..., description="Unweighted sample mean under selection bias")
    ht_weighted_mean: float = Field(..., description="Horvitz-Thompson IPW reconstructed mean")
    hajek_weighted_mean: float = Field(..., description="Self-normalized Hajek IPW mean")
    unweighted_error: float
    ipw_error: float
    ipw_recovery_successful: bool

class MeasurementErrorAudit(BaseModel):
    true_beta: float = Field(..., description="True underlying structural slope")
    var_x: float = Field(..., description="Variance of true latent predictor X")
    var_u_group0: float = Field(..., description="Sensor noise variance for Group 0")
    var_u_group1: float = Field(..., description="Sensor noise variance for Group 1")
    theoretical_lambda_group0: float = Field(..., description="Reliability ratio for Group 0")
    theoretical_lambda_group1: float = Field(..., description="Reliability ratio for Group 1")
    empirical_slope_group0: float
    empirical_slope_group1: float
    group0_attenuation_pct: float
    attenuation_proven: bool

class ProxyLabelBiasAudit(BaseModel):
    target_enrolled_rate_privileged: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    target_enrolled_rate_unprivileged: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    mean_illness_enrolled_privileged: float
    mean_illness_enrolled_unprivileged: float
    illness_severity_disparity: float
    proxy_bias_confirmed: bool

def audit_sampling_selection() -> SamplingBiasAudit:
    np.random.seed(42)
    n = 60000
    x = np.random.normal(50.0, 10.0, n)
    y = 2.0 * x + np.random.normal(0, 5.0, n)
    pop_mean = float(np.mean(y))

    # Selection probability: pi(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(x - 50) / 8))
    pi = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(x - 50.0) / 8.0))
    s = (np.random.uniform(0, 1, n) < pi).astype(int)

    unweighted_mean = float(np.mean(y[s == 1]))
    ht_mean = float(np.sum((s * y) / pi) / n)
    hajek_mean = float(np.sum((s * y) / pi) / np.sum(s / pi))

    unw_err = abs(unweighted_mean - pop_mean)
    ipw_err = abs(hajek_mean - pop_mean)

    return SamplingBiasAudit(
        true_population_mean=round(pop_mean, 4),
        biased_sample_mean=round(unweighted_mean, 4),
        ht_weighted_mean=round(ht_mean, 4),
        hajek_weighted_mean=round(hajek_mean, 4),
        unweighted_error=round(unw_err, 4),
        ipw_error=round(ipw_err, 4),
        ipw_recovery_successful=(ipw_err < 0.10 and unw_err > 5.0)
    )

def audit_measurement_error() -> MeasurementErrorAudit:
    np.random.seed(42)
    n = 80000
    sigma_x = 1.5
    var_x = sigma_x ** 2
    true_beta = 2.40

    x = np.random.normal(0, sigma_x, n)
    y = true_beta * x + np.random.normal(0, 1.0, n)

    # Differential noise
    sigma_u0 = 2.60 # Noisy sensor
    var_u0 = sigma_u0 ** 2
    sigma_u1 = 0.30 # Clean sensor
    var_u1 = sigma_u1 ** 2

    x_star0 = x + np.random.normal(0, sigma_u0, n)
    x_star1 = x + np.random.normal(0, sigma_u1, n)

    lambda0 = var_x / (var_x + var_u0)
    lambda1 = var_x / (var_x + var_u1)

    slope0 = float(np.cov(x_star0, y)[0, 1] / np.var(x_star0))
    slope1 = float(np.cov(x_star1, y)[0, 1] / np.var(x_star1))

    att_pct = (1.0 - slope0 / true_beta) * 100.0
    match = abs(slope0 - (true_beta * lambda0)) < 0.05

    return MeasurementErrorAudit(
        true_beta=true_beta,
        var_x=round(var_x, 4),
        var_u_group0=round(var_u0, 4),
        var_u_group1=round(var_u1, 4),
        theoretical_lambda_group0=round(lambda0, 4),
        theoretical_lambda_group1=round(lambda1, 4),
        empirical_slope_group0=round(slope0, 4),
        empirical_slope_group1=round(slope1, 4),
        group0_attenuation_pct=round(att_pct, 2),
        attenuation_proven=match
    )

def audit_proxy_label_bias() -> ProxyLabelBiasAudit:
    np.random.seed(42)
    n = 20000
    # Group 0 (Black, 20%), Group 1 (White, 80%)
    group = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=n, p=[0.2, 0.8])
    true_illness = np.random.normal(3.0, 1.0, size=n)

    # Expenditure proxy: $4000 per illness unit for Group 1, but only $2600 for Group 0
    costs = np.where(group == 1, 4000.0 * true_illness, 2600.0 * true_illness) + np.random.normal(0, 400, size=n)

    # Healthcare management enrollment threshold: top 15% predicted by cost
    tau = np.percentile(costs, 85)
    enrolled = costs >= tau

    rate_0 = float(np.mean(enrolled[group == 0]))
    rate_1 = float(np.mean(enrolled[group == 1]))

    mean_ill_0 = float(np.mean(true_illness[enrolled & (group == 0)]))
    mean_ill_1 = float(np.mean(true_illness[enrolled & (group == 1)]))

    return ProxyLabelBiasAudit(
        target_enrolled_rate_privileged=round(rate_1, 4),
        target_enrolled_rate_unprivileged=round(rate_0, 4),
        mean_illness_enrolled_privileged=round(mean_ill_1, 2),
        mean_illness_enrolled_unprivileged=round(mean_ill_0, 2),
        illness_severity_disparity=round(mean_ill_0 - mean_ill_1, 2),
        proxy_bias_confirmed=(rate_0 < 0.05 and (mean_ill_0 - mean_ill_1) > 1.5)
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    samp_audit = audit_sampling_selection()
    meas_audit = audit_measurement_error()
    proxy_audit = audit_proxy_label_bias()

    print("=== 1. Sampling Selection Bias & Horvitz-Thompson IPW Audit ===")
    print(f"  True Population Mean : {samp_audit.true_population_mean}")
    print(f"  Biased Sample Mean   : {samp_audit.biased_sample_mean} (Error: {samp_audit.unweighted_error})")
    print(f"  Hajek Reconstructed  : {samp_audit.hajek_weighted_mean} (Error: {samp_audit.ipw_error})")
    print(f"  IPW Recovery Success : {samp_audit.ipw_recovery_successful}")

    print("\n=== 2. Measurement Error & Attenuation Dilution Audit ===")
    print(f"  True Beta Slope      : {meas_audit.true_beta}")
    print(f"  Group 1 OLS Slope    : {meas_audit.empirical_slope_group1} (Reliability: {meas_audit.theoretical_lambda_group1})")
    print(f"  Group 0 OLS Slope    : {meas_audit.empirical_slope_group0} (Reliability: {meas_audit.theoretical_lambda_group0})")
    print(f"  Group 0 Attenuation  : -{meas_audit.group0_attenuation_pct}%")
    print(f"  Attenuation Proven   : {meas_audit.attenuation_proven}")

    print("\n=== 3. Proxy Label Bias (Obermeyer Science 2019) Audit ===")
    print(f"  Group 1 Enrolled Rate: {proxy_audit.target_enrolled_rate_privileged * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Group 0 Enrolled Rate: {proxy_audit.target_enrolled_rate_unprivileged * 100:.1f}% (Severe Under-Enrollment)")
    print(f"  Illness at Admission : Group 0 = {proxy_audit.mean_illness_enrolled_unprivileged} vs Group 1 = {proxy_audit.mean_illness_enrolled_privileged}")
    print(f"  Severity Disparity   : +{proxy_audit.illness_severity_disparity} Illness Units")
    print(f"  Proxy Bias Confirmed : {proxy_audit.proxy_bias_confirmed}")

    assert samp_audit.ipw_recovery_successful, "IPW population recovery audit failed!"
    assert meas_audit.attenuation_proven, "Measurement attenuation proof failed!"
    assert proxy_audit.proxy_bias_confirmed, "Proxy label bias audit failed!"
    print("\n[PASS] All Pydantic V2 Dataset Bias Mechanisms Validated Successfully.")

docs.title: 🔬 Empirical Case Studies: Physical & Algorithmic Reality
docs.text:
1. Pulse Oximeter Optical Hypoxemia Disparity in COVID-19:
  2. Clinical Context: Pulse oximeters estimate arterial oxygen saturation (\(SpO_2\)) non-invasively by emitting red (\(660\,\text{nm}\)) and infrared (\(940\,\text{nm}\)) light through tissue.
  3. Differential Measurement Mechanism: The calibration curves connecting light absorption to oxygen saturation were fitted almost exclusively on fair-skinned European cohorts. Melanin absorbs light in the same optical window, introducing differential measurement error on patients with darker skin pigmentation.

  4. Clinical Consequence: The sensor systematically overestimated blood oxygen saturation on Black and Hispanic COVID-19 patients, causing occult hypoxemia (\(SaO_2 < 88\%\)) to go undetected at nearly triple the frequency of White patients, delaying supplemental oxygen therapy and emergency ICU admissions [Sjoding2020].

  5. Computer Vision Geographic & Cultural Benchmark Skew:

  6. The Dollar Street & ImageNet Audits: Shankar et al. (2017) and DeVries et al. (2019) demonstrated that \(>80\%\) of images in standard computer vision benchmarks (ImageNet, Open Images) originated from the United States and Europe.
  7. Representation Failure: State-of-the-art vision models recognized US wedding dresses and dish soap brands with \(>98\%\) accuracy, but failed completely on traditional Nigerian or Indian bridal attire, classifying them as "costumes" or "theatrical performers."

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment 1: Deriving the Reliability Ratio for Attenuation Bias

In a simple linear regression \(Y = \beta X + \epsilon\) with \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_X^2)\), suppose \(X\) is measured through a noisy sensor \(X^* = X + u\) with \(u \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)\) and \(u \perp X\). Prove why \(\text{plim} \; \hat{\beta}_{\text{OLS}} = \beta \frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_u^2}\).

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: The OLS estimator of slope is: $\(\hat{\beta} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i^* - \bar{X}^*)(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i^* - \bar{X}^*)^2}\)$ By the Weak Law of Large Numbers: $\(\text{plim} \; \hat{\beta} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X^*, Y)}{\text{Var}(X^*)} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X + u, \beta X + \epsilon)}{\text{Var}(X + u)}\)$ Expanding numerator covariance: $\(\text{Cov}(X + u, \beta X + \epsilon) = \beta \text{Cov}(X, X) + \text{Cov}(X, \epsilon) + \beta \text{Cov}(u, X) + \text{Cov}(u, \epsilon)\)$ Since disturbances \(\epsilon\) and sensor noise \(u\) are mutually independent of each other and of \(X\), the last three terms vanish to 0, leaving \(\beta \text{Var}(X) = \beta \sigma_X^2\).

Expanding denominator variance: $\(\text{Var}(X + u) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(u) + 2\text{Cov}(X, u) = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_u^2\)$ Therefore: $\(\text{plim} \; \hat{\beta} = \beta \cdot \left( \frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_u^2} \right) = \beta \lambda_{\text{rel}} < \beta \quad \blacksquare\)$

Self-Assessment 2: Unbiasedness of Horvitz-Thompson Estimator

Why does standard sample mean \(\bar{Y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\) fail under selection bias, and how does weighting by \(w_i = 1 / \pi_i\) restore unbiasedness?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - Under selection bias, inclusion indicator \(S_i\) is correlated with \(Y_i\) (or covariates \(\mathbf{X}_i\) predictive of \(Y\)). Thus \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid S_i = 1] \neq \mathbb{E}[Y_i]\), meaning the observed sample mean is systematically biased. - In the Horvitz-Thompson estimator \(\hat{\mu}_{\text{HT}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{S_i Y_i}{\pi_i}\), taking conditional expectations over \(S_i\) yields: $\(\mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{S_i Y_i}{\pi_i} \,\middle|\, \mathbf{X}_i, Y_i \right] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[S_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i, Y_i] Y_i}{\pi_i} = \frac{\pi_i Y_i}{\pi_i} = Y_i\)$ - Weighting each observed unit inversely by its sampling probability accounts for the underrepresented fraction of the target population that the unit represents.

Self-Assessment 3: The Obermeyer Proxy Trap

Suppose an automated hiring algorithm seeks to predict "Employee Productivity" \(Y^*\), but uses "Manager Performance Ratings" \(\tilde{Y}\) as a training target. Explain why this constitutes proxy label bias if female employees receive lower ratings for identical output due to subjective evaluator stereotypes.

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - The true target is productive output \(Y^*\). The operational training label is \(\tilde{Y} = Y^* - \delta \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{Gender} = F) + \epsilon\), where \(\delta > 0\) reflects cognitive evaluator bias. - An ML model optimized to minimize loss on \(\tilde{Y}\) will internalize that female employees have lower expected labels for identical skill profiles: $\(\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y} \mid \mathbf{X}, F] < \mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y} \mid \mathbf{X}, M]\)$ - The model will actively discriminate against qualified female candidates, not because female employees are less productive, but because the engineered proxy conflated productivity with subjective human appraisal bias.

Self-Assessment 4: Simpson's Paradox in Aggregation Bias

Can an algorithm produce a negative predicted relationship between income and creditworthiness across the whole population if the relationship is positive within every single ethnic subgroup?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - Yes. This is the classic definition of Simpson's Paradox (Aggregation Bias). - If Group 1 has high average income but faces a lower historical credit scale due to regional or baseline differences, while Group 0 has low average income but a higher baseline credit score, pooling the data into a single regression line connects the low-income/high-score cluster to the high-income/low-score cluster, generating a negative pooled slope. - Minimizing global empirical risk without group stratification forces the model to learn an inverse relationship that is false for all individuals within every subgroup.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & Statistical Formulations
docs.text:
Auditing tabular datasets and model outputs for systematic bias requires quantitative statistical testing across demographic slices. Rather than relying on intuition or raw aggregate accuracy, modern fairness engineering employs distribution divergence bounds [Feldman2015, Hardt2016], optimal transport distances, individual-group entropy decompositions [Speicher2018], and hypothesis testing suites provided by standard toolkits like Fairlearn [Weerts2023] and AIF360 [Bellamy2019].

docs.title: 1. Mathematical Formulations of Continuous Distributional Divergence
docs.text: Let \(A \in \{0, 1\}\) denote the binary sensitive demographic attribute (where \(A=0\) represents the unprivileged cohort and \(A=1\) represents the privileged cohort). Let \(S \in \mathbb{R}\) denote a continuous prediction score (e.g., credit rating, insurance premium, probability of recidivism), with group conditional cumulative distribution functions \(F_0(s) = \Pr(S \le s \mid A = 0)\) and \(F_1(s) = \Pr(S \le s \mid A = 1)\).

docs.title: 1. Two-Sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov Statistic (\(D_{\text{KS}}\))
docs.text:
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic quantifies the maximal vertical distance between the two empirical CDFs:

\[D_{\text{KS}} = \sup_{s \in \mathbb{R}} |F_0(s) - F_1(s)|\]

Under the null hypothesis of distributional parity (\(H_0: F_0 = F_1\)), the normalized statistic converges asymptotically to the Kolmogorov distribution:

\[\sqrt{\frac{n_0 n_1}{n_0 + n_1}} D_{\text{KS}} \xrightarrow{d} K, \quad \Pr(K \le x) = 1 - 2 \sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1} e^{-2 k^2 x^2}\]

A statistically significant \(p < 0.01\) provides strong evidence that the continuous scoring mechanism treats the two demographic cohorts as fundamentally different statistical populations.

docs.title: 2. Wasserstein-1 Distance & Kantorovitch-Rubinstein Duality
docs.text:
While the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test measures only the single largest vertical discrepancy, it is completely insensitive to horizontal tail translations (e.g., whether scores in the privileged group extend far higher into executive tiers).

The Wasserstein-1 Distance (Earth Mover's Distance) measures the minimal total probability-weighted work required to transport distribution \(P_0\) into \(P_1\):

\[\mathcal{W}_1(P_0, P_1) = \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(P_0, P_1)} \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y) \sim \gamma}[|X - Y|]\]

By the Kantorovitch-Rubinstein Duality Theorem, this primal formulation equates to a maximization over all 1-Lipschitz test functions:

\[\mathcal{W}_1(P_0, P_1) = \sup_{\|f\|_{\text{Lip}} \le 1} \left( \mathbb{E}_{X \sim P_0}[f(X)] - \mathbb{E}_{Y \sim P_1}[f(Y)] \right)\]

In one dimension, this dual form simplifies to the exact closed-form integrated horizontal area between the two cumulative distributions, or equivalently the \(L_1\) distance between their quantile functions \(F_0^{-1}\) and \(F_1^{-1}\):

\[\mathcal{W}_1(P_0, P_1) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty |F_0(x) - F_1(x)| \, dx = \int_0^1 |F_0^{-1}(u) - F_1^{-1}(u)| \, du\]

[!NOTE] Why Wasserstein-1 is Superior for Continuous Fairness Audits: Wasserstein-1 preserves the actual metric units of the underlying feature (e.g., credit points, dollar wage gaps). If an employer shifts male salaries upward by USD 10,000, \(D_{\text{KS}}\) reports an abstract vertical divergence bounded in \([0, 1]\), whereas \(\mathcal{W}_1\) directly reports \(\mathcal{W}_1 = \text{USD } 10,000\) in exact monetary transport work [Feldman2015].

docs.title: 3. Theil Index of Inequality & Between-Group Entropy Decomposition
docs.text:
Originating from econometric welfare theory, the Theil index provides a mathematically rigorous bridge connecting individual fairness (treating similar individuals similarly via Lipschitz metric constraints [Dwork2012]) with group fairness (statistical parity and predictive rate consistency [Chouldechova2017], [Kleinberg2016], [Speicher2018]).

Let individual benefit be defined as \(b_i = \hat{y}_i - y_i + 1 > 0\) (a strictly positive measure of algorithmic advantage relative to true status). The population Theil index is:

\[T = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}} \ln\left( \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}} \right), \quad \bar{b} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N b_i\]

docs.title: Additive Decomposition Proof
docs.text:
Partition the population of size \(N\) into \(K\) disjoint demographic subgroups of size \(N_k\), with subgroup mean benefits \(\bar{b}_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_{i \in G_k} b_i\).

Expanding the summand by introducing \(\bar{b}_k\):

\[T = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i \in G_k} \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}} \ln\left( \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}_k} \cdot \frac{bar{b}_k}{\bar{b}} \right) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i \in G_k} \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}} \left[ \ln\left( \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}_k} \right) + \ln\left( \frac{\bar{b}_k}{\bar{b}} \right) \right]\]

Splitting into two distinct additive components:

\[T = \sum_{k=1}^K \left( \frac{N_k}{N} \frac{\bar{b}_k}{\bar{b}} \right) \underbrace{\left[ \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_{i \in G_k} \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}_k} \ln\left( \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}_k} \right) \right]}_{T_k \text{ (Within-Group Theil)}} + \sum_{k=1}^K \left( \frac{N_k}{N} \frac{\bar{b}_k}{\bar{b}} \right) \ln\left( \frac{\bar{b}_k}{\bar{b}} \right)\]

Defining group benefit weights \(w_k = \frac{N_k}{N} \frac{\bar{b}_k}{\bar{b}}\):

\[T = \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^K w_k T_k}_{T_{\text{within}} \text{ (Individual Unfairness)}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^K w_k \ln\left( \frac{\bar{b}_k}{\bar{b}} \right)}_{T_{\text{between}} \text{ (Group Disparity)}} \quad \blacksquare\]
  • \(T_{\text{within}}\) measures unfairness within demographic slices (inconsistent treatment of individuals with identical profiles).
  • \(T_{\text{between}}\) measures systematic disparity between groups. If demographic parity is achieved (\(\bar{b}_k = \bar{b}\) for all \(k\)), then \(\ln(1) = 0\), driving \(T_{\text{between}} = 0\) while leaving individual performance differences in \(T_{\text{within}}\).

docs.title: 2. Hypothesis Testing for Disparate Selection Rates
docs.text: When decisions are binarized (\(\\hat{Y} \\in \\{0, 1\\}\)), compliance is governed by civil rights statutes (e.g., EEOC Four-Fifths Rule).

docs.title: 1. Disparate Impact Ratio (DIR) & The 80% Rule
docs.text:
Let \(\hat{p}_0 = \Pr(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 0)\) and \(\hat{p}_1 = \Pr(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 1)\). The Disparate Impact Ratio is:

\[\text{DIR} = \frac{\hat{p}_0}{\hat{p}_1}\]

Adverse impact is legally presumed if \(\text{DIR} < 0.80\).

docs.title: 2. Two-Proportion Pooled Z-Test
docs.text:
To test whether an observed selection gap is statistically significant rather than finite-sample noise (\(H_0: p_0 = p_1\)):

\[Z = \frac{\hat{p}_0 - \hat{p}_1}{\sqrt{\bar{p}(1 - \bar{p}) \left( \frac{1}{n_0} + \frac{1}{n_1} \right)}}, \quad \bar{p} = \frac{Y_0 + Y_1}{n_0 + n_1}\]

where \(Y_g\) is the count of positive selections in group \(g\). Under \(H_0\), \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), and the two-tailed \(p\)-value is \(2(1 - \Phi(|Z|))\).

docs.title: 3. Exact Non-Parametric Permutation Resampling
docs.text:
When demographic sub-slices are small (\(n_0 < 50\)), asymptotic normality fails. Permutation testing shuffles sensitive group labels \(B = 10,000\) times across pooled data to compute an exact finite-sample empirical null distribution:

\[p_{\text{perm}} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \mathbb{I}\left( |\bar{S}_{0, b} - \bar{S}_{1, b}| \ge |\bar{S}_{0, \text{obs}} - \bar{S}_{1, \text{obs}}| \right)\] 
flowchart TD
    Pool["Pool Observations (N = n0 + n1)"] --> Obs["1. Calculate Observed Gap T_obs = |mean_0 - mean_1|"]
    Obs --> Perm["2. Randomly Permute Protected Labels A in {0, 1} (B = 10,000 rounds)"]
    Perm --> Null["3. Compute Disparity T_b under H0: Group Invariance"]
    Null --> PVal["4. Calculate Exact p-value: (1/B) sum(I(T_b >= T_obs))"]

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation & Pydantic V2 Verification Suite
docs.text:
Below is a self-contained, typed Python testing suite with Pydantic V2 validating the three key pillars of statistical fairness auditing: 1. Continuous Divergence Audit: Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and Wasserstein-1 transport work. 2. Theil Entropy Subgroup Decomposition: Verifies exact additive decomposition into \(T_{\text{within}}\) and \(T_{\text{between}}\) (\(|T - (T_{\text{within}} + T_{\text{between}})| < 10^{-10}\)). 3. Exact Permutation Resampling & Disparate Impact Z-Test: Evaluates Title VII compliance against the Four-Fifths rule with statistical significance.

# test_ch7_p3_pydantic.py
# Production Implementation & Pydantic V2 Verification Suite for Lesson 7.3

from typing import Dict, List, Any
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class ContinuousDivergenceAudit(BaseModel):
    n_group0: int
    n_group1: int
    mean_group0: float
    mean_group1: float
    ks_statistic: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    ks_p_value: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    wasserstein_1_distance: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    theil_total_entropy: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    theil_within_group: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    theil_between_group: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    theil_decomposition_exact: bool

class PermutationTestAudit(BaseModel):
    n_permutations: int
    observed_difference: float
    permutation_p_value: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    two_proportion_z_score: float
    asymptotic_p_value: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    statistically_significant: bool

class DisparateImpactHypothesisAudit(BaseModel):
    selection_rate_unprivileged: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    selection_rate_privileged: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    disparate_impact_ratio: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    violates_four_fifths_rule: bool
    confidence_interval_95: List[float]

def audit_continuous_divergence() -> ContinuousDivergenceAudit:
    np.random.seed(42)
    n0, n1 = 1500, 2000
    s0 = np.random.normal(0.50, 0.15, n0)
    s1 = np.random.normal(0.66, 0.15, n1)

    ks_stat, ks_pval = stats.ks_2samp(s0, s1)
    w1_dist = float(stats.wasserstein_distance(s0, s1))

    # Theil Index Subgroup Decomposition
    min_val = min(np.min(s0), np.min(s1))
    b0 = s0 - min_val + 0.05
    b1 = s1 - min_val + 0.05
    b_all = np.concatenate([b0, b1])

    b_bar = float(np.mean(b_all))
    b0_bar = float(np.mean(b0))
    b1_bar = float(np.mean(b1))

    t_total = float(np.mean((b_all / b_bar) * np.log(b_all / b_bar)))
    t0 = float(np.mean((b0 / b0_bar) * np.log(b0 / b0_bar)))
    t1 = float(np.mean((b1 / b1_bar) * np.log(b1 / b1_bar)))

    w0 = (n0 / (n0 + n1)) * (b0_bar / b_bar)
    w1_wt = (n1 / (n0 + n1)) * (b1_bar / b_bar)

    t_within = w0 * t0 + w1_wt * t1
    t_between = w0 * np.log(b0_bar / b_bar) + w1_wt * np.log(b1_bar / b_bar)

    decomp_match = abs(t_total - (t_within + t_between)) < 1e-10

    return ContinuousDivergenceAudit(
        n_group0=n0,
        n_group1=n1,
        mean_group0=round(float(np.mean(s0)), 4),
        mean_group1=round(float(np.mean(s1)), 4),
        ks_statistic=round(float(ks_stat), 4),
        ks_p_value=float(ks_pval),
        wasserstein_1_distance=round(w1_dist, 4),
        theil_total_entropy=round(t_total, 4),
        theil_within_group=round(t_within, 4),
        theil_between_group=round(t_between, 4),
        theil_decomposition_exact=decomp_match
    )

def audit_permutation_resampling(b_rounds: int = 2000) -> PermutationTestAudit:
    np.random.seed(42)
    n0, n1 = 60, 140
    s0 = np.random.normal(0.50, 0.15, n0)
    s1 = np.random.normal(0.58, 0.15, n1)

    t_obs = abs(float(np.mean(s1) - np.mean(s0)))
    pooled = np.concatenate([s0, s1])
    n_total = len(pooled)

    extreme_count = 0
    for _ in range(b_rounds):
        perm = np.random.permutation(n_total)
        p0_mean = np.mean(pooled[perm[:n0]])
        p1_mean = np.mean(pooled[perm[n0:]])
        if abs(p1_mean - p0_mean) >= t_obs:
            extreme_count += 1

    p_perm = float(extreme_count / b_rounds)

    # Asymptotic Z-test benchmark
    pooled_var = float(np.var(pooled, ddof=1))
    se = np.sqrt(pooled_var * (1.0 / n0 + 1.0 / n1))
    z = t_obs / se
    p_asymp = float(2.0 * (1.0 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z))))

    return PermutationTestAudit(
        n_permutations=b_rounds,
        observed_difference=round(t_obs, 4),
        permutation_p_value=round(p_perm, 4),
        two_proportion_z_score=round(float(z), 4),
        asymptotic_p_value=round(p_asymp, 6),
        statistically_significant=(p_perm < 0.05)
    )

def audit_disparate_impact_proportions(hired0: int = 35, total0: int = 100, 
                                      hired1: int = 120, total1: int = 200) -> DisparateImpactHypothesisAudit:
    p0 = hired0 / total0
    p1 = hired1 / total1
    dir_val = p0 / p1

    # 95% Confidence Interval for Relative Risk (DIR) via Katz log-method
    log_dir = np.log(dir_val)
    se_log = np.sqrt((1 - p0) / (total0 * p0) + (1 - p1) / (total1 * p1))
    ci_lower = float(np.exp(log_dir - 1.96 * se_log))
    ci_upper = float(np.exp(log_dir + 1.96 * se_log))

    return DisparateImpactHypothesisAudit(
        selection_rate_unprivileged=round(p0, 4),
        selection_rate_privileged=round(p1, 4),
        disparate_impact_ratio=round(dir_val, 4),
        violates_four_fifths_rule=(dir_val < 0.80),
        confidence_interval_95=[round(ci_lower, 4), round(ci_upper, 4)]
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cont_res = audit_continuous_divergence()
    perm_res = audit_permutation_resampling(b_rounds=2000)
    di_res = audit_disparate_impact_proportions()

    print("=== 1. Continuous Distribution Divergence & Theil Audit ===")
    print(f"  Wasserstein-1 Distance    : {cont_res.wasserstein_1_distance}")
    print(f"  Kolmogorov-Smirnov D_KS   : {cont_res.ks_statistic} (p-val: {cont_res.ks_p_value:.2e})")
    print(f"  Total Theil Entropy       : {cont_res.theil_total_entropy}")
    print(f"  Theil Within (Individual) : {cont_res.theil_within_group}")
    print(f"  Theil Between (Group Gap) : {cont_res.theil_between_group}")
    print(f"  Additive Proof Exact      : {cont_res.theil_decomposition_exact}")

    print("\n=== 2. Non-Parametric Permutation Resampling Audit ===")
    print(f"  Observed Disparity T_obs  : {perm_res.observed_difference}")
    print(f"  Permutation p-value       : {perm_res.permutation_p_value}")
    print(f"  Asymptotic Z-Score        : {perm_res.two_proportion_z_score}")
    print(f"  Statistically Significant : {perm_res.statistically_significant}")

    print("\n=== 3. Disparate Impact Ratio & Katz 95% Confidence Bounds ===")
    print(f"  Selection Rate (A=0, A=1) : {di_res.selection_rate_unprivileged} vs {di_res.selection_rate_privileged}")
    print(f"  Disparate Impact Ratio    : {di_res.disparate_impact_ratio}")
    print(f"  Four-Fifths Violation     : {di_res.violates_four_fifths_rule}")
    print(f"  Katz 95% CI Range         : {di_res.confidence_interval_95}")

    assert cont_res.theil_decomposition_exact, "Theil additive decomposition check failed!"
    assert perm_res.statistically_significant, "Permutation significance test failed!"
    assert di_res.violates_four_fifths_rule, "Title VII violation detection failed!"
    print("\n[PASS] All Pydantic V2 Statistical Fairness Auditing Schemas Validated Successfully.")

docs.title: 🔬 Empirical Case Study: Automated Hiring Algorithms & Mortgage Lending
docs.text:
1. Amazon's Automated Resume Screener:
  2. Audit Findings: The algorithm assigned resume relevance scores on a continuous scale \([0.0, 1.0]\). A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on applicant cohorts revealed \(D_{\text{KS}} = 0.38\) between male and female candidates.

  3. The Role of Wasserstein-1: While binarized hiring at top \(5\%\) showed adverse impact, the Wasserstein metric revealed that the entire female score distribution was shifted downward by \(\mathcal{W}_1 = 0.14\) across all percentiles due to penalty weights attached to gendered resume tokens.

  4. FinTech Mortgage Lending Audits (HMDA Data):

  5. Context: Automated underwriting systems evaluated loan approval probability based on financial telemetry.
  6. Theil Index Decomposition: By decomposing applicant entropy across racial cohorts, regulators proved that between-group inequality (\(T_{\text{between}}\)) accounted for \(>28\%\) of total entropy variation, establishing evidence of systemic disparate impact even after controlling for applicant creditworthiness [Speicher2018].

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment 1: Kolmogorov-Smirnov Distance vs. Wasserstein-1 Distance

Contrast how the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (\(D_{\text{KS}}\)) and Wasserstein-1 (\(\mathcal{W}_1\)) metrics evaluate distributional divergence between two demographic score distributions. In what scenario does \(D_{\text{KS}}\) fail to capture severe distributional unfairness?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - Kolmogorov-Smirnov (\(D_{\text{KS}}\)): Measures the single maximal vertical difference between two CDF curves: $\(D_{\text{KS}} = \sup_s |F_0(s) - F_1(s)|\)$ - Wasserstein-1 (\(\mathcal{W}_1\)): Measures the integrated horizontal work required to transform one distribution into the other: $\(\mathcal{W}_1 = \int_0^1 |F_0^{-1}(u) - F_1^{-1}(u)| \, du\)$

Failure Scenario for \(D_{\text{KS}}\): Suppose \(F_0\) and \(F_1\) have a modest maximum vertical gap (\(D_{\text{KS}} = 0.12\)), but in the upper tail (scores \(> 800\)), Group 1 scores extend to \(950\) while Group 0 scores truncate at \(810\). \(D_{\text{KS}}\) treats this massive horizontal tail gap identically to a minor local shift, whereas \(\mathcal{W}_1\) directly integrates the huge distance, correctly flagging the severe tail exclusion [Feldman2015].

Self-Assessment 2: Why Is the Theil Index Uniquely Decomposable?

Why is the Theil Index preferred over the Gini Coefficient when auditing individual versus group unfairness in machine learning?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - The Gini coefficient is not strictly additively decomposable; when group distributions overlap, its decomposition includes an intractable residual "transvariation" term. - The Theil Index belongs to the family of Generalized Entropy Indices (\(I(1)\)), which satisfies the axiom of strong additive decomposability: $\(T = T_{\text{within}} + T_{\text{between}}\)$ - This allows auditors to isolate exactly what fraction of overall inequality is caused by systematic demographic disparity (\(T_{\text{between}}\)) versus within-group performance dispersion (\(T_{\text{within}}\)) [Speicher2018].

Self-Assessment 3: Minimum Sample Size & Type II Error in Bias Auditing

Suppose an audit evaluates an unprivileged subgroup with \(n_0 = 16\) applicants and a privileged group with \(n_1 = 200\). The selection rates are \(\hat{p}_0 = 0.25\) and \(\hat{p}_1 = 0.45\) (DIR = \(0.55\), severe violation). Calculate why a standard two-tailed proportion test might yield \(p > 0.05\) and explain the regulatory danger of confusing non-significance with fairness.

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - With \(n_0 = 16\), the standard error of the difference in proportions is: $\(\text{SE} \approx \sqrt{0.43 \times 0.57 \times \left( \frac{1}{16} + \frac{1}{200} \right)} \approx \sqrt{0.245 \times 0.0675} \approx 0.128\)$ - The \(Z\)-score is \(Z = \frac{0.25 - 0.45}{0.128} = -1.56\), yielding \(p \approx 0.118 > 0.05\). - Regulatory Danger: A test underpowered by small sample size fails to reject the null hypothesis. Concluding that the algorithm is "fair" commits a fatal Type II error. Auditors must report confidence intervals and minimum detectable effect sizes rather than relying solely on \(p\)-values.

Self-Assessment 4: The Katz Logarithmic Confidence Interval for DIR

Why do auditors compute confidence intervals on \(\ln(\text{DIR})\) rather than directly on \(\text{DIR} = \hat{p}_0 / \hat{p}_1\)?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - The ratio of two random variables \(\text{DIR} = \hat{p}_0 / \hat{p}_1\) has a highly skewed, non-normal distribution in finite samples (bounded below by 0, but unbounded above). - By taking the natural logarithm \(\ln(\text{DIR}) = \ln(\hat{p}_0) - \ln(\hat{p}_1)\), the distribution converges much more rapidly to asymptotic normality via the Delta Method: $\(\text{Var}(\ln(\text{DIR})) \approx \frac{1 - p_0}{n_0 p_0} + \frac{1 - p_1}{n_1 p_1}\)$ - Transforming the symmetric confidence interval back via exponentiation guarantees that the lower bound remains strictly non-negative and correctly reflects asymmetric ratio variance.

Visualizing disparities is crucial for communicating complex fairness tradeoffs to multi-disciplinary stakeholders, auditors, and legal compliance officers. Tabular accuracy numbers alone obscure the fundamental tensions between false-positive burdens and true-positive allocations, particularly across intersectional demographic groups [Buolamwini2018]. Modern fairness engineering synthesizes multi-metric disparity matrices, subgroup calibration curves, and ROC Pareto frontiers to guide threshold adjustments and post-processing mitigations [Weerts2023, Bellamy2019].

docs.title: 1. The Rank-2 Metric Disparity Tensor
docs.text:
To evaluate multi-faceted disparities across intersecting demographic slices, fairness auditing engines construct a rank-2 Disparity Metric Tensor \(\mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{G \times K}\):

\[\mathbf{M}_{g, k} = \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y) \sim \mathcal{D}_g}\left[ \mu_k(f(X), Y) \right]\]

where \(g \in \{1, \dots, G\}\) indexes demographic subgroups and \(\mu_k\) represents the \(k\)-th fairness evaluation metric (e.g., Selection Rate, Accuracy, True Positive Rate, False Positive Rate).

From this tensor, auditors compute the Extreme Disparity Spread \(\Delta_k\) and the Disparate Impact Ratio \(\rho_k\):

\[\Delta_k = \max_{g} \mathbf{M}_{g, k} - \min_{g'} \mathbf{M}_{g', k}, \qquad \rho_k = \frac{\min_{g'} \mathbf{M}_{g', k}}{\max_{g} \mathbf{M}_{g, k}}\]

The Four-Fifths rule requires \(\rho_{\text{selection}} \ge 0.80\), while Equalized Odds demands \(\Delta_{\text{TPR}} \le \epsilon\) and \(\Delta_{\text{FPR}} \le \epsilon\).

docs.title: 2. Subgroup Calibration Geometry & Expected Calibration Error (ECE)
docs.text:
A continuous risk score or predicted probability \(R \in [0, 1]\) is perfectly calibrated within protected demographic group \(A\) if the observed empirical success rate matches the nominal confidence score [Pleiss2017]:

\[\Pr(Y = 1 \mid R = r, A = a) = r \quad \forall a \in \{0, 1\}, \; \forall r \in [0, 1]\]

On a visual calibration plot (reliability diagram): - Diagonal Parity Line (\(45^\circ\)): Indicates perfect statistical calibration. - Points Above the Diagonal (\(y > x\)): The model under-estimates true capability/risk (e.g., predicting \(40\%\) probability of repayment for a group that repays at \(60\%\)). - Points Below the Diagonal (\(y < x\)): The model over-estimates risk, injecting systematic punitive bias into allocation decisions.

docs.title: Quantitative Metric: Subgroup Expected Calibration Error (ECE)
docs.text:
Partition the prediction range \([0, 1]\) into \(B\) discrete bins \(\{I_b\}_{b=1}^B\) with bin width \(1/B\). For group \(a\):

\[\text{ECE}_a = \sum_{b=1}^B \frac{|I_b^{(a)}|}{|D_a|} \left| \text{acc}(I_b^{(a)}) - \text{conf}(I_b^{(a)}) \right|\]

where \(|I_b^{(a)}|\) is the number of group \(a\) instances falling into bin \(b\), \(\text{conf}(I_b^{(a)}) = \frac{1}{|I_b^{(a)}|} \sum_{i \in I_b^{(a)}} R_i\) is the average predicted confidence, and \(\text{acc}(I_b^{(a)}) = \frac{1}{|I_b^{(a)}|} \sum_{i \in I_b^{(a)}} Y_i\) is the empirical ground truth accuracy.

docs.title: 3. Group-Specific ROC Convex Hulls & Equalized Odds Operating Thresholds
docs.text:
Each demographic group \(a \in \{0, 1\}\) generates a distinct Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve parameterized by continuous decision threshold \(\tau_a \in [0, 1]\):

\[\text{ROC}_a(\tau_a) = \left( \text{FPR}_a(\tau_a), \; \text{TPR}_a(\tau_a) \right)\]

Under a single uniform decision threshold \(\tau_0 = \tau_1 = 0.50\), differing score distributions almost always produce unequal error rates:

\[\text{FPR}_0(0.50) \neq \text{FPR}_1(0.50) \quad \text{or} \quad \text{TPR}_0(0.50) \neq \text{TPR}_1(0.50)\]

Achieving Equalized Odds requires locating a pair of group-specific operating thresholds \((\tau_0^*, \tau_1^*)\) where the two coordinates coincide:

\[\text{FPR}_0(\tau_0^*) = \text{FPR}_1(\tau_1^*), \qquad \text{TPR}_0(\tau_0^*) = \text{TPR}_1(\tau_1^*)\]

By the Hardt-Price-Srebro Theorem [Hardt2016], any point in the intersection of the convex hulls of the two group ROC curves is achievable through randomized or group-specific thresholding.

docs.title: Multi-Objective Threshold Optimization
docs.text:
Auditors solve the constrained Pareto optimization problem:

\[\max_{\tau_0, \tau_1} \sum_{a \in \{0, 1\}} p_a \text{Acc}_a(\tau_a) \quad \text{subject to } \Delta_{\text{AOD}}(\tau_0, \tau_1) \le \epsilon\]

where Average Absolute Odds Disparity is defined as:

\[\Delta_{\text{AOD}}(\tau_0, \tau_1) = \frac{1}{2} \left( |\text{FPR}_0(\tau_0) - \text{FPR}_1(\tau_1)| + |\text{TPR}_0(\tau_0) - \text{TPR}_1(\tau_1)| \right)\]

[!TIP] Industrial Best Practice: Fairlearn MetricFrame in Automated CI/CD Gates Never compute global accuracy without subgroup stratification. In enterprise continuous integration (CI/CD) pipelines, instantiate a MetricFrame tracking selection rate, false positive rate, and error rate across every demographic slice on every model checkpoint commit [Weerts2023]. If \(\text{DIR} < 0.80\) or \(\Delta_{\text{AOD}} > 0.10\), fail the deployment build automatically.

[!WARNING] Common Pitfall / Anti-Pattern: Visualizing Calibration Without Group Disaggregation A predictive model can be globally perfectly calibrated across the pooled population while suffering catastrophic miscalibration within every demographic subgroup (the subgroup calibration paradox). Always plot separate calibration curves per protected group [Pleiss2017].

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation & Pydantic V2 Verification Suite
docs.text:
Below is a self-contained, typed Python testing suite with Pydantic V2 validating: 1. Subgroup Calibration & ECE Audit: Evaluates 10-bin expected calibration error across demographic slices. 2. Dual-Threshold ROC Optimization: Computes the Pareto frontier coordinates that minimize \(\Delta_{\text{AOD}}\). 3. Multi-Metric Disparity Matrix: Validates extreme disparity spreads across accuracy, selection rate, and error margins.

# test_ch7_p4_pydantic.py
# Production Implementation & Pydantic V2 Verification Suite for Lesson 7.4

from typing import Dict, List, Tuple, Any
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class CalibrationECEAudit(BaseModel):
    n_bins: int = Field(default=10)
    ece_group0: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    ece_group1: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    disparity_delta_ece: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    global_pooled_ece: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    subgroup_miscalibration_detected: bool

class EqualizedOddsOptimizationAudit(BaseModel):
    uncalibrated_threshold: float
    uncalibrated_aod_disparity: float
    optimal_threshold_group0: float
    optimal_threshold_group1: float
    minimized_aod_disparity: float
    disparity_mitigated: bool

class FairnessMetricFrameAudit(BaseModel):
    selection_rate_group0: float
    selection_rate_group1: float
    accuracy_group0: float
    accuracy_group1: float
    tpr_group0: float
    tpr_group1: float
    fpr_group0: float
    fpr_group1: float
    disparate_impact_ratio: float
    average_odds_difference: float

def audit_subgroup_ece() -> CalibrationECEAudit:
    np.random.seed(42)
    n = 3000
    group = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=n, p=[0.4, 0.6])

    # Group 1 well calibrated
    p1 = np.random.beta(2.5, 2.5, size=n)
    # Group 0 under-confident / miscalibrated
    p0 = np.random.beta(1.8, 3.2, size=n)
    probs = np.where(group == 1, p1, p0)
    labels = (np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=n) < probs).astype(int)

    def calc_ece(y_true, y_prob, n_bins=10):
        bin_edges = np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1)
        ece = 0.0
        for b in range(n_bins):
            in_bin = (y_prob >= bin_edges[b]) & (y_prob < bin_edges[b+1])
            if np.sum(in_bin) > 0:
                acc = np.mean(y_true[in_bin])
                conf = np.mean(y_prob[in_bin])
                weight = np.sum(in_bin) / len(y_true)
                ece += weight * abs(acc - conf)
        return float(ece)

    ece0 = calc_ece(labels[group == 0], probs[group == 0])
    ece1 = calc_ece(labels[group == 1], probs[group == 1])
    glob_ece = calc_ece(labels, probs)
    d_ece = abs(ece0 - ece1)

    return CalibrationECEAudit(
        n_bins=10,
        ece_group0=round(ece0, 4),
        ece_group1=round(ece1, 4),
        disparity_delta_ece=round(d_ece, 4),
        global_pooled_ece=round(glob_ece, 4),
        subgroup_miscalibration_detected=(ece0 > 0.035 and ece1 < 0.035)
    )

def audit_equalized_odds_optimization() -> EqualizedOddsOptimizationAudit:
    np.random.seed(42)
    n = 2500
    group = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=n, p=[0.4, 0.6])
    # Group 1 scores higher baseline
    probs = np.where(group == 1, 
                     np.random.beta(3.0, 2.0, size=n), 
                     np.random.beta(2.0, 3.0, size=n))
    labels = (np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=n) < probs).astype(int)

    # Baseline uniform threshold at 0.50
    pred_base = (probs >= 0.50).astype(int)
    tpr0_b = np.sum((pred_base == 1) & (labels == 1) & (group == 0)) / np.sum((labels == 1) & (group == 0))
    tpr1_b = np.sum((pred_base == 1) & (labels == 1) & (group == 1)) / np.sum((labels == 1) & (group == 1))
    fpr0_b = np.sum((pred_base == 1) & (labels == 0) & (group == 0)) / np.sum((labels == 0) & (group == 0))
    fpr1_b = np.sum((pred_base == 1) & (labels == 0) & (group == 1)) / np.sum((labels == 0) & (group == 1))
    uncal_aod = 0.5 * (abs(tpr0_b - tpr1_b) + abs(fpr0_b - fpr1_b))

    # ROC Curves
    fpr0, tpr0, th0 = roc_curve(labels[group == 0], probs[group == 0])
    fpr1, tpr1, th1 = roc_curve(labels[group == 1], probs[group == 1])

    best_disp = float("inf")
    best_t0, best_t1 = 0.5, 0.5
    for i in range(1, len(th0) - 1):
        for j in range(1, len(th1) - 1):
            disp = 0.5 * (abs(fpr0[i] - fpr1[j]) + abs(tpr0[i] - tpr1[j]))
            if disp < best_disp:
                best_disp = disp
                best_t0 = float(th0[i])
                best_t1 = float(th1[j])

    return EqualizedOddsOptimizationAudit(
        uncalibrated_threshold=0.50,
        uncalibrated_aod_disparity=round(float(uncal_aod), 4),
        optimal_threshold_group0=round(best_t0, 4),
        optimal_threshold_group1=round(best_t1, 4),
        minimized_aod_disparity=round(float(best_disp), 4),
        disparity_mitigated=(best_disp < 0.05 and uncal_aod > 0.20)
    )

def audit_metric_frame() -> FairnessMetricFrameAudit:
    np.random.seed(42)
    n = 2000
    group = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=n, p=[0.4, 0.6])
    probs = np.where(group == 1, 
                     np.random.normal(0.65, 0.15, size=n), 
                     np.random.normal(0.48, 0.15, size=n))
    probs = np.clip(probs, 0.0, 1.0)
    labels = (np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=n) < probs).astype(int)

    preds = (probs >= 0.50).astype(int)

    def group_stats(g_val):
        mask = (group == g_val)
        y_g = labels[mask]
        p_g = preds[mask]
        acc = float(np.mean(y_g == p_g))
        sel = float(np.mean(p_g == 1))
        tp = np.sum((p_g == 1) & (y_g == 1))
        fp = np.sum((p_g == 1) & (y_g == 0))
        fn = np.sum((p_g == 0) & (y_g == 1))
        tn = np.sum((p_g == 0) & (y_g == 0))
        tpr = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0.0
        fpr = fp / (fp + tn) if (fp + tn) > 0 else 0.0
        return acc, sel, tpr, fpr

    acc0, sel0, tpr0, fpr0 = group_stats(0)
    acc1, sel1, tpr1, fpr1 = group_stats(1)

    dir_val = sel0 / sel1 if sel1 > 0 else 0.0
    aod = 0.5 * (abs(tpr0 - tpr1) + abs(fpr0 - fpr1))

    return FairnessMetricFrameAudit(
        selection_rate_group0=round(sel0, 4),
        selection_rate_group1=round(sel1, 4),
        accuracy_group0=round(acc0, 4),
        accuracy_group1=round(acc1, 4),
        tpr_group0=round(tpr0, 4),
        tpr_group1=round(tpr1, 4),
        fpr_group0=round(fpr0, 4),
        fpr_group1=round(fpr1, 4),
        disparate_impact_ratio=round(dir_val, 4),
        average_odds_difference=round(aod, 4)
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ece_audit = audit_subgroup_ece()
    opt_audit = audit_equalized_odds_optimization()
    mf_audit = audit_metric_frame()

    print("=== 1. Subgroup Calibration & ECE Audit ===")
    print(f"  Group 0 ECE              : {ece_audit.ece_group0}")
    print(f"  Group 1 ECE              : {ece_audit.ece_group1}")
    print(f"  Delta ECE Disparity      : {ece_audit.disparity_delta_ece}")
    print(f"  Miscalibration Detected  : {ece_audit.subgroup_miscalibration_detected}")

    print("\n=== 2. Dual ROC Convex Hull Equalized Odds Optimization ===")
    print(f"  Uncalibrated AOD (tau=0.50): {opt_audit.uncalibrated_aod_disparity}")
    print(f"  Optimal Group 0 Threshold  : {opt_audit.optimal_threshold_group0}")
    print(f"  Optimal Group 1 Threshold  : {opt_audit.optimal_threshold_group1}")
    print(f"  Optimized AOD Disparity    : {opt_audit.minimized_aod_disparity}")
    print(f"  Disparity Mitigated        : {opt_audit.disparity_mitigated}")

    print("\n=== 3. Fairlearn Disparity Metric Tensor Audit ===")
    print(f"  Selection Rates (G0 / G1)  : {mf_audit.selection_rate_group0} vs {mf_audit.selection_rate_group1}")
    print(f"  Disparate Impact Ratio     : {mf_audit.disparate_impact_ratio}")
    print(f"  Average Absolute Odds Gap  : {mf_audit.average_odds_difference}")

    assert ece_audit.subgroup_miscalibration_detected, "ECE audit check failed!"
    assert opt_audit.disparity_mitigated, "Equalized odds threshold optimization check failed!"
    assert mf_audit.disparate_impact_ratio < 0.80, "DIR violation detection check failed!"
    print("\n[PASS] All Pydantic V2 Bias Visualization & Auditing Schemas Validated Successfully.")

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment 1: Why Does a Single Global Threshold Fail on Disparate Groups?

If Group 0 and Group 1 have different risk score distributions due to historical measurement disparities, why does enforcing a single uniform decision threshold $ au = 0.50$ inevitably create disparate impact or disparate false positive rates?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: A single threshold $ au$ operates on absolute score values, not percentiles.

If Group 0 scores are systematically depressed by historical measurement bias (\(\\mathbb{E}[S \\mid A=0] < \\mathbb{E}[S \\mid A=1]\)), a threshold at \(0.50\) will select a vastly smaller fraction of Group 0, directly violating demographic parity (\(\\text{DIR} \\ll 0.80\)). Furthermore, if the score distributions have different variances, a uniform threshold forces divergent True Positive and False Positive rates between the groups. Achieving Equalized Odds requires group-specific threshold calibration \((\\tau_0^*, \\tau_1^*)\) [Hardt2016, Pleiss2017].

Self-Assessment 2: Group Calibration vs. Equalized Odds Conflict

Can an algorithmic predictor simultaneously achieve perfect within-group calibration and equalized odds if the base rates of the two groups are different (\(\\Pr(Y=1 \\mid A=0) \\neq \\Pr(Y=1 \\mid A=1)\))?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: No. As mathematically proven by Kleinberg et al. [Kleinberg2016] and Chouldechova [Chouldechova2017], within-group calibration and equalized odds are mutually incompatible whenever base rates differ, unless the prediction is \(100\%\) accurate (zero error rate). Visual displays must explicitly present this tradeoff to policymakers rather than promising impossible mathematical perfection.

Self-Assessment 3: Why Does Global Calibration Hide Subgroup Miscalibration?

Explain why a model with a near-zero overall Expected Calibration Error (\(\\text{ECE}_{\\text{pooled}} = 0.015\)) can still inflict severe representational and allocative harm on an unprivileged subgroup.

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - Pooled ECE computes a weighted average across all instances regardless of group identity: $\(\\text{ECE}_{\\text{pooled}} = \\sum_{b=1}^B \\frac{|I_b|}{N} |\\text{acc}(I_b) - \\text{conf}(I_b)|\)$ - If Group 1 comprises \(85\\%\) of the population and is well-calibrated, its low error completely dominates the global sum. - Group 0 (15% of the data) can have severe systematic under-prediction (\(\\text{ECE}_0 = 0.15\)), but its contribution is diluted in the pooled metric: $\(0.85 \\times 0.01 + 0.15 \\times 0.15 \\approx 0.031\)$ - Auditors must inspect subgroup reliability diagrams individually to detect localized miscalibration [Pleiss2017].

Self-Assessment 4: The Geometry of the ROC Convex Hull

In the context of the Hardt-Price-Srebro (2016) post-processing framework, why is the convex hull of the group ROC curve used rather than the raw empirical step curve?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - A classifier can randomize between any two deterministic threshold operating points \((\\text{FPR}_A, \\text{TPR}_A)\) and \((\\text{FPR}_B, \\text{TPR}_B)\) with coin-flip probability \(\\alpha \\in [0, 1]\). - By linearity of expectation, any convex combination \(\\alpha (\\text{FPR}_A, \\text{TPR}_A) + (1-\\alpha) (\\text{FPR}_B, \\text{TPR}_B)\) is empirically achievable. - Taking the convex hull fills in all non-concave dips and gaps in the empirical ROC curve, expanding the feasible space of operating points and enabling exact Equalized Odds intersections without requiring continuous retrainings.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & Cascading Harm Dynamics
docs.text:
Algorithmic bias is not an abstract statistical curiosity confined to academic benchmarks; it produces devastating, cumulative real-world externalities across civil liberties, criminal justice, access to capital, clinical survival, and corporate solvency [Dressel2018, Obermeyer2019, Chouldechova2017]. When automated decision systems operate at scale without rigorous bias controls, allocative distortions compound over time, transforming transient algorithmic errors into persistent intergenerational structural inequality [Selbst2019].

docs.title: 1. Mathematical Formulations of Compounding Harm Dynamics
1. Economic Allocative Utility Disparity
docs.text:
Consider an institutional allocator distributing access to loans, housing, or employment. The net expected social utility achieved by demographic group \(a \in \{0, 1\}\) under decision policy \(\hat{Y} = f(\mathbf{X}) \in \{0, 1\}\) is:

\[U_a = \int_{\mathbf{x}} \left( b \cdot y(\mathbf{x}) - c \right) \Pr(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) \, dF_a(\mathbf{x})\]

where \(b > 0\) represents the economic utility of an opportunity granted to a qualified candidate, and \(c > 0\) is the institutional loss of an erroneous assignment.

When an algorithm suffers from disparate error rates (e.g., lower true positive rates for unprivileged candidates: \(\text{TPR}_0 \ll \text{TPR}_1\)), the expected utility extraction from Group 0 is severe:

\[\Delta U = U_1 - U_0 = b \cdot (\text{TPR}_1 \cdot p_1 - \text{TPR}_0 \cdot p_0) - c \cdot (\text{FPR}_1 \cdot (1 - p_1) - \text{FPR}_0 \cdot (1 - p_0))\]

docs.title: 2. Dynamic Intergenerational Wealth Divergence
docs.text:
When credit, mortgage lending, or employment opportunities are denied at round \(t\), the compounding capital accumulation is stunted across operational generations \(t = 1, \dots, T\):

\[W_{t+1}(a) = (1 + r) W_t(a) + b \cdot \mathbb{I}(\hat{Y}_t = 1) - c_L\]

where \(r\) is the compound annual capital return rate, \(b\) is the economic benefit of loan or job approval, \(\mathbb{I}(\hat{Y}_t = 1)\) is the Bernoulli indicator of selection with probability \(p_a = \Pr(\hat{Y}_t = 1 \mid A = a)\), and \(c_L\) is baseline living costs.

docs.title: Closed-Form Wealth Trajectory Derivation
docs.text:
Taking expectations over the allocation distribution:

\[\mathbb{E}[W_{t+1}(a)] = (1 + r) \mathbb{E}[W_t(a)] + (b \cdot p_a - c_L)\]

Unrolling the first-order linear difference equation from initial wealth \(W_0(a)\):

\[\mathbb{E}[W_T(a)] = (1 + r)^T W_0(a) + \sum_{k=0}^{T-1} (1 + r)^k (b \cdot p_a - c_L)\]

Using the finite geometric series formula \(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1} (1+r)^k = \frac{(1+r)^T - 1}{r}\):

\[\mathbb{E}[W_T(a)] = (1 + r)^T W_0(a) + \frac{(1 + r)^T - 1}{r} \left( b \cdot p_a - c_L \right) \quad \blacksquare\]

[!IMPORTANT] The Compounding Divergence Multiplier: Notice that the wealth gap \(\mathbb{E}[W_T(1)] - \mathbb{E}[W_T(0)]\) expands exponentially with horizon \(T\): $\(\mathbb{E}[W_T(1)] - \mathbb{E}[W_T(0)] = (1 + r)^T \left( W_0(1) - W_0(0) \right) + \frac{(1 + r)^T - 1}{r} b \cdot (p_1 - p_0)\)$ Even if initial wealth is equal (\(W_0(1) = W_0(0)\)), a modest allocative gap (e.g., \(p_0 = 0.35\) vs. \(p_1 = 0.55\), \(\text{DIR} = 0.64\)) compounds over a 30-year mortgage horizon into a \(>2.4\times\) wealth chasm!

docs.title: 3. Chouldechova's Impossibility Law for Recidivism Scoring
docs.text:
Alexandra Chouldechova [Chouldechova2017] proved that for any risk assessment instrument (such as Northpointe's COMPAS), if base rates of recidivism differ (\(p_0 \neq p_1\)), the False Positive Rate is algebraically determined by Positive Predictive Value (PPV) calibration:

\[\text{FPR}_a = \left( \frac{p_a}{1 - p_a} \right) \left( \frac{1 - \text{PPV}_a}{\text{PPV}_a} \right) \cdot \text{TPR}_a\]

Taking the ratio of False Positive Rates under equal calibration (\(\text{PPV}_0 = \text{PPV}_1 = v\)) and equal sensitivity (\(\text{TPR}_0 = \text{TPR}_1\)):

\[\frac{\text{FPR}_0}{\text{FPR}_1} = \frac{\frac{p_0}{1 - p_0}}{\frac{p_1}{1 - p_1}} = \frac{\text{Odds}(p_0)}{\text{Odds}(p_1)}\]

Consequently:

\[p_0 > p_1 \implies \text{FPR}_0 > \text{FPR}_1\]

This mathematical identity proves that the racial disparity uncovered by ProPublica [Angwin2016] was not an engineering bug or isolated anomaly—it was an unavoidable algebraic consequence of enforcing predictive calibration across demographic cohorts with unequal arrest base rates [Dressel2018].

docs.title: 2. Legal Liabilities & Regulatory Enforcement Frameworks
docs.text:
Modern regulatory authorities treat dataset bias as an actionable legal violation rather than an academic concern:

Regulation / Statute Jurisdiction Legal Liability & Enforcement Scope Maximum Penalty EU Artificial Intelligence Act (2024) European Union Article 10 (Data Governance): Mandates that training datasets for High-Risk AI systems must be relevant, representative, and free of discriminatory errors. Up to €35 Million or 7% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher) GDPR Article 22 European Union Right not to be subject to solely automated decisions producing legal effects; mandates meaningful human intervention and explainability. Up to €20 Million or 4% of global annual turnover US Title VII & ECOA United States Prohibits facially neutral policies that produce unlawful disparate impact in employment, credit, and housing underwriting [Barocas2016]. Civil compensatory damages, federal consent decrees, mandatory operational restructuring FTC Act Section 5 United States Regulates unfair or deceptive trade practices; enforces the strict remedy of Algorithmic Disgorgement. Mandatory destruction of models, algorithms, and training weights

docs.title: 3. The Threat of Algorithmic Disgorgement
docs.text:
Beyond monetary penalties, regulatory agencies (specifically the US Federal Trade Commission) increasingly enforce Algorithmic Disgorgement (model deletion) against companies caught deploying systems trained on tainted or discriminatory datasets:

    FTCOrder --> Mandate2["2. Compulsory Destruction of All Weights W (Disgorgement)"]

docs.title: Precedent Enforcement Actions:
docs.text:
1. FTC v. Everalbum (2021): Photo storage company trained facial recognition algorithms on consumer photos without explicit opt-in consent. The FTC ordered Everalbum to completely delete all facial recognition algorithms, code, and neural network weights derived from the data.
  2. FTC v. Kurbo / Weight Watchers (2022): Ordered the destruction of all machine learning algorithms developed using data collected from children under 13 without verifiable parental consent.

[!WARNING] Operational Risk: Model disgorgement represents the total forfeiture of engineering R&D capital. A company cannot simply "patch" a disgorged model; it must start model development from zero with compliant data [Selbst2019].

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation & Pydantic V2 Verification Suite
docs.text:
Below is a self-contained, typed Python testing suite with Pydantic V2 validating: 1. Dynamic Intergenerational Wealth Compounding: Verifies closed-form geometric series expansion against step-by-step simulation. 2. Chouldechova's Impossibility Theorem: Mathematically verifies that the FPR disparity strictly equals the base rate odds ratio. 3. Regulatory Liability Exposure Assessment: Evaluates statutory penalty exposure under the EU AI Act and FTC Algorithmic Disgorgement doctrines.

# test_ch7_p5_pydantic.py
# Production Implementation & Pydantic V2 Verification Suite for Lesson 7.5

from typing import Dict, List, Any
import numpy as np
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class IntergenerationalWealthAudit(BaseModel):
    initial_wealth_g0: float
    initial_wealth_g1: float
    horizon_years: int
    annual_return_rate: float
    approval_rate_g0: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    approval_rate_g1: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    simulated_final_wealth_g0: float
    simulated_final_wealth_g1: float
    closed_form_wealth_g0: float
    closed_form_wealth_g1: float
    wealth_chasm_ratio: float
    closed_form_exact: bool

class ChouldechovaTheoremAudit(BaseModel):
    base_rate_g0: float
    base_rate_g1: float
    calibrated_ppv: float
    tpr: float
    theoretical_fpr_g0: float
    theoretical_fpr_g1: float
    empirical_fpr_ratio: float
    theoretical_odds_ratio: float
    impossibility_proven: bool

class RegulatoryLiabilityAudit(BaseModel):
    disparate_impact_ratio: float
    fpr_disparity_ratio: float
    eu_ai_act_violation: bool
    eu_max_fine_millions: float
    ftc_disgorgement_threat_level: str

def audit_wealth_compounding() -> IntergenerationalWealthAudit:
    r = 0.05
    T = 30
    w0_0 = 10000.0
    w0_1 = 15000.0
    b = 5000.0
    cL = 1500.0
    p0 = 0.35
    p1 = 0.55

    traj0 = [w0_0]
    traj1 = [w0_1]
    for _ in range(T):
        traj0.append(traj0[-1] * (1.0 + r) + (b * p0 - cL))
        traj1.append(traj1[-1] * (1.0 + r) + (b * p1 - cL))

    cf0 = (1.0 + r)**T * w0_0 + (((1.0 + r)**T - 1.0) / r) * (b * p0 - cL)
    cf1 = (1.0 + r)**T * w0_1 + (((1.0 + r)**T - 1.0) / r) * (b * p1 - cL)

    ratio = cf1 / cf0
    match = abs(traj0[-1] - cf0) < 1e-4 and abs(traj1[-1] - cf1) < 1e-4

    return IntergenerationalWealthAudit(
        initial_wealth_g0=w0_0,
        initial_wealth_g1=w0_1,
        horizon_years=T,
        annual_return_rate=r,
        approval_rate_g0=p0,
        approval_rate_g1=p1,
        simulated_final_wealth_g0=round(traj0[-1], 2),
        simulated_final_wealth_g1=round(traj1[-1], 2),
        closed_form_wealth_g0=round(cf0, 2),
        closed_form_wealth_g1=round(cf1, 2),
        wealth_chasm_ratio=round(ratio, 2),
        closed_form_exact=match
    )

def audit_chouldechova_law() -> ChouldechovaTheoremAudit:
    p0 = 0.52
    p1 = 0.32
    ppv = 0.62
    tpr = 0.68

    odds_factor = (1.0 - ppv) / ppv
    fpr0 = (p0 / (1.0 - p0)) * odds_factor * tpr
    fpr1 = (p1 / (1.0 - p1)) * odds_factor * tpr

    emp_ratio = fpr0 / fpr1
    theo_odds_ratio = (p0 / (1.0 - p0)) / (p1 / (1.0 - p1))
    proven = abs(emp_ratio - theo_odds_ratio) < 1e-12

    return ChouldechovaTheoremAudit(
        base_rate_g0=p0,
        base_rate_g1=p1,
        calibrated_ppv=ppv,
        tpr=tpr,
        theoretical_fpr_g0=round(float(fpr0), 4),
        theoretical_fpr_g1=round(float(fpr1), 4),
        empirical_fpr_ratio=round(float(emp_ratio), 4),
        theoretical_odds_ratio=round(float(theo_odds_ratio), 4),
        impossibility_proven=proven
    )

def audit_regulatory_liability(dir_val: float = 0.64, fpr_ratio: float = 2.30) -> RegulatoryLiabilityAudit:
    violates_eu = (dir_val < 0.80 or fpr_ratio > 1.50)
    disgorgement_threat = "CRITICAL" if dir_val < 0.70 else "MODERATE"

    return RegulatoryLiabilityAudit(
        disparate_impact_ratio=dir_val,
        fpr_disparity_ratio=fpr_ratio,
        eu_ai_act_violation=violates_eu,
        eu_max_fine_millions=35.0,
        ftc_disgorgement_threat_level=disgorgement_threat
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    wealth_res = audit_wealth_compounding()
    chould_res = audit_chouldechova_law()
    reg_res = audit_regulatory_liability()

    print("=== 1. Intergenerational Wealth Compounding Audit ===")
    print(f"  Year 30 Wealth Group 0   : ${wealth_res.closed_form_wealth_g0:,.2f}")
    print(f"  Year 30 Wealth Group 1   : ${wealth_res.closed_form_wealth_g1:,.2f}")
    print(f"  Intergenerational Gap    : {wealth_res.wealth_chasm_ratio}x divergence")
    print(f"  Closed-Form Verification : {wealth_res.closed_form_exact}")

    print("\n=== 2. Chouldechova Recidivism Law Audit ===")
    print(f"  Group 0 FPR              : {chould_res.theoretical_fpr_g0 * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Group 1 FPR              : {chould_res.theoretical_fpr_g1 * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  FPR Disparity Ratio      : {chould_res.empirical_fpr_ratio:.2f}x higher")
    print(f"  Impossibility Law Proven : {chould_res.impossibility_proven}")

    print("\n=== 3. Corporate Regulatory Liability Audit ===")
    print(f"  EU AI Act Article 10 Flag: {reg_res.eu_ai_act_violation}")
    print(f"  Maximum Statutory Fine   : €{reg_res.eu_max_fine_millions}M or 7% Turnover")
    print(f"  FTC Disgorgement Threat  : {reg_res.ftc_disgorgement_threat_level}")

    assert wealth_res.closed_form_exact, "Wealth calculation check failed!"
    assert chould_res.impossibility_proven, "Chouldechova theorem proof check failed!"
    assert reg_res.eu_ai_act_violation, "Regulatory liability check failed!"
    print("\n[PASS] All Pydantic V2 Societal Impact & Legal Schemas Validated Successfully.")

docs.title: 🔬 Empirical Case Study: Netherlands SyRI Welfare Scandal & Apple Card
docs.text:
1. Netherlands SyRI Welfare Fraud Scandal (2020):
  2. Context: The Dutch government deployed the Systeem Risico Indicatie (SyRI) algorithm across municipalities to identify social assistance fraud.
  3. The Harm: Trained predominantly on low-income immigrant neighborhoods, SyRI manufactured thousands of false-positive fraud accusations. Families suffered catastrophic tax clawbacks, bank account seizures, and unpayable debt.

  4. Judicial Reversal: In 2020, The Hague District Court struck down SyRI for violating Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (Right to Respect for Private and Family Life), holding that opaque automated profiling without statistical accountability is unlawful in a democratic society.

  5. Apple Card Credit Limit Gender Disparity (2019):

  6. Context: Apple Card (underwritten by Goldman Sachs) assigned automated credit lines to applicants.
  7. Disparity: Spouses filing joint tax returns with identical assets discovered husbands received \(10\times\) to \(20\times\) higher credit limits than their wives, even when wives possessed higher independent FICO scores.
  8. Consequence: Regulators launched formal civil probes under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA), illustrating that relying on facially neutral machine learning proxies does not shield institutions from disparate impact scrutiny.

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment 1: The Closed-Form Intergenerational Wealth Divergence

In the wealth compounding equation \(\mathbb{E}[W_T(a)] = (1+r)^T W_0(a) + \frac{(1+r)^T - 1}{r} (b p_a - c_L)\), why does an initially minor allocative disparity (\(p_1 - p_0 = 0.20\)) expand into an insurmountable wealth gap over 30 years?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - The multiplier on the annual economic net flow \((b p_a - c_L)\) is \(\frac{(1+r)^T - 1}{r}\). - At an annual interest rate \(r = 0.05\) over \(T = 30\) years: $\(\frac{(1 + 0.05)^{30} - 1}{0.05} = \frac{4.322 - 1}{0.05} = \frac{3.322}{0.05} = 66.44\)$ - Every dollar difference in annual approval flow is amplified by a factor of \(66.44\times\) over three decades. - Consequently, a small difference in algorithmic loan approvals compounds into a structural economic chasm between demographic communities.

Self-Assessment 2: What Is Algorithmic Disgorgement?

Explain why an FTC Algorithmic Disgorgement enforcement order is far more damaging to a tech company than a conventional civil monetary fine.

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - A monetary fine is an accounting expense that can be absorbed as a cost of business. - Algorithmic Disgorgement mandates the complete destruction of: 1. The underlying training data. 2. The trained model weights, parameters, and latent embeddings derived from that data. 3. Downstream APIs, applications, and services built upon those weights. - Disgorgement eradicates the company's core intellectual property, nullifying years of engineering investment and requiring total re-development from scratch [Selbst2019].

Self-Assessment 3: Chouldechova's Impossibility Theorem in Bail Systems

State Chouldechova's Impossibility Theorem in plain mathematical terms. Why is it impossible for a predictive bail algorithm to satisfy both Predictive Parity and Equalized Odds simultaneously when base recidivism rates differ?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - Chouldechova proved that: $\(\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1 - p} \left( \frac{1 - \text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}} \right) \text{TPR}\)$ - If an algorithm enforces Predictive Parity (\(\text{PPV}_0 = \text{PPV}_1\)) and equal sensitivity (\(\text{TPR}_0 = \text{TPR}_1\)), the False Positive Rate is strictly proportional to the base rate odds \(\frac{p}{1 - p}\). - Because societal re-arrest base rates differ (\(p_0 \ne p_1\)), the False Positive Rates must differ (\(\text{FPR}_0 \ne \text{FPR}_1\)). Satisfying Predictive Parity guarantees the violation of Equal False Positive Rates [Chouldechova2017, Dressel2018].

Self-Assessment 4: Article 10 of the EU AI Act

Under Article 10 of the EU AI Act, what data governance obligations are imposed on providers of High-Risk AI systems regarding training datasets?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - Providers of High-Risk AI systems must implement comprehensive data governance practices covering: 1. Explicit design choices and data collection mechanisms. 2. Data origin, lineage, and representation auditing. 3. Prior assessment of potential biases and mitigation of discriminatory flaws. - Datasets must be relevant, representative, free of errors, and complete in view of the intended purpose. - Violations risk administrative fines of up to €35 Million or 7% of total global annual turnover.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & The Inherent Impossibility Theorem
docs.text:
A pervasive misconception in applied machine learning assumes that given sufficiently large datasets, deep neural architectures, and optimal feature engineering, an algorithmic predictor can simultaneously satisfy all intuitive concepts of fairness. In 2016 and 2017, foundational mathematical theorems proved that the three primary families of group fairness—Independence (Demographic Parity), Separation (Equalized Odds), and Sufficiency (Predictive Calibration)—are mutually exclusive whenever demographic groups exhibit unequal ground-truth base rates (Kleinberg et al., 2017; Chouldechova, 2017).

Fairness is not a single engineering optimization constraint to be solved in a loss function; it represents a set of contradictory normative ethical philosophies. An algorithm cannot simultaneously satisfy an individual's right to group-blind calibrated scoring and a group's right to equalized erroneous accusation rates. Engineering teams deploying high-stakes decision systems must navigate this trilemma deliberately, establishing explicit ethical and legal trade-offs.
