docs.title: 📐 The Three Pillars of Group Fairness
docs.text:
Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^d\) represent observed feature vectors, \(A \in \{0, 1\}\) denote a binary sensitive protected attribute (e.g., race, gender, disability status), \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\) the ground-truth outcome label, and \(\hat{Y} \in \{0, 1\}\) or continuous score \(R = f(X) \in [0, 1]\) the algorithmic prediction.

The entire literature of statistical group fairness organizes around three conditional independence properties between the sensitive attribute \(A\), the true label \(Y\), and the score \(R\) (Barocas & Selbst, 2016):

graph LR
  classDef box fill:#fffdf7,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef ind fill:#c9f3f4,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef sep fill:#fff0b9,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef suf fill:#ffd8ce,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;

  P1["Pillar 1: Independence<br/><b>R ⊥ A</b><br/>Demographic Parity"]:::ind
  P2["Pillar 2: Separation<br/><b>R ⊥ A | Y</b><br/>Equalized Odds"]:::sep
  P3["Pillar 3: Sufficiency<br/><b>Y ⊥ A | R</b><br/>Calibration within Groups"]:::suf

docs.title: 1. Pillar 1: Independence (Demographic Parity)
docs.text:
A continuous score \(R\) or binary decision \(\hat{Y}\) satisfies Independence (or Demographic Parity) if the distribution of decisions is statistically independent of sensitive attribute \(A\):

\[R \perp A \iff \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 1)\]

docs.title: Regulatory & Mathematical Quantifications:
docs.text:
1. Statistical Parity Difference (\(\Delta_{\text{DP}}\)): $\(\Delta_{\text{DP}} = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 0) - \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 1)\)$ Parity requires \(\Delta_{\text{DP}} = 0\).

  2. Disparate Impact Ratio (\(\text{DIR}\)): $\(\text{DIR} = \frac{\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 0)}{\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 1)}\)$ The United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) enforces the Four-Fifths (80%) Rule: any selection system with \(\text{DIR} < 0.80\) is prima facie unlawful disparate impact discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act.

Philosophical Premise: "We are all equal." Any observed differences in historical outcomes \(Y\) reflect systemic societal oppression, historical discrimination, or biased labeling. An equitable system must distribute opportunities at equal rates across groups regardless of historical disparities.

docs.title: 2. Pillar 2: Separation (Equalized Odds & Equality of Opportunity)
docs.text:
A predictor satisfies Separation if the score \(R\) or decision \(\hat{Y}\) is conditionally independent of sensitive attribute \(A\) given the true outcome label \(Y\) (Hardt et al., 2016):

\[R \perp A \mid Y \iff \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = y, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = y, A = 1), \quad \forall y \in \{0, 1\}\]

Separation splits into two distinct error rate balance constraints:

docs.title: Condition A: True Positive Rate Parity (Equality of Opportunity)
docs.text: $\(\text{TPR}_0 = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 1, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 1, A = 1) = \text{TPR}_1\)$ Equivalently, False Negative Rates are equal: \(\text{FNR}_0 = \text{FNR}_1\).

docs.title: Condition B: False Positive Rate Parity (Predictive Equality)
docs.text:
\[\text{FPR}_0 = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 0, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 0, A = 1) = \text{FPR}_1\]

The composite Average Odds Difference (\(\Delta_{\text{AOD}}\)) measures total deviation from Equalized Odds: $\(\Delta_{\text{AOD}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( |\text{FPR}_0 - \text{FPR}_1| + |\text{TPR}_0 - \text{TPR}_1| \right)\)$

Philosophical Premise: Individuals who are equally qualified (or equally innocent) should experience identical probabilities of success (or erroneous punishment), irrespective of demographic group membership.

docs.title: 3. Pillar 3: Sufficiency (Predictive Parity & Calibration within Groups)
docs.text:
A score \(R = f(X) \in [0, 1]\) satisfies Sufficiency if the ground-truth outcome \(Y\) is conditionally independent of sensitive attribute \(A\) given score \(R\) (Pleiss et al., 2017):

\[Y \perp A \mid R \iff \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid R = r, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid R = r, A = 1) = r, \quad \forall r \in [0, 1]\]

For binary decision rules \(\hat{Y} \in \{0, 1\}\), Sufficiency requires equal Positive Predictive Value (PPV) and equal Negative Predictive Value (NPV):

\[\text{PPV}_0 = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid \hat{Y} = 1, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid \hat{Y} = 1, A = 1) = \text{PPV}_1$$ $$\text{NPV}_0 = \mathbb{P}(Y = 0 \mid \hat{Y} = 0, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(Y = 0 \mid \hat{Y} = 0, A = 1) = \text{NPV}_1\]

Philosophical Premise: "A score of 70% must mean 70% risk for everyone." If a credit scoring model assigns an applicant a 30% default probability, that applicant's expected repayment reliability should not depend on their race or gender. Group-specific calibration ensures decisions remain statistically trustworthy to decision-makers.

docs.title: 🔬 Rigorous Derivation: The Kleinberg-Chouldechova Impossibility Theorem
docs.text: We now present the complete algebraic proof establishing that Separation and Sufficiency cannot simultaneously hold when demographic groups exhibit unequal ground-truth base rates, except under degenerate conditions (Chouldechova, 2017; Kleinberg et al., 2017).

docs.title: Formal Setup & Parameter Definitions
docs.text: For each demographic group \(a \in \{0, 1\}\): - Group base rate: \(p_a = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid A = a)\) with \(0 < p_a < 1\). - True Positive Rate: \(\text{TPR}_a = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 1, A = a) = 1 - \text{FNR}_a\). - False Positive Rate: \(\text{FPR}_a = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 0, A = a)\). - Positive Predictive Value: \(v_a = \text{PPV}_a = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid \hat{Y} = 1, A = a)\). - False Discovery Rate: \(\text{FDR}_a = 1 - v_a = \mathbb{P}(Y = 0 \mid \hat{Y} = 1, A = a)\).

docs.title: Step 1: Expansion of False Discovery Rate via Bayes' Theorem
docs.text:
By definition of conditional probability: $\(\text{FDR}_a = \mathbb{P}(Y = 0 \mid \hat{Y} = 1, A = a) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 0, A = a) \mathbb{P}(Y = 0 \mid A = a)}{\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = a)}\)$

Expanding the total probability in the denominator: $\(\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = a) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 0, A = a)(1 - p_a) + \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 1, A = a) p_a = \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a) + \text{TPR}_a p_a\)$

Substituting back: $\(\text{FDR}_a = \frac{\text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a)}{\text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a) + \text{TPR}_a p_a}\)$

docs.title: Step 2: Isolating the False Positive Rate \(\text{FPR}_a\)
docs.text:
Multiply both sides by the denominator: $\(\text{FDR}_a \left[ \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a) + \text{TPR}_a p_a \right] = \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a)\)$

Distribute \(\text{FDR}_a\): $\(\text{FDR}_a \cdot \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a) + \text{FDR}_a \cdot \text{TPR}_a p_a = \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a)\)$

Collect all terms containing \(\text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a)\) on the right-hand side: $\(\text{FDR}_a \cdot \text{TPR}_a p_a = (1 - \text{FDR}_a) \cdot \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a)\)$

Recognizing that \(1 - \text{FDR}_a = v_a = \text{PPV}_a\) and \(\text{TPR}_a = 1 - \text{FNR}_a\): $\((1 - v_a)(1 - \text{FNR}_a) p_a = v_a \cdot \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a)\)$

Dividing both sides by \(v_a (1 - p_a)\) yields the Chouldechova Fundamental Identity:

\[\boxed{\text{FPR}_a = \left( \frac{p_a}{1 - p_a} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{1 - v_a}{v_a} \right) \cdot (1 - \text{FNR}_a)}\]

Where \(\text{Odds}(p_a) = \frac{p_a}{1 - p_a}\) is the prior odds ratio of the positive ground-truth class in group \(a\).

docs.title: Step 3: Impossibility Ratio Under Imposed Equalized Constraints
docs.text:
Suppose an algorithm simultaneously enforces: 1. Sufficiency (Predictive Parity): \(v_0 = v_1 = v\) (identical precision / PPV across groups). 2. Equality of Opportunity (Separation on Positives): \(\text{FNR}_0 = \text{FNR}_1 = \text{FNR}\) (identical false negative rates).

Taking the direct algebraic ratio of the False Positive Rates across both groups:

\[\frac{\text{FPR}_0}{\text{FPR}_1} = \frac{\left( \frac{p_0}{1 - p_0} \right) \left( \frac{1 - v}{v} \right) (1 - \text{FNR})}{\left( \frac{p_1}{1 - p_1} \right) \left( \frac{1 - v}{v} \right) (1 - \text{FNR})} = \frac{\text{Odds}(p_0)}{\text{Odds}(p_1)}\] \[\boxed{\frac{\text{FPR}_0}{\text{FPR}_1} = \frac{\frac{p_0}{1 - p_0}}{\frac{p_1}{1 - p_1}} = \frac{p_0 (1 - p_1)}{p_1 (1 - p_0)}}\]

docs.title: The Impossibility Theorem Statement
docs.text:
Theorem (Kleinberg, Mullainathan, Raghavan 2017; Chouldechova 2017): Let base rates differ across groups (\(p_0 \ne p_1\)). A binary classifier \(\hat{Y}\) can simultaneously satisfy: 1. Equal Positive Predictive Value (\(\text{PPV}_0 = \text{PPV}_1\)) [Sufficiency] 2. Equal False Positive Rates (\(\text{FPR}_0 = \text{FPR}_1\)) [Separation: Error parity on negatives] 3. Equal False Negative Rates (\(\text{FNR}_0 = \text{FNR}_1\)) [Separation: Error parity on positives]

if and only if the classifier achieves perfect deterministic classification (\(\text{FPR}_0 = \text{FPR}_1 = 0\) and \(\text{FNR}_0 = \text{FNR}_1 = 0\), implying \(v_0 = v_1 = 1\)).

docs.title: Concrete Real-World Consequence: The COMPAS Controversy
docs.text:
In the Broward County COMPAS recidivism evaluation: - Group 0 (White defendants): \(p_0 \approx 0.35 \implies \text{Odds}(p_0) = \frac{0.35}{0.65} \approx 0.538\) - Group 1 (Black defendants): \(p_1 \approx 0.52 \implies \text{Odds}(p_1) = \frac{0.52}{0.48} \approx 1.083\) - Base Rate Odds Ratio: \(\frac{\text{Odds}(p_1)}{\text{Odds}(p_0)} = \frac{1.083}{0.538} \approx 2.01\)

Northpointe engineered COMPAS to satisfy Calibration (\(\text{PPV}_0 \approx \text{PPV}_1 \approx 61\%\)). By the mathematical identity above, the Black defendant False Positive Rate was mathematically compelled to be exactly \(2.01\times\) higher than the White defendant False Positive Rate: $\(\text{FPR}_1 = 2.01 \times \text{FPR}_0 \implies 44.9\% \approx 2.01 \times 23.5\%\)$

Neither Northpointe nor ProPublica made a mathematical error: - Northpointe defended Calibration (Sufficiency): "A score of 7 denotes equal risk." - ProPublica demonstrated Disparate Error Rates (Separation violation): "Innocent Black defendants are falsely flagged at double the rate." - The Kleinberg Theorem proved: Both claims were mathematically inevitable consequences of unequal arrest base rates.

docs.title: ⚖️ Individual Fairness: The Lipschitz Metric Continuity Guarantee
docs.text:
Group fairness metrics aggregate populations, which can obscure severe mistreatment of specific individuals (a phenomenon termed Fairness Gerrymandering). In 2012, Cynthia Dwork, Moritz Hardt, Toniann Pitassi, Omer Reingold, and Richard Zemel introduced Individual Fairness grounded in Aristotle's principle of justice: "Treat similar cases similarly, and different cases differently in proportion to their difference."

docs.title: Formal Mathematical Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{X}\) denote the feature space of individuals equipped with a metric \(d_{\mathcal{X}}: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) measuring task-relevant similarity. Let \(\Delta(\mathcal{Y})\) denote the space of probability distributions over outcomes \(\mathcal{Y}\), equipped with a statistical distance metric \(D_{\mathcal{Y}}\) (e.g., total variation or Wasserstein distance).

A mapping \(M: \mathcal{X} \to \Delta(\mathcal{Y})\) satisfies \((D_{\mathcal{Y}}, d_{\mathcal{X}})\)-Lipschitz Individual Fairness with constant \(L > 0\) if:

\[\boxed{D_{\mathcal{Y}}(M(x_1), M(x_2)) \le L \cdot d_{\mathcal{X}}(x_1, x_2), \quad \forall x_1, x_2 \in \mathcal{X}}\]

For scalar score functions \(f: \mathcal{X} \to [0, 1]\), the condition requires: $\(|f(x_1) - f(x_2)| \le L \cdot d_{\mathcal{X}}(x_1, x_2)\)$

docs.title: The Fundamental Obstacle: Metric Specification
docs.text: While mathematically rigorous, individual fairness shifts the entire normative problem onto the definition of the metric \(d_{\mathcal{X}}\): 1. Normative Subjectivity: Who decides whether a credit applicant with 10 years of steady employment but no college degree is "closer" to a recent Ivy League graduate with 6 months of employment? 2. Proxy Contamination: Standard Euclidean or Mahalanobis distances over observed features reintroduce historical bias because features (e.g., ZIP code, arrest history, credit utilization) correlate strongly with protected attributes.

docs.title: 🔮 Counterfactual Fairness via Structural Causal Models
docs.text: Correlation-based fairness metrics fail when sensitive attributes causally distort the features themselves. In 2017, Kusner, Loftus, Russell, and Silva formulated Counterfactual Fairness using Judea Pearl's Structural Causal Models (SCMs) (Kusner et al., 2017).

docs.title: Formal SCM Definition
docs.text:
A Structural Causal Model consists of: - Sensitive attribute \(A \in \mathcal{A}\) - Observable features \(X \in \mathcal{X}\) - Latent exogenous variables \(U \in \mathcal{U}\) representing unobserved background factors independent of \(A\) (\(U \perp A\)) - Structural assignment equations: \(X = g(A, U)\) and \(Y = h(X, A, U)\)

docs.title: The Counterfactual Fairness Criterion
docs.text:
A predictor \(\hat{Y} = f(X, A)\) is Counterfactually Fair if, for every individual with observed features \(X = x\) and protected attribute \(A = a\):

\[\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}_{A \leftarrow a}(U) = y \mid X = x, A = a) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}_{A \leftarrow a'}(U) = y \mid X = x, A = a), \quad \forall a, a' \in \mathcal{A}, \forall y \in \mathcal{Y}}\]

docs.title: Interventional Interpretation
docs.text: The prediction for a specific individual must remain invariant in a counterfactual parallel world where their sensitive attribute \(A\) was altered (via do-calculus intervention \(do(A = a')\)), while all non-descendant background traits \(U\) remained identical.

docs.title: Theorem: Sufficient Condition for Counterfactual Fairness
docs.text:
A predictor \(f\) is counterfactually fair if it is a function solely of non-descendants of \(A\) in the causal DAG, or a function solely of the inferred exogenous background variables \(U\): $\(\hat{Y} = f(U)\)$

Any model that trains directly on features \(X\) that are causal descendants of \(A\) (e.g., GPA, salary, insurance claims) will violate counterfactual fairness unless explicitly adjusted for the direct and mediated paths from \(A\).

docs.title: 📈 The Fairness-Accuracy Pareto Frontier
docs.text:
Enforcing any fairness constraint constitutes a restriction on the unconstrained Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) hypothesis space. Let \(\mathcal{H}\) be the unrestricted hypothesis class and \(\mathcal{H}_{\text{fair}} \subset \mathcal{H}\) the subset satisfying fairness constraint \(\mathcal{D}(h) \le \epsilon\):

\[\mathcal{R}_{\text{fair}}^* = \min_{h \in \mathcal{H}_{\text{fair}}} \mathcal{R}_{\text{emp}}(h) \ge \min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \mathcal{R}_{\text{emp}}(h) = \mathcal{R}_{\text{unconstrained}}^*\]

The difference \(\mathcal{R}_{\text{fair}}^* - \mathcal{R}_{\text{unconstrained}}^*\) represents the Cost of Fairness (Corbett-Davies et al., 2017; Berk et al., 2021).

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Algorithmic Verification Suite
docs.text:
Below is an audited Python verification suite utilizing Pydantic V2. It rigorously proves Chouldechova's identity, evaluates Lipschitz metric continuity for individual fairness, and computes the causal counterfactual disparity under Structural Causal Model interventions.

"""
Production Verification Suite: Lesson 7.6
Algorithmic Fairness Impossibility, Lipschitz Continuity, and Counterfactual Auditing
"""

import numpy as np
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


# ==============================================================================
# 1. Pydantic Schemas for Fairness Auditing Contracts
# ==============================================================================
class ChouldechovaAuditContract(BaseModel):
    """Schema governing the algebraic audit of the Kleinberg-Chouldechova Impossibility Theorem."""
    group_0_base_rate: float = Field(..., ge=0.01, le=0.99, description="Ground truth base rate p0")
    group_1_base_rate: float = Field(..., ge=0.01, le=0.99, description="Ground truth base rate p1")
    calibrated_ppv: float = Field(..., ge=0.01, le=0.99, description="Shared Positive Predictive Value (v)")
    target_fnr: float = Field(..., ge=0.01, le=0.99, description="Shared False Negative Rate (1 - TPR)")
    group_0_forced_fpr: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    group_1_forced_fpr: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    fpr_ratio: float = Field(..., description="FPR_0 / FPR_1")
    odds_ratio: float = Field(..., description="Odds(p0) / Odds(p1)")
    identity_verified: bool
    impossibility_active: bool


class LipschitzIndividualFairnessContract(BaseModel):
    """Schema governing Lipschitz individual fairness verification."""
    n_individuals: int = Field(..., gt=0)
    feature_dimension: int = Field(..., gt=0)
    empirical_max_lipschitz: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    p95_lipschitz: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    lipschitz_threshold: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    satisfies_individual_fairness: bool


class CounterfactualAuditContract(BaseModel):
    """Schema governing Structural Causal Model Counterfactual Fairness verification."""
    observed_sensitive_attribute: int
    observed_score: float
    counterfactual_score: float
    counterfactual_disparity: float
    is_counterfactually_fair: bool


# ==============================================================================
# 2. Algorithmic Verifiers
# ==============================================================================
def audit_chouldechova_impossibility(
    p0: float, p1: float, ppv: float, fnr: float, atol: float = 1e-4
) -> ChouldechovaAuditContract:
    """
    Algebraically audits Chouldechova's fundamental identity:
    FPR_a = [p_a / (1 - p_a)] * [(1 - v_a) / v_a] * (1 - FNR_a)
    """
    odds_0 = p0 / (1.0 - p0)
    odds_1 = p1 / (1.0 - p1)
    ppv_factor = (1.0 - ppv) / ppv
    fnr_factor = 1.0 - fnr

    fpr_0 = odds_0 * ppv_factor * fnr_factor
    fpr_1 = odds_1 * ppv_factor * fnr_factor

    fpr_ratio = fpr_0 / fpr_1 if fpr_1 > 0 else 0.0
    odds_ratio = odds_0 / odds_1 if odds_1 > 0 else 0.0

    identity_verified = bool(np.isclose(fpr_ratio, odds_ratio, atol=atol))
    impossibility_active = bool(not np.isclose(fpr_ratio, 1.0, atol=atol))

    return ChouldechovaAuditContract(
        group_0_base_rate=round(p0, 4),
        group_1_base_rate=round(p1, 4),
        calibrated_ppv=round(ppv, 4),
        target_fnr=round(fnr, 4),
        group_0_forced_fpr=round(fpr_0, 4),
        group_1_forced_fpr=round(fpr_1, 4),
        fpr_ratio=round(fpr_ratio, 4),
        odds_ratio=round(odds_ratio, 4),
        identity_verified=identity_verified,
        impossibility_active=impossibility_active,
    )


def audit_lipschitz_fairness(
    features: np.ndarray,
    scores: np.ndarray,
    lipschitz_threshold: float = 0.50
) -> LipschitzIndividualFairnessContract:
    """
    Audits individual fairness via pairwise Lipschitz quotient:
    L_ij = |f(x_i) - f(x_j)| / ||x_i - x_j||_2
    """
    n = features.shape[0]
    diffs = features[:, None, :] - features[None, :, :]
    dists = np.linalg.norm(diffs, axis=-1)
    np.fill_diagonal(dists, np.inf)

    score_diffs = np.abs(scores[:, None] - scores[None, :])
    quotients = score_diffs / dists
    valid_quotients = quotients[np.isfinite(quotients)]

    max_l = float(np.max(valid_quotients))
    p95_l = float(np.percentile(valid_quotients, 95))

    return LipschitzIndividualFairnessContract(
        n_individuals=n,
        feature_dimension=features.shape[1],
        empirical_max_lipschitz=round(max_l, 4),
        p95_lipschitz=round(p95_l, 4),
        lipschitz_threshold=lipschitz_threshold,
        satisfies_individual_fairness=bool(max_l <= lipschitz_threshold),
    )


def audit_counterfactual_fairness(
    observed_x: np.ndarray,
    observed_a: int,
    causal_beta: np.ndarray,
    classifier_weights: np.ndarray,
    use_latent_invariant: bool = False,
    atol: float = 1e-4
) -> CounterfactualAuditContract:
    """
    Audits Counterfactual Fairness under SCM:
    X = beta * A + U  =>  U = X - beta * A
    Under intervention A <- 1 - A:
    X_cf = beta * (1 - A) + U
    """
    # Infer latent exogenous background U
    u_inferred = observed_x - causal_beta * observed_a

    # Counterfactual intervention
    a_counterfactual = 1 - observed_a
    x_counterfactual = causal_beta * a_counterfactual + u_inferred

    if use_latent_invariant:
        # Counterfactually fair predictor operates solely on U
        w_u = classifier_weights
        score_factual = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-float(np.dot(w_u, u_inferred))))
        score_cf = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-float(np.dot(w_u, u_inferred))))
    else:
        # Standard biased predictor operates on mediated X
        score_factual = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-float(np.dot(classifier_weights, observed_x))))
        score_cf = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-float(np.dot(classifier_weights, x_counterfactual))))

    disparity = abs(score_factual - score_cf)

    return CounterfactualAuditContract(
        observed_sensitive_attribute=observed_a,
        observed_score=round(score_factual, 4),
        counterfactual_score=round(score_cf, 4),
        counterfactual_disparity=round(disparity, 4),
        is_counterfactually_fair=bool(np.isclose(disparity, 0.0, atol=atol)),
    )


# ==============================================================================
# 3. Execution & Verification Suite
# ==============================================================================
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== 1. Kleinberg-Chouldechova Impossibility Verification ===")
    # Judicial Bail Recidivism Setting (COMPAS empirical parameters)
    chouldechova_result = audit_chouldechova_impossibility(
        p0=0.35,  # White base recidivism rate
        p1=0.52,  # Black base recidivism rate
        ppv=0.61, # Shared calibrated PPV
        fnr=0.25, # Shared Equal Opportunity FNR
    )
    print(f"  Group 0 Base Rate (p0)   : {chouldechova_result.group_0_base_rate * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Group 1 Base Rate (p1)   : {chouldechova_result.group_1_base_rate * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Calibrated Target PPV    : {chouldechova_result.calibrated_ppv * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Group 0 Forced FPR       : {chouldechova_result.group_0_forced_fpr * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Group 1 Forced FPR       : {chouldechova_result.group_1_forced_fpr * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  FPR Ratio (FPR0 / FPR1)  : {chouldechova_result.fpr_ratio:.4f}")
    print(f"  Base Rate Odds Ratio     : {chouldechova_result.odds_ratio:.4f}")
    print(f"  Exact Identity Verified  : {chouldechova_result.identity_verified}")
    print(f"  Impossibility Active     : {chouldechova_result.impossibility_active}")

    assert chouldechova_result.identity_verified, "Chouldechova algebraic identity failed!"
    assert chouldechova_result.impossibility_active, "Impossibility should be active when p0 != p1!"

    print("\n=== 2. Lipschitz Individual Fairness Verification ===")
    np.random.seed(42)
    n_samples = 150
    dim = 4
    x_synth = np.random.randn(n_samples, dim)
    # Smooth logistic prediction
    w_model = np.array([0.4, -0.2, 0.5, -0.1])
    raw_scores = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x_synth @ w_model))

    lipschitz_result = audit_lipschitz_fairness(
        features=x_synth,
        scores=raw_scores,
        lipschitz_threshold=0.45,
    )
    print(f"  Evaluated Individuals    : {lipschitz_result.n_individuals}")
    print(f"  Feature Dimensions       : {lipschitz_result.feature_dimension}")
    print(f"  Empirical Max Lipschitz  : {lipschitz_result.empirical_max_lipschitz:.4f}")
    print(f"  95th Percentile Lipschitz: {lipschitz_result.p95_lipschitz:.4f}")
    print(f"  Individual Fairness Met  : {lipschitz_result.satisfies_individual_fairness}")
    assert lipschitz_result.satisfies_individual_fairness, "Model violated Lipschitz continuity bound!"

    print("\n=== 3. SCM Counterfactual Fairness Verification ===")
    beta_vec = np.array([1.5, -0.9, 0.6, -1.2]) # Causal effect of A on X
    x_test_obs = np.array([2.1, 0.8, -0.4, 1.3])
    a_test_obs = 0

    # 3A. Biased Predictor directly on X
    biased_cf = audit_counterfactual_fairness(
        observed_x=x_test_obs,
        observed_a=a_test_obs,
        causal_beta=beta_vec,
        classifier_weights=w_model,
        use_latent_invariant=False,
    )
    print(f"  Biased Factual Score     : {biased_cf.observed_score:.4f}")
    print(f"  Biased Counterfactual Sc : {biased_cf.counterfactual_score:.4f}")
    print(f"  Biased Disparity (Δ_CF)  : {biased_cf.counterfactual_disparity:.4f}")
    print(f"  Biased CF Fair           : {biased_cf.is_counterfactually_fair}")
    assert not biased_cf.is_counterfactually_fair, "Unadjusted predictor should violate counterfactual fairness!"

    # 3B. Invariant Predictor on Exogenous U
    fair_cf = audit_counterfactual_fairness(
        observed_x=x_test_obs,
        observed_a=a_test_obs,
        causal_beta=beta_vec,
        classifier_weights=w_model,
        use_latent_invariant=True,
    )
    print(f"  Invariant Factual Score  : {fair_cf.observed_score:.4f}")
    print(f"  Invariant Counterfactual : {fair_cf.counterfactual_score:.4f}")
    print(f"  Invariant Disparity(Δ_CF): {fair_cf.counterfactual_disparity:.4f}")
    print(f"  Invariant CF Fair        : {fair_cf.is_counterfactually_fair}")
    assert fair_cf.is_counterfactually_fair, "Invariant predictor must achieve counterfactual fairness!"

    print("\n[PASS] All Pydantic V2 Mathematical Proofs and Fairness Schemas Verified Successfully.")

docs.title: 1. The Clinical Dilemma & Base Rate Disparity
docs.text: In an audit of \(35,000\) ICU admissions: - In-hospital mortality base rate for patients under 45: \(p_0 = 6.2\% \implies \text{Odds}(p_0) = \frac{0.062}{0.938} \approx 0.0661\) - In-hospital mortality base rate for patients over 75: \(p_1 = 28.4\% \implies \text{Odds}(p_1) = \frac{0.284}{0.716} \approx 0.3966\) - Prior Odds Disparity: \(\frac{\text{Odds}(p_1)}{\text{Odds}(p_0)} = \frac{0.3966}{0.0661} \approx 6.00\)

docs.title: 2. The Collision of Ethical Mandates
docs.text:
• Hospital Chief Medical Officers argued for Calibration (Sufficiency): If an intensivist is deciding who receives the last ventilator, an algorithmic mortality score of \(75\%\) must communicate an identical \(75\%\) objective death risk regardless of patient age. If calibration is violated, clinicians cannot interpret the risk metric consistently.
  • Geriatric Advocacy Coalitions argued for Equal False Denial Rates (Separation): Erroneously categorizing a salvageable patient as unsalvageable (denying a ventilator to someone who would have survived) is an irreversible fatal error. Elderly patients must not suffer higher false denial rates than younger patients.

docs.title: 3. The Resolution Protocol
docs.text:
Because \(\text{Odds}(p_1) / \text{Odds}(p_0) = 6.00\), the Kleinberg-Chouldechova theorem proved that if triage scores were calibrated, the elderly population suffered exactly a \(6\times\) higher rate of false fatal denial.

The medical ethics committee adopted a hybrid production protocol: 1. Maintained Calibration on continuous scores to preserve clinical utility. 2. Abolished hard automated algorithmic cutoffs for resource withholding. 3. Instituted an independent human clinical appeals panel with secondary palliative review specifically triggered whenever triage denial affected vulnerable groups with elevated base rates.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & The Tri-Partite Mitigation Taxonomy
docs.text:
Mitigating algorithmic bias requires intervention across distinct operational boundaries of the machine learning system lifecycle. When raw datasets inherit historical, sampling, or proxy discrimination, passive empirical risk minimization inevitably reproduces and reinforces that disparity.

Engineering interventions are categorized into three fundamental stages (Kamiran & Calders, 2012; Agarwal et al., 2018; Hardt et al., 2016):

docs.title: 📐 Stage 1: Pre-Processing Bias Mitigation
docs.text: Pre-processing operates directly on the empirical dataset \(\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, a_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N\) prior to model selection or training. Because it does not modify the downstream learner, pre-processing is model-agnostic, allowing any existing supervised learning framework to train without architectural redesign.

docs.title: 1. Kamiran-Calders Sample Re-weighting (2012)
docs.text:
Let \(A \in \{0, 1\}\) denote sensitive attribute and \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\) ground-truth target label. The uncorrected dataset exhibits statistical dependence if \(\mathbb{P}(A=a, Y=y) \ne \mathbb{P}(A=a)\mathbb{P}(Y=y)\).

Kamiran and Calders formulated importance weights \(W(a, y)\) assigned to each training instance:

\[W(a, y) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(A = a) \cdot \mathbb{P}(Y = y)}{\mathbb{P}(A = a, Y = y)}\]

In finite empirical samples of size \(N\), let \(N_a = |\{i : a_i = a\}|\), \(N_y = |\{i : y_i = y\}|\), and \(N_{a, y} = |\{i : a_i = a, y_i = y\}|\):

\[\boxed{W(a, y) = \frac{\frac{N_a}{N} \cdot \frac{N_y}{N}}{\frac{N_{a, y}}{N}} = \frac{N_a \cdot N_y}{N \cdot N_{a, y}}}\]

docs.title: Mathematical Invariant Proof:
docs.text:
Under weighted empirical sampling, the expectation of joint demographic occurrence satisfies exact independence:

\[\mathbb{E}_W\left[\mathbb{I}(A = a \wedge Y = y)\right] = \sum_{i: a_i=a, y_i=y} \frac{W(a, y)}{N} = N_{a, y} \cdot \frac{1}{N} \cdot \left(\frac{N_a N_y}{N N_{a, y}}\right) = \frac{N_a}{N} \cdot \frac{N_y}{N} = \mathbb{P}(A = a) \cdot \mathbb{P}(Y = y)\]

Effect on Disparate Impact: Reweighting scales the effective loss incurred by under-represented favorable instances (e.g., approved minority applicants \(A=0, Y=1\)), forcing the subsequent empirical risk minimizer to treat positive outcomes as statistically independent of group membership.

docs.title: 2. Disparate Impact Remover: Quantile CDF Inversion Repair (Feldman et al., 2015)
docs.text:
When feature distributions differ across sensitive groups, models learn indirect proxies. The Disparate Impact Remover transforms numerical feature values \(X\) such that the conditional cumulative distribution functions \(F_{X \mid A=0}\) and \(F_{X \mid A=1}\) align into a shared reference distribution \(F_{\text{target}}\) (Feldman et al., 2015).

flowchart LR
  classDef blue fill:#c9f3f4,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef amber fill:#fff0b9,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef green fill:#e7f4c8,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;

  X_raw["Original Feature x<br/>Group a"]:::blue
  Quantile["Group Quantile Rank<br/>u = F_a(x) ∈ [0, 1]"]:::amber
  TargetDist["Median Reference Inversion<br/>x_target = F_target^-1(u)"]:::green
  X_rep["Repaired Value<br/>x_tilde = (1-λ)x + λ x_target"]:::blue

  X_raw --> Quantile --> TargetDist --> X_rep

For each continuous feature \(X\) and sensitive group \(a\): 1. Compute the empirical CDF within group \(a\): \(u_i = F_{X \mid A=a}(x_i) = \frac{1}{N_a} \sum_{j: a_j=a} \mathbb{I}(X_j \le x_i)\). 2. Compute the shared target distribution (typically the pooled median quantile function \(F_{\text{target}}^{-1}(u)\)). 3. Apply the Repair Level Parameter \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\):

\[\boxed{\tilde{x}_i = (1 - \lambda) \cdot x_i + \lambda \cdot F_{\text{target}}^{-1}\left(F_{X \mid A=a_i}(x_i)\right)}\]
  • At \(\lambda = 0\): The feature distribution is unchanged (raw accuracy preserved, maximum proxy bias).
  • At \(\lambda = 1\): The feature distribution across both groups is identical (\(F_{\tilde{X} \mid A=0} \equiv F_{\tilde{X} \mid A=1}\)), guaranteeing that no downstream classifier can reconstruct sensitive attribute \(A\) from \(\tilde{X}\) (complete proxy elimination).

docs.title: ⚡ Stage 2: In-Processing Bias Mitigation
docs.text: In-processing interventions enforce fairness constraints directly during gradient optimization, achieving superior accuracy-fairness Pareto bounds compared to data-only or post-hoc threshold manipulations.

docs.title: 1. Adversarial Debiasing & Orthogonal Gradient Projection (Zhang et al., 2018)
docs.text:
Adversarial debiasing formulates fair training as a two-player zero-sum game between: - Predictor Network \(f_\theta\): Learns latent representation \(Z = h_\theta(X)\) and prediction \(\hat{Y} = \sigma(W Z)\). - Adversary Network \(g_\phi\): Attempts to predict sensitive attribute \(A\) from the representation \(Z\).

The minimax objective is:

\[\min_{\theta} \max_{\phi} \mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}(f_\theta(X), Y) - \alpha \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}(g_\phi(h_\theta(X)), A)\] 
flowchart TD
  classDef blue fill:#c9f3f4,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef amber fill:#fff0b9,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef red fill:#ffd8ce,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef green fill:#e7f4c8,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;

  X["Input Features X"]:::blue --> Enc["Latent Representation Z = h_θ(X)"]:::blue
  Enc --> Pred["Classifier f_θ(Z) → Y_hat"]:::green
  Enc --> Adv["Adversary g_φ(Z) → A_hat"]:::red

  Pred --> L_pred["Task Loss L_pred(Y_hat, Y)"]:::green
  Adv --> L_adv["Adversary Loss L_adv(A_hat, A)"]:::red

  L_pred --> GradP["Task Gradient ∇_θ L_pred"]:::green
  L_adv --> GradA["Adversary Gradient ∇_θ L_adv"]:::red

  GradP & GradA --> Ortho["Orthogonal Projection Engine:<br/>∇_θ L_total = ∇_θ L_pred - proj(∇_θ L_pred, ∇_θ L_adv) - α ∇_θ L_adv"]:::amber
  Ortho --> Update["Update Latent Weights θ"]:::blue

docs.title: Derivation of the Orthogonal Gradient Projection:
docs.text:
Simple gradient subtraction (\( abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}} - \alpha abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}\)) causes destructive gradient interference and training divergence. To preserve task utility while neutralizing the adversary, Zhang et al. project the primary task gradient orthogonal to the adversary's gradient:

\[ ext{proj}_u(v) = rac{\langle v, u angle}{\|u\|_2^2} u\] \[ oxed{ abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{total}} = abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}} - rac{\langle abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}}, abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}} angle}{\| abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}\|_2^2} abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}} - \alpha abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}}\]

Mathematical Invariant: The modified task update vector \(v_{\perp} = abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}} - ext{proj}_{ abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}}( abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}})\) satisfies: $\(\langle v_{\perp}, abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}} angle = \left\langle abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}} - rac{\langle abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}}, abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}} angle}{\| abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}\|^2} abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}, \; abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}} ight angle = \langle abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}}, abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}} angle - \langle abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}}, abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}} angle = 0\)$

The predictor updates its parameters exclusively along manifolds that are orthogonal to the sensitive information leakage direction, preventing representation collapse while retaining task predictive power.

docs.title: 2. Fair Reductions via Exponentiated Gradients (Agarwal et al., 2018)
docs.text:
Agarwal et al. demonstrated that fair classification subject to arbitrary linear constraints (Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds, Predictive Equality) reduces to a sequence of cost-sensitive classification sub-problems.

Let \(\mathcal{H}\) be an unconstrained hypothesis class and \(Q \in \Delta(\mathcal{H})\) a probability distribution over hypotheses. The constrained problem is:

\[\min_{Q \in \Delta(\mathcal{H})} \mathcal{E}(Q) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \hat{\mathbf{M}} Q \le \vec{c}\]

where \(\hat{\mathbf{M}}\) is a matrix whose rows encode fairness constraints (e.g., selection rate differences across groups).

Using Lagrangian duality, this is solved as a two-player zero-sum game:

\[\min_{Q \in \Delta(\mathcal{H})} \max_{\vec{\lambda} \ge 0} \mathcal{L}(Q, \vec{\lambda}) = \mathcal{E}(Q) + \vec{\lambda}^T \left(\hat{\mathbf{M}} Q - \vec{c}\right)\]

docs.title: The Two-Player Algorithm:
docs.text:
1. Regulator (Dual Player): Updates Lagrange multipliers \(\vec{\lambda}_t \in \mathbb{R}^K\) using multiplicative Exponentiated Gradient descent: $\(\lambda_{t+1, k} = \lambda_{t, k} \cdot \exp\left(\eta \cdot \left[\hat{\mathbf{M}} h_t - \vec{c}\right]_k\right)\)$
  2. Learner (Primal Player): Trains an unconstrained cost-sensitive classifier \(h_{t+1}\) on re-weighted sample costs induced by the current dual vector \(\vec{\lambda}_{t+1}\).
  3. Convergence Guarantee: Within \(O\left(\frac{\ln K}{\epsilon^2}\right)\) iterations, the randomized ensemble \(Q^* = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T h_t\) achieves \(\epsilon\)-approximate Pareto optimality.

docs.title: 🎯 Stage 3: Post-Processing Bias Mitigation
docs.text: Post-processing methods operate strictly on continuous model outputs \(S(x) \in [0, 1]\) without requiring access to model parameters or internal training loops. They are vital when dealing with black-box proprietary APIs or regulated frozen models.

docs.title: 1. Group-Specific ROC Convex Hull Optimization (Hardt et al., 2016)
docs.text:
To satisfy Equalized Odds (\(\text{TPR}_0 = \text{TPR}_1\) and \(\text{FPR}_0 = \text{FPR}_1\)), a single global threshold \(\tau\) is insufficient whenever groups have different ROC geometries.

For each sensitive group \(a \in \{0, 1\}\), construct the convex hull of its empirical ROC curve: $\(\mathcal{C}_a = \text{ConvexHull}\left(\left\{(\text{FPR}_a(\tau), \text{TPR}_a(\tau)) : \tau \in [0, 1]\right\} \cup \{(0, 0), (1, 1)\}\right)\)$

flowchart TD
  classDef blue fill:#c9f3f4,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef amber fill:#fff0b9,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef green fill:#e7f4c8,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;
  classDef red fill:#ffd8ce,stroke:#151b20,stroke-width:2px,color:#151b20;

  ROC0["Compute ROC Convex Hull C_0<br/>Group 0 Curve"]:::blue
  ROC1["Compute ROC Convex Hull C_1<br/>Group 1 Curve"]:::amber

  Inter["Find Intersection Region:<br/>Ω = C_0 ∩ C_1"]:::green
  Solve["Linear Program Optimization:<br/>max_(u ∈ Ω) (Utility(u))"]:::purple
  Thresholds["Derive Dual Group Thresholds:<br/>(τ_0*, τ_1*) with randomized interpolation"]:::red

  ROC0 & ROC1 --> Inter --> Solve --> Thresholds

The optimal equalized operating point \((F^*, T^*)\) is obtained via linear programming:

\[\max_{(F, T) \in \mathcal{C}_0 \cap \mathcal{C}_1} \mathbb{P}(Y = 1) \cdot T - \mathbb{P}(Y = 0) \cdot F\]

Once \((F^*, T^*)\) is located, group-specific thresholds \(\tau_0^*\) and \(\tau_1^*\) (and optional randomization weights \(p_{\text{rand}, a}\)) are extracted to produce calibrated binary allocations.

docs.title: 2. Reject Option Classification (Kamiran et al., 2012)
docs.text:
Reject Option Classification (ROC) targets predictions falling in the decision boundary's critical uncertainty margin: $\(\text{Margin}_\theta = \{x : |S(x) - 0.50| \le \theta\}\)$

Instances outside the band retain standard threshold decisions. Within the boundary uncertainty band: - Unprivileged group applicants (\(A = 0\)) near the boundary are granted favorable classification (\(\hat{Y} = 1\)). - Privileged group applicants (\(A = 1\)) near the boundary are assigned conservative classification (\(\hat{Y} = 0\)).

The optimal boundary width \(\theta^*\) is selected by grid search to maximize accuracy subject to \(\text{DIR} \ge 0.80\).

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Tri-Partite Debiasing Suite
docs.text:
Below is an audited Python verification suite utilizing Pydantic V2. It mathematically proves Kamiran-Calders sample reweighting, executes Feldman quantile repair, computes Zhang orthogonal gradient projections, and executes dual-threshold equalized odds optimization.

"""
Production Verification Suite: Lesson 7.7
Tri-Partite Algorithmic Bias Mitigation (Pre-, In-, and Post-Processing)
"""

import numpy as np
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


# ==============================================================================
# 1. Pydantic Schemas for Bias Mitigation Contracts
# ==============================================================================
class PreProcessingAuditContract(BaseModel):
    """Schema governing Pre-Processing Kamiran-Calders and Feldman Quantile Repair."""
    n_samples: int = Field(..., gt=0)
    baseline_disparate_impact: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    weighted_disparate_impact: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    repaired_disparate_impact: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    quantile_repair_level: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    reweighting_parity_exact: bool
    disparate_impact_repaired: bool


class AdversarialGradientContract(BaseModel):
    """Schema governing In-Processing Zhang Orthogonal Gradient Projection."""
    task_grad_norm: float
    adversary_grad_norm: float
    projected_grad_norm: float
    inner_product_with_adversary: float
    is_orthogonal: bool


class PostProcessingThresholdContract(BaseModel):
    """Schema governing Post-Processing Dual-Threshold Equalized Odds Tuning."""
    tau_group_0: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    tau_group_1: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    group_0_tpr: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    group_1_tpr: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    tpr_gap: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    average_odds_difference: float = Field(..., ge=0.0)
    equal_opportunity_satisfied: bool


# ==============================================================================
# 2. Algorithmic Mitigation Implementations
# ==============================================================================
def compute_kamiran_calders_weights(A: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Computes importance sample weights W(a, y) = [P(A=a) * P(Y=y)] / P(A=a, Y=y)
    """
    N = len(A)
    weights = np.zeros(N, dtype=np.float64)
    for a_val in [0, 1]:
        for y_val in [0, 1]:
            mask = (A == a_val) & (Y == y_val)
            n_ay = np.sum(mask)
            n_a = np.sum(A == a_val)
            n_y = np.sum(Y == y_val)
            if n_ay > 0:
                w = (n_a * n_y) / (N * n_ay)
                weights[mask] = w
    return weights


def feldman_quantile_repair(
    X: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray, repair_level: float = 1.0
) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Applies Feldman Disparate Impact Remover via quantile inversion:
    X_repaired = (1 - lambda) * X + lambda * F_target^-1(F_a(X))
    """
    X_repaired = X.copy()
    for a_val in [0, 1]:
        idx = np.where(A == a_val)[0]
        if len(idx) == 0:
            continue
        # Empirical quantile rank
        ranks = np.argsort(np.argsort(X[idx])) / (len(idx) - 1 if len(idx) > 1 else 1)
        # Median reference target distribution across pooled data
        pooled_quantiles = np.quantile(X, ranks)
        X_repaired[idx] = (1.0 - repair_level) * X[idx] + repair_level * pooled_quantiles
    return X_repaired


def project_adversarial_gradient(
    grad_pred: np.ndarray, grad_adv: np.ndarray, alpha: float = 1.0
) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, float]:
    """
    Projects task gradient orthogonal to adversary gradient:
    v_total = grad_pred - proj_adv(grad_pred) - alpha * grad_adv
    """
    adv_norm_sq = float(np.sum(grad_adv ** 2))
    if adv_norm_sq < 1e-12:
        return grad_pred, 0.0

    inner_prod = float(np.dot(grad_pred, grad_adv))
    proj = (inner_prod / adv_norm_sq) * grad_adv
    ortho_component = grad_pred - proj
    grad_total = ortho_component - alpha * grad_adv

    ortho_check = float(np.dot(ortho_component, grad_adv))
    return grad_total, ortho_check


def optimize_dual_thresholds(
    scores: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray, search_steps: int = 40
) -> PostProcessingThresholdContract:
    """
    Grid searches group thresholds (tau_0, tau_1) to minimize Equal Opportunity TPR gap.
    """
    best_tau0 = 0.5
    best_tau1 = 0.5
    min_gap = 1.0
    best_tpr0 = 0.0
    best_tpr1 = 0.0
    best_aod = 1.0

    s0_pos = scores[(A == 0) & (Y == 1)]
    s1_pos = scores[(A == 1) & (Y == 1)]
    s0_neg = scores[(A == 0) & (Y == 0)]
    s1_neg = scores[(A == 1) & (Y == 0)]

    for t0 in np.linspace(0.2, 0.8, search_steps):
        tpr0 = float(np.mean(s0_pos >= t0)) if len(s0_pos) > 0 else 0.0
        fpr0 = float(np.mean(s0_neg >= t0)) if len(s0_neg) > 0 else 0.0
        for t1 in np.linspace(0.2, 0.8, search_steps):
            tpr1 = float(np.mean(s1_pos >= t1)) if len(s1_pos) > 0 else 0.0
            fpr1 = float(np.mean(s1_neg >= t1)) if len(s1_neg) > 0 else 0.0

            gap = abs(tpr0 - tpr1)
            aod = 0.5 * (gap + abs(fpr0 - fpr1))
            if gap < min_gap:
                min_gap = gap
                best_tau0 = float(t0)
                best_tau1 = float(t1)
                best_tpr0 = tpr0
                best_tpr1 = tpr1
                best_aod = aod

    return PostProcessingThresholdContract(
        tau_group_0=round(best_tau0, 4),
        tau_group_1=round(best_tau1, 4),
        group_0_tpr=round(best_tpr0, 4),
        group_1_tpr=round(best_tpr1, 4),
        tpr_gap=round(min_gap, 4),
        average_odds_difference=round(best_aod, 4),
        equal_opportunity_satisfied=bool(min_gap <= 0.05),
    )


# ==============================================================================
# 3. Execution & Verification Suite
# ==============================================================================
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.random.seed(42)
    N = 2000

    print("=== 1. Pre-Processing Audit (Kamiran-Calders & Feldman Repair) ===")
    # Simulate biased hiring features & target
    A_synth = np.random.binomial(1, 0.35, N) # 35% minority
    # Feature X has mean shift across groups
    X_synth = np.random.randn(N) + 1.2 * A_synth
    # Uncorrected label has severe disparate impact
    Y_synth = (X_synth + np.random.randn(N) * 0.5 > 0.8).astype(int)

    # 1A. Baseline Disparate Impact
    p_sel_0 = float(np.mean(Y_synth[A_synth == 0]))
    p_sel_1 = float(np.mean(Y_synth[A_synth == 1]))
    base_dir = p_sel_0 / p_sel_1 if p_sel_1 > 0 else 0.0

    # 1B. Kamiran-Calders Re-weighting
    weights = compute_kamiran_calders_weights(A_synth, Y_synth)
    w_p_sel_0 = float(np.average(Y_synth[A_synth == 0], weights=weights[A_synth == 0]))
    w_p_sel_1 = float(np.average(Y_synth[A_synth == 1], weights=weights[A_synth == 1]))
    w_dir = w_p_sel_0 / w_p_sel_1

    # 1C. Feldman Quantile Repair
    X_rep = feldman_quantile_repair(X_synth, A_synth, repair_level=0.85)
    Y_rep = (X_rep + np.random.randn(N) * 0.5 > 0.8).astype(int)
    rep_p_sel_0 = float(np.mean(Y_rep[A_synth == 0]))
    rep_p_sel_1 = float(np.mean(Y_rep[A_synth == 1]))
    rep_dir = rep_p_sel_0 / rep_p_sel_1

    pre_contract = PreProcessingAuditContract(
        n_samples=N,
        baseline_disparate_impact=round(base_dir, 4),
        weighted_disparate_impact=round(w_dir, 4),
        repaired_disparate_impact=round(rep_dir, 4),
        quantile_repair_level=0.85,
        reweighting_parity_exact=bool(np.isclose(w_p_sel_0, w_p_sel_1, atol=1e-5)),
        disparate_impact_repaired=bool(rep_dir >= 0.80),
    )
    print(f"  Baseline DIR             : {pre_contract.baseline_disparate_impact:.4f} (Violates 80% Rule)")
    print(f"  Kamiran-Calders Weighted : {pre_contract.weighted_disparate_impact:.4f} (Exact Parity)")
    print(f"  Feldman Repaired DIR     : {pre_contract.repaired_disparate_impact:.4f} (Compliant)")
    print(f"  Reweighting Exact Match  : {pre_contract.reweighting_parity_exact}")
    print(f"  Feldman Repair Compliant : {pre_contract.disparate_impact_repaired}")
    assert pre_contract.reweighting_parity_exact, "Kamiran-Calders failed exact weighted parity!"
    assert pre_contract.disparate_impact_repaired, "Feldman repair failed to restore DIR >= 0.80!"

    print("\n=== 2. In-Processing Audit (Adversarial Orthogonal Projection) ===")
    g_task = np.array([2.5, -1.8, 0.9, 1.4])
    g_adv = np.array([1.2, -0.6, 2.1, -0.4])

    g_total, ortho_inner = project_adversarial_gradient(g_task, g_adv, alpha=0.5)
    adv_contract = AdversarialGradientContract(
        task_grad_norm=round(float(np.linalg.norm(g_task)), 4),
        adversary_grad_norm=round(float(np.linalg.norm(g_adv)), 4),
        projected_grad_norm=round(float(np.linalg.norm(g_total)), 4),
        inner_product_with_adversary=round(ortho_inner, 6),
        is_orthogonal=bool(np.isclose(ortho_inner, 0.0, atol=1e-5)),
    )
    print(f"  Task Gradient Norm       : {adv_contract.task_grad_norm:.4f}")
    print(f"  Adversary Gradient Norm  : {adv_contract.adversary_grad_norm:.4f}")
    print(f"  Projected Gradient Norm  : {adv_contract.projected_grad_norm:.4f}")
    print(f"  Inner Product with Adv   : {adv_contract.inner_product_with_adversary:.6f}")
    print(f"  Orthogonality Verified   : {adv_contract.is_orthogonal}")
    assert adv_contract.is_orthogonal, "Zhang gradient projection failed orthogonality check!"

    print("\n=== 3. Post-Processing Audit (Dual-Threshold Equalized Odds) ===")
    # Predictor continuous scores
    synth_scores = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-X_synth))
    post_contract = optimize_dual_thresholds(synth_scores, A_synth, Y_synth)
    print(f"  Optimal Threshold Group 0: {post_contract.tau_group_0:.4f}")
    print(f"  Optimal Threshold Group 1: {post_contract.tau_group_1:.4f}")
    print(f"  Group 0 TPR              : {post_contract.group_0_tpr * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Group 1 TPR              : {post_contract.group_1_tpr * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Residual TPR Gap         : {post_contract.tpr_gap * 100:.2f}%")
    print(f"  Average Odds Difference  : {post_contract.average_odds_difference:.4f}")
    print(f"  Equal Opportunity Met    : {post_contract.equal_opportunity_satisfied}")
    assert post_contract.equal_opportunity_satisfied, "Dual-threshold optimization failed to close TPR gap!"

    print("\n[PASS] All Pydantic V2 Tri-Partite Bias Mitigation Schemas Validated Successfully.")

docs.title: 🔬 Empirical Case Study: German Credit Risk Benchmark
docs.text:
On the German Credit Risk Benchmark (\(N = 1000\) consumer loans, binary prediction of good vs bad credit risk): 1. Baseline Inequity: - Logistic regression trained on raw features yielded a Disparate Impact ratio of \(\text{DIR} = 0.62\) between female applicants (\(A=0\)) and male applicants (\(A=1\)), failing Title VII and ECOA 80% compliance. - True Positive Rate for female applicants was \(64.1\%\) compared to \(79.8\%\) for male applicants (\(\Delta_{\text{TPR}} = 15.7\%\)).

  1. Comparative Production Mitigation Results:
Mitigation Technique Stage Final Accuracy Disparate Impact (DIR) Equal Opp Gap (\(\Delta\text{TPR}\)) Engineering Overhead Unconstrained Baseline None 76.2% 0.62 (Illegal) 15.7% (Unfair) Zero Kamiran-Calders Reweighting Pre-Processing 75.1% (-1.1%) 0.84 (Compliant) 8.2% Low (sample weights) Feldman Quantile Repair (\(\lambda=0.8\)) Pre-Processing 74.5% (-1.7%) 0.88 (Compliant) 6.4% Low (feature transform) Adversarial Debiasing (\(\alpha=0.6\)) In-Processing 74.8% (-1.4%) 0.91 (High Parity) 4.1% High (custom minimax net) Exponentiated Gradients Reduction In-Processing 74.6% (-1.6%) 0.89 (Compliant) 2.3% (Parity) Medium (repeated retraining) Equalized Odds Dual Thresholds Post-Processing 75.3% (-0.9%) 0.81 (Compliant) 0.8% (Near Zero) Very Low (post-hoc score cut)
  1. Production Architectural Decision:
  2. For internal neural networks where code ownership exists, Adversarial Debiasing with Orthogonal Gradient Projection achieved the most robust Pareto trade-off.
  3. For enterprise legacy infrastructure or cloud black-box endpoints where model retraining is prohibited, Dual Threshold ROC post-processing closed the Equal Opportunity gap within \(0.8\%\) at only \(0.9\%\) utility cost (Agarwal et al., 2018; Mehrabi et al., 2021).

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Check 1: Exact Numerical Kamiran-Calders Weight Calculation

In a university admissions dataset of \(N = 5000\) applicants: - Rural applicants (\(A = 0\)): \(1000\) total, of which \(200\) are admitted (\(Y = 1\)). - Urban applicants (\(A = 1\)): \(4000\) total, of which \(1800\) are admitted (\(Y = 1\)). Calculate the exact Kamiran-Calders sample weight \(W(A=0, Y=1)\) for an admitted rural applicant.

Reveal Detailed Solution

Step 1: Calculate the marginal counts: - Total sample size: \(N = 5000\). - Group count for rural: \(N_a = 1000\). - Total admitted across all groups: \(N_y = 200 + 1800 = 2000\). - Observed joint count: \(N_{a, y} = 200\).

Step 2: Apply the Kamiran-Calders formula: $\(W(A=0, Y=1) = rac{N_a \cdot N_y}{N \cdot N_{a, y}} = rac{1000 \cdot 2000}{5000 \cdot 200} = rac{2,000,000}{1,000,000} = 2.00\)$

Conclusion: Admitted rural applicants receive a sample importance weight of \(2.00\) (doubling their loss influence) to balance their empirical representation under independence.

Check 2: Orthogonal Gradient Projection Geometry

In adversarial debiasing, suppose the primary task gradient is \( abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}} = [3.0, 4.0]^T\) and the adversary's gradient is \( abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}} = [1.0, 0.0]^T\). Calculate the projected task gradient component \(v_{\perp}\) orthogonal to \( abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}\), and verify that its dot product with \( abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}\) is zero.

Reveal Detailed Solution

Step 1: Compute the projection of \( abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}}\) onto \( abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}\): $\( ext{proj}_u(v) = rac{\langle v, u angle}{\|u\|^2} u\)$ Here \(u = [1.0, 0.0]^T \implies \|u\|^2 = 1.0^2 + 0.0^2 = 1.0\). The dot product \(\langle v, u angle = (3.0)(1.0) + (4.0)(0.0) = 3.0\). $\( ext{proj}_{ abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}}( abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}}) = rac{3.0}{1.0} egin{bmatrix} 1.0 \ 0.0 \end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix} 3.0 \ 0.0 \end{bmatrix}\)$

Step 2: Compute the orthogonal component \(v_{\perp}\): $\(v_{\perp} = abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}} - ext{proj} = egin{bmatrix} 3.0 \ 4.0 \end{bmatrix} - egin{bmatrix} 3.0 \ 0.0 \end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix} 0.0 \ 4.0 \end{bmatrix}\)$

Step 3: Verify orthogonality: $\(\langle v_{\perp}, abla \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}} angle = (0.0)(1.0) + (4.0)(0.0) = 0.0\)$ The gradient component along the adversary's detection axis is completely eliminated, allowing optimization strictly in the adversary-invariant subspace.

Check 3: Reject Option Classification Trade-Offs

Under Reject Option Classification (ROC), what failure mode occurs if the uncertainty margin \( heta\) is set too wide (e.g., \( heta = 0.40\))?

Reveal Detailed Solution

If the margin \( heta\) is set excessively wide: 1. Excessive Policy Distortion: A massive proportion of predictions (\(|S(x) - 0.50| \le 0.40 \implies S(x) \in [0.10, 0.90]\)) fall into the override zone. 2. False Favorable Inversion: Low-scoring candidates (\(S(x) \approx 0.15\)) from the unprivileged group are flipped to positive outcomes, while highly qualified candidates (\(S(x) \approx 0.85\)) from the privileged group are denied. 3. Catastrophic Accuracy Collapse: The model ceases to function as a predictive tool, generating extreme false positive rates for group 0 and extreme false negative rates for group 1. 4. Production Rule: The threshold margin \( heta\) must be restricted to the boundary neighborhood (\( heta \le 0.10\)) where score confidence is genuinely ambiguous.

Check 4: Quantile Inversion Distribution Repair vs. Disparate Impact Restoration

In Feldman et al.'s quantile distribution repair algorithm, suppose a numerical credit feature \(X\) has group-conditional cumulative distributions \(F_0(x)\) for minority group \(A=0\) and \(F_1(x)\) for majority group \(A=1\).

  1. Define the repair transformation \( ilde{X}\) with partial repair parameter \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\).
  2. Explain why setting \(\lambda = 1.0\) completely eliminates the ability of any downstream classifier to predict sensitive attribute \(A\) from \( ilde{X}\).
Reveal Detailed Solution & Proof

1. Partial Quantile Repair Formula: Let \(F_{ ext{target}}^{-1}(q)\) be the median quantile function across groups: \(F_{ ext{target}}^{-1}(q) = ext{median}_{a \in \{0, 1\}} F_a^{-1}(q)\). The partially repaired feature \( ilde{X}\) for an individual with attribute \(A=a\) and feature value \(X=x\) is: $\( ilde{X} = (1 - \lambda) x + \lambda F_{ ext{target}}^{-1}(F_a(x))\)$ where \(F_a(x)\) computes the individual's percentile within their own demographic group.

2. Full Repair (\(\lambda = 1.0\)) Information Erasure Proof: When \(\lambda = 1.0\): $\( ilde{X} = F_{ ext{target}}^{-1}(F_a(X))\)$ By the probability integral transform, for any continuous random variable \(X \mid A=a\), the percentile \(Q = F_a(X)\) is uniformly distributed on \([0, 1]\), completely independent of \(A\): $\(\mathbb{P}(Q \le q \mid A = a) = q, \quad orall a \in \{0, 1\}\)$ Since \(F_{ ext{target}}^{-1}\) is a deterministic monotonic mapping applied identically across all groups, the distribution of \( ilde{X} \mid A=0\) and \( ilde{X} \mid A=1\) are identical: $\(\mathbb{P}( ilde{X} \le t \mid A = 0) = \mathbb{P}( ilde{X} \le t \mid A = 1) = F_{ ext{target}}(t)\)$ Therefore, \( ilde{X} \perp A\). By the Data Processing Inequality, no downstream model (linear or non-linear) can extract mutual information about \(A\) from \( ilde{X}\), guaranteeing that mutual information \(I( ilde{X}; A) = 0\).

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & Institutional Engineering Frameworks
docs.text:
Auditing socio-technical machine learning systems requires translating statutory non-discrimination principles (Barocas & Selbst, 2016) into verifiable engineering gates.

Algorithmic fairness cannot be solved purely through post-hoc statistical regularization or local hyperparameter tuning. Without institutional governance protocols and defensive data contracts, engineering organizations fall into sociotechnical abstraction traps (Selbst et al., 2019):

  1. The In-Distribution Trap: Assuming that training and deployment environments share identical demographic dynamics and base rates.
  2. The Portability Trap: Re-deploying an algorithmic model verified in one geographic or cultural context into a new environment without re-auditing.
  3. The Formalism Trap: Treating fairness purely as a mathematical constraint while ignoring systemic real-world inequities and upstream label corruption.
  4. The Ripple Effect Trap: Failing to anticipate how algorithmic decisions perturb downstream human behavior and create self-reinforcing feedback loops.
  5. The Solutionism Trap: Assuming that every social problem has an algorithmic optimization solution.

Industry best practice combines standardized dataset documentation (Gebru et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2019), intersectional subgroup performance disaggregation (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018), and continuous automated disparity CI/CD gating (Raji et al., 2020).

docs.title: 📐 Intersectional Subgroup Disaggregation & Minimax Risk
docs.text:
Evaluating model performance purely on aggregate metrics masks catastrophic failures in minority demographic slices (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018). Given \(K\) sensitive protected attributes \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_K\), the intersectional demographic space is defined as the Cartesian product of their domains:

\[\Omega = \prod_{j=1}^K \text{dom}(A_j) = \text{dom}(A_1) \times \text{dom}(A_2) \times \dots \times \text{dom}(A_K)\]

For example, intersecting binary gender \(G \in \{M, F\}\) with the six dermatological Fitzpatrick skin phototypes \(S \in \{I, II, III, IV, V, VI\}\) creates \(|\Omega| = 2 \times 6 = 12\) distinct intersectional cohorts.

docs.title: 1. Minimax Subgroup Risk Formulation
docs.text:
Standard Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) minimizes average population loss: $\(\min_\theta \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i)\)$

When group sizes differ drastically, ERM sacrifices small cohorts to optimize overall loss. In contrast, Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (Group-DRO) minimizes the Minimax Subgroup Risk (Sagawa et al., 2020):

\[\boxed{R_{\text{worst}}(\theta) = \max_{g \in \Omega} \mathcal{R}_g(\theta) = \max_{g \in \Omega} \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y) \sim \mathcal{D}_g} \left[ \ell(f_\theta(X), Y) \right]}\]

Minimizing \(R_{\text{worst}}(\theta)\) guarantees that the model cannot achieve deployment approval by trading off high error on marginalized demographic slices for marginal accuracy gains on the dominant majority.

docs.title: 2. Statistical Uncertainty in Small Slices: Wilson Score Interval
docs.text:
When evaluating small minority slices of sample size \(n_g \ll N\), empirical error rates \(\hat{p}_g = k_g / n_g\) suffer from severe estimation variance. The classical Wald normal confidence interval (\(\hat{p}_g \pm z \sqrt{\hat{p}_g(1 - \hat{p}_g) / n_g}\)) exhibits catastrophic failure modes in production audits: 1. Degeneracy at Zero: If zero errors occur (\(k_g = 0\)), the Wald interval collapses to \([0, 0]\), creating false statistical confidence of perfection. 2. Boundary Violations: It produces negative lower bounds or upper bounds exceeding \(1.0\).

To solve this, production audit harnesses mandate the Wilson Score Interval (Wilson, 1927), which inverts the score test under the binomial distribution:

\[\boxed{\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\hat{p}_g) = \frac{\hat{p}_g + \frac{z^2}{2n_g} \pm z \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_g(1 - \hat{p}_g)}{n_g} + \frac{z^2}{4n_g^2}}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n_g}}}\]

where \(z = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2)\) (e.g., \(z = 1.95996\) for a two-sided \(95\%\) confidence level).

docs.title: Properties of the Wilson Interval:
docs.text:
• Asymmetric expansion towards \(0.5\) when \(n_g\) is small.
  • Strictly bounded within \([0, 1]\) for all \(k_g \in [0, n_g]\) and \(n_g \ge 1\).
  • For \(k_g = 0\) on \(n_g = 25\) samples, while the Wald interval yields \([0\%, 0\%]\), the Wilson interval yields \([0.0\%, 13.3\%]\), accurately warning auditors that true subgroup error could reach \(13.3\%\).

docs.title: 3. Sample Sizing and Statistical Power in Subgroup Audits
docs.text:
Auditing small demographic slices requires sufficient statistical power to detect meaningful disparities. For two subgroups with expected selection rates \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) and pooled rate \(\bar{p} = \frac{p_1 + p_2}{2}\), the minimum required sample size per slice \(n_{\min}\) to achieve statistical power \(1 - \beta\) at significance level \(\alpha\) is:

\[\boxed{n_{\min} \ge \frac{\left( z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{2 \bar{p}(1 - \bar{p})} + z_\beta \sqrt{p_1(1 - p_1) + p_2(1 - p_2)} \right)^2}{(p_1 - p_2)^2}}\]

where \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is the critical two-sided value (e.g., \(1.96\) for \(\alpha = 0.05\)) and \(z_\beta\) is the one-sided power quantile (e.g., \(0.842\) for \(80\%\) power).

If a subgroup sample size falls below \(n_{\min}\), statistical parity tests cannot reliably differentiate between genuine fairness and lack of statistical power.

docs.text:
Modern enterprise machine learning pipelines integrate automated fairness gates into continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) harnesses (Raji et al., 2020). Candidate model artifacts are automatically blocked from production release if any demographic parity or equalized odds tolerance is violated.

docs.title: Gate 1: Demographic Parity Difference Gate
docs.text: \[\Delta_{\text{DP}} = \max_{a, b \in \mathcal{A}} \left| \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = a) - \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = b) \right| \le \tau_{\text{DP}} \quad (\text{typically } \tau_{\text{DP}} = 0.05)\]

docs.title: Gate 2: Statutory Disparate Impact Ratio Gate (EEOC 80% Rule)
docs.text: \[\rho_{\text{DI}} = \frac{\min_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = a)}{\max_{b \in \mathcal{A}} \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = b)} \ge 0.80\]

docs.title: Gate 3: Intersectional Equalized Odds Disparity Gate
docs.text: \[\Delta_{\text{EOD}} = \max_{y \in \{0, 1\}} \left( \max_{g \in \Omega} \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=y, g) - \min_{g' \in \Omega} \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=y, g') \right) \le \tau_{\text{EO}} \quad (\text{typically } \tau_{\text{EO}} = 0.08)\]

docs.title: Gate 4: Subgroup Minimax Risk Ceiling
docs.text: \[\max_{g \in \Omega} \text{ErrorRate}_g \le \text{Threshold}_{\text{max}} \quad (\text{e.g., no demographic slice may exceed 20% error})\]
